Old Park Star, Sober Glory and Baron Noir clash at Ffos Las
Having been declared to clash at Cheltenham over the weekend, Old Park Star and Sober Glory both swerved commitments at Prestbury Park in favour of more suitable conditions in South Wales on Wednesday, and we are treated to a fascinating contest with Baron Noir also thrown into the mix.
Tuesday 17 November 2026 17:32, UK
Cheltenham's loss is Ffos Las' gain on Wednesday as old rivals Old Park Star, Sober Glory and Baron Noir are set to face-off on chase debut and At The Races' Declan Rix previewed the contest.
You always need a bit of luck in this game, no matter what your role or ability. While the elements have unfortunately conspired against those at Exeter so far this season, Ffos Las is the beneficiary of what they are calling The Welsh Arkle on Wednesday, live on Sky Sports Racing.
The race got a huge boost with the somewhat surprise addition of 2026 Supreme Novices' Hurdle winner Old Park Star, a high-profile non-runner on Cheltenham's Saturday card due to the ground being deemed too quick. His inclusion means we have a huge early season clash with an old foe in Sober Glory, last season's unlucky Supreme runner-up.
The inclusion of Old Park Star is no doubt bad luck for those connected to Sober Glory et al; after all, the Henderson-trained horse was meant to run last Saturday, but it's a huge stroke of luck for Ffos Las and indeed, Sky Sports Racing. Exciting early season clashes like this are incredibly rare for novice chasers in Britain - and in general given the monster that the Cheltenham Festival has morphed into - so it's understandable there is a bit of a buzz around the industry ahead of the five-runner Golwg Gwendraeth Beginners' Chase, due off at 13:18pm.
Ground and weather
As of 8.37am on Tuesday, on the back of 16mm since 6pm on Monday, the ground is officially Good (good to soft in places), but with significant rain due. According to the BHA site, tomorrow's forecast reads as, 'blustery with persistent rain, heavy at times throughout the day'. Hopefully it leads to beautiful soft ground which the horses will get through nicely.
The big guns
As the official ratings and betting suggests, Old Park Star (155; 4/6) and Sober Glory (153; 15/8) are the standouts and are set to renew their rivalry having served up a fantastic Cheltenham Festival curtain raiser in March, along with Mydaddypaddy back in third. At the line, the winning margins were 1½ lengths and a nose, with the also reopposing Baron Noir (146; 10/1), Wednesday's third favourite, a further 6 lengths back in fourth.
Wednesday's prices and a glance at the formbook in black and white could lead you down the garden path of just siding the unbeaten hurdler Old Park Star, but replaying the final flight of their Supreme clash is wise, given it had such a significant impact on the race.
Heading to the last in the Supreme, Sober Glory looked to have everything in trouble with a good 1½+ lengths lead before he put in an extra stride, hit the hurdle and landed steeply, losing critical momentum. It was a huge shame for his connections because up to that point he had jumped so well and looked the best horse in the race going to the last.
That mistake cost him dearly, along with many punters having been a huge gamble from 16/1 in the morning to an SP of 9/2. The Philip Hobbs & Johnson White yard clearly felt like they had their charge in great order, produced him beautifully on the day only for that famous last flight on the Old Course at Prestbury Park to scupper a dream start to the 2026 Festival.
His disappointing run 31 days later at Aintree is easily excused on the back of a long season after a huge Cheltenham run and now with his attentions turned to chasing, this former Irish point-to-point winner for Cormac Doyle rates an exciting prospect for the upcoming campaign for owners Brocade Racing.
Standing in his way again is fellow six-year-old Old Park Star, who, to be fair, didn't exactly ping the final flight in the Supreme himself, also putting in an extra stride which led to the son of Well Chosen landing awkwardly but crucially, not losing as much momentum as Sober Glory.
That saw him stay unbeaten in four hurdle starts, after wins at Kempton, Cheltenham and Haydock, showing good versatility in terms of the tracks he could handle along with also displaying tactical adaptability. Having jumped right in places on debut, his hurdling got better and slicker as the campaign progressed and he looked a straight-forward character throughout.
Having been put away after Cheltenham, Old Park Star's attentions now to turn chasing, a game he possesses the physical scope and athleticism for, although unlike Sober Glory he has no point-to-point background. While not ideal, it's possibly a good sign that Nicky Henderson was willing to pitch him into Grade 2 company at Cheltenham on chasing debut before the ground ruled him out.
A horse said to be big and weak last season, there could be much more to come from Old Park Star, his trainer's comments of 'he's still a shell of a horse' last year continually playing on my mind. If he was able to achieve what he did last season when weak, you cannot but be excited about him after another summer on his back.
Chasing to put manners on Baron Noir?
Baron Noir is certainly no no-hoper against Old Park Star and Sober Glory, with 7½ lengths and 6 lengths, respectively, to find with the leading pair, especially if he has settled down for a summer's break and/or fences curb his keen-going ways.
It's in his breeding to be highly-strung, being by Vadamos out of a Dylan Thomas mare, but he's a horse with plenty of ability and it was a clear sign of the belief his trainer Alan King had in him to run in a Supreme when only rated 130.
While essentially well-held at the line, the six-year-old shaped better than the distance beaten, not getting up the hill as well as his Wednesday rivals. With that in mind, the much flatter nature of Ffos Las should suit.
He too has no point-to-point background, but with the King yard ticking along nicely, he is certainly worth a market check.
Skelton pair make up the field
It's not often you would get prices of 33/1 about a Grade 2-winning novice hurdler from the Skelton yard who looks all-over a chaser on novice chase debut, but that's the task facing Carlenrig. His odds are not just about the horses he is taking on, but also the trip, mind.
A winner of the Grade 2 Bristol Novices' Hurdle at Cheltenham last December, he showed a good attitude to win over that 3m trip. On the back of that given his unexposed nature, he looked a big player in the River Don Novices' Hurdle at Doncaster 42 days later - despite carrying a penalty - but having been a stinking drifter (4/1 out to 14/1), fell two out when his race looked to be run.
The former winning Irish pointer picked up a small injury that day and hasn't been seen in 298 days so this looks like a starting point to get his campaign up and running.
Stablemate Bobby's Nelson has his first run for the Skeltons and should be more at home over this 2m trip. He also looks a chaser physically and his three-quarter of a length defeat to Baron Noir last December at Uttoxeter doesn't half look bad now; indeed, you could argue he is overpriced at 80/1 on that effort, but is probably best watched.
A bet?
In truth, this looks a race to watch for the future, but if forced to have a bet, at the prices, it would certainly be SOBER GLORY. I don't think it's far fetched to say he looked the best horse in the Supreme before his final flight mistake, and with his point-to-point background, might have a jumping experience edge over Old Park Star. That said, the Hobbs and White yard are only operating at a 5% strike-rate currently, for all they've had plenty of others run well. Either way, I am very much looking forward to seeing how all these horses take to fences.

The Tamil Nadu Medical Officers Association (TNMOA) has urged the Chief Minister, Health Minister and Managing Director of Tamil Nadu Medical Services (TNMSC) to cancel the corporation’s recent tenders to carry out repair works at warehouses of Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation (TASMAC) and to direct that the works be undertaken through the Public Works Department or another agency.

TNMSC was established to procure quality medical equipment and medicines at affordable cost for the Health department, it said. The association expressed concern that instead of addressing the shortcomings and strengthening TNMSC, a model agency in the country, the State government is taking steps that undermine the institution.

Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.
Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.
Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.
Theonila Roka Matbob, a cabinet minister in Bougainville’s autonomous government and Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.
“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.
“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”
Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”
The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.
“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”
The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”
Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.
The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.
Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.
A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.
The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.
But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

NEW DELHI: India and Sweden are looking to move industrial decarbonization from commitments to execution, with the third phase of their Leadership Group for Industry Transition (LeadIT) initiative focusing on scaling low-carbon projects, mobilising private capital and accelerating emissions cuts in hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, cement and transport. LeadIT 3.0, covering 2027-30, was announced by Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav at an industry leaders' roundtable on the sidelines of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on Tuesday, according to a government statement. The roundtable was co-chaired by Yadav and Sweden's state secretary for Climate and Enterprise Helena Dyrssen. The new phase will shift the initiative's focus from establishing partnerships to scaling industrial projects, mobilizing capital and delivering tangible results. Its three priorities are technology development and diffusion through industrial projects; capital mobilization and de-risking to connect projects with finance; and capacity building and policy support, including carbon markets and workforce transition. Quick answers to key questions LeadIT 3.0 is the 2027–30 phase of the India-Sweden Leadership Group for Industry Transition initiative. It aims to turn industrial decarbonisation commitments into projects and measurable emissions cuts. Its priorities are developing and sharing technology through industrial projects, mobilising and de-risking capital, and providing capacity-building and policy support. The policy work includes carbon markets and workforce transition. The initiative focuses on hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, cement and transport. Earlier projects explored hydrogen-based ironmaking, industrial heat electrification, carbon capture and utilisation, and lower-carbon cement production. The new phase shifts the focus from establishing partnerships to scaling projects, mobilising finance and delivering results. The second phase facilitated 11 pre-pilot projects in steel and cement. India says the transition should create opportunities for workers and communities, particularly in developing economies, rather than focus only on emissions cuts. It also needs to progress alongside priorities such as poverty alleviation, energy access, jobs and infrastructure. “Geopolitical conflicts, volatile energy markets and competing development priorities make international cooperation even more important, particularly in hard-to-abate industrial sectors,” Yadav said, adding that India's priorities of poverty alleviation, energy access, job creation and infrastructure development must progress alongside its transition to a low-carbon economy. The launch comes as governments and industries face mounting pressure to cut emissions from energy-intensive sectors, where decarbonization often requires substantial capital investment, technological innovation and changes in production processes. India and Sweden launched LeadIT in 2019. Its second phase facilitated 11 pre-pilot projects in steel and cement under the India-Sweden Industry Transition Partnership. These cover hydrogen-based ironmaking, electrification of industrial heat, carbon capture and utilisation, clinker substitution, industrial circularity and the use of artificial intelligence to reduce cement demand. LeadIT has also supported South Africa's investment plan under the Climate Investment Funds and Ethiopia's engagement on low-carbon cement, Yadav said. The initiative's membership has since expanded to 20 countries and 33 companies, with Brazil joining as its latest country member, strengthening participation from the Global South. Yadav called on countries and companies to move beyond feasibility studies towards pilot projects, demonstrations and replication, arguing that industrial transition commitments must translate into measurable outcomes. Highlighting India's climate progress, the minister said the country had reduced its emissions intensity by 37.38% between 2005 and 2022 and achieved 50% of its installed electricity capacity from non-fossil fuel sources, five years ahead of its target. India's additional forest carbon sink has reached around 2.44 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, he added. Yadav said the industrial transition must create opportunities for workers and communities, particularly in developing economies, rather than focus solely on reducing emissions. The launch at COP31, which the Turkish presidency has described as the 'COP of Implementation', is intended to strengthen international cooperation and accelerate the shift from industrial transition commitments to on-ground projects. An issue keeps nagging at Waymo's robotaxi operations: The company's self-driving cars struggle to navigate highway construction zones.
Now, California's vehicle regulatory agency has stepped in.
In a statement to Business Insider on Tuesday, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said it was restricting Waymo from operating and testing on highways, citing three incidents in which Waymo's robotaxis "entered an active construction closure." The restriction took effect on November 11.
The restriction will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the DMV that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the problems that prompted it.
"The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026," a DMV spokesperson said.
A Waymo spokesperson said that the recent incidents did not involve injuries or collisions and that, while the DMV order only limits freeway operations in California, the company will temporarily pause highway operations nationwide.
"We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," the spokesperson said.
As the DMV points out, the restrictions come several months after Waymo tried to address this exact issue.
In May, Waymo said it self-suspended highway operations to improve how its autonomous cars behaved around construction zones.
On July 29, Waymo announced that it was "gradually resuming" freeway routes. The company told TechCrunch at the time that it had implemented "software updates designed to improve the performance around freeway construction zones."
The updates appeared insufficient to prevent the latest incidents. The DMV spokesperson cited two cases in which Waymo entered an active construction closure: one on November 5 when it entered a construction zone on US Route 101 near Burlingame, and another on November 6 involving California Highway Patrol vehicles.
Waymo now has to provide evidence that it can detect construction zones, emergency vehicles, and other roadway situations before it can resume freeway operations.

On Monday, the Department of Health and Human Services issued a long-awaited update to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act privacy rule. Originally proposed in January 2021, HHS’ Office for Civil Rights finalized several updates to the rule intended to make it easier to share health information — to coordinate patients’ care between health providers, but also to make it easier for patients to access and share their own data.
The HIPAA privacy rule update puts a particular focus on measures to support patients’ access to their own records. “It’s fair to say that two-thirds of the content of the rule is about this problem, the problem of individual access,” said Lucia Savage, former chief privacy officer at HHS’s Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT.
The final rule reduces the maximum time for covered entities to respond to patient requests from 30 to 15 days. It prevents them from imposing unreasonable measures for individuals requesting records to prove their identity. And it establishes standards for accessing those records through a newly defined category of tools called “personal health applications,” which can include wellness apps and tools linked to fitness trackers. Some of those products have been headlined by other federal agencies during the Trump administration, including the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

క్లెయిమ్: త్రిపురలో బీఎస్ఎఫ్ సిబ్బందిపై దాడికి పాల్పడిన నిందితులను పోలీసులు అరెస్ట్ చేస్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియో త్రిపురకు చెందినది కాదు. నేపాల్లోని సప్తరి జిల్లాలో, సప్తకోశి మున్సిపాలిటీ-5లోని గంగాజలిలో నిర్వహించిన ‘Indigenous and Tribal Literature Festival’ సందర్భంగా మద్యం మత్తులో ఉన్న ఒక వ్యక్తి దుకాణం వద్ద గొడవ సృష్టించడంతో పోలీసులు అతడిని అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్న దృశ్యాలు ఇవి. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోను జాగ్రత్తగా పరిశీలించగా అందులో ఉన్న పోలీసు వాహనంపై “Nepal Police” అని రాసి ఉండటాన్ని గుర్తించాము. దీంతో ఈ వీడియో త్రిపురకు చెందినది కాదనే అనుమానం కలిగింది.
తదుపరి, దీని గురించి మరింత తెలుసుకోడానికి వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేములను ఉపయోగిస్తూ రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చైయగా, ఇదే వీడియో 31 అక్టోబర్ 2026న నేపాల్కు చెందిన వార్తా సంస్థ ‘జన చర్చా టైమ్స్’ ఫేస్బుక్ పేజీలో షేర్ చేయటాన్ని గమనించాము. ఆ పోస్టులో తెలిపిన వివరాల ప్రకారం, నేపాల్లోని సప్తరి జిల్లాలో, సప్తకోశి మున్సిపాలిటీ-5లోని గంగాజలిలో నిర్వహించిన ‘Indigenous and Tribal Literature Festival’ సందర్భంగా మద్యం మత్తులో ఉన్న ఒక వ్యక్తి దుకాణం వద్ద గొడవ సృష్టించాడు. దీంతో పోలీసులు అతడిని అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.
అదే వీడియోను మరో నేపాలీ వార్తా సంస్థకు చెందిన ఫేస్బుక్, ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీలలో కూడా 31 అక్టోబర్ 2026న షేర్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాము. అక్కడ కూడా ఇదే ఘటనకు సంబంధించిన వివరాలను పేర్కొన్నారు.

As Kolkata choked on toxic air following Diwali and Kali Puja celebrations, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari accused those raising concerns over firecracker pollution of being communists opposed to Hindu traditions. His remarks were consistent with the concerted push by a section of the Right wing to portray criticism of firecrackers as an attack on Hindu religious practices. However, among those complaining about noise levels and pollution in Kolkata were members of Adhikari’s own party and cabinet.
The Bengal CM made the remarks while addressing the media during a visit to the coastal town of Digha on Monday, where he had gone to attend an administrative meeting and visit the Kali Puja organised by the Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Traders Association.
Speaking to reporters, Adhikari said, “There has been an awakening of Sanatan in this state, and some people have a problem with that. The people making these allegations (about firecrackers) had turned Hindu religious festivals into cultural fests… These people do not apply ‘tika’ or religious markings on their foreheads, they do not wear ‘dors’ or religious threads on their wrists, nor do they wear tulsi beads around their necks.”
Adhikari further said, “The communists are raising this issue of firecrackers. We have controlled it in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directives. Firecrackers were burst in some places even after 10 pm, and the police took necessary action. We have stopped DJs, and we do not want environmental pollution. But people will have fun during Diwali. They will celebrate with lights and burst firecrackers. Where is the problem with that?”
While acknowledging that firecrackers had been burst beyond the time limit prescribed by the Supreme Court, Adhikari sought to deflect criticism by pointing to action taken by the administration.
“Those complaining that sound crackers were burst for a few hours longer than the time stipulated by the Supreme Court should know that the Pollution Control Board and the police are taking action against such violations. I would request those complaining about firecrackers to also congratulate the state government for stopping DJs. I will not say that DJ incidents did not happen in remote corners, but I did not hear them blaring, at least near the roads,” he said.
Firecrackers can Cure Diseases, Says Bengal Minister, then Apologises
According to the Supreme Court’s directives, only green firecrackers were allowed to be burst between 8 pm and 10 pm on Diwali. However, statements by ministers, the West Bengal Police’s deletion of a post urging responsible Diwali celebrations, and the general perception that a BJP government would not impose restrictions on Hindu festivals had collectively sent out a clear message: When it came to celebrating a majoritarian festival, the rules could be bent, if not ignored altogether.
BJP leader and Tollygunge MLA Papia Adhikary said on Monday, “Our honourable chief minister has said that people will definitely burst firecrackers. How can we celebrate Kali Puja without firecrackers? But we will burst them in accordance with the instructions of the local police station. Also, many diseases can be prevented simply by lighting firecrackers.”
Although Adhikary later apologised and backtracked on her statement, claiming that the media had misinterpreted her remarks, the message had already got across.
A section of social media users also began targeting dissenting voices who tried to reason with their fellow citizens. A user named Partha Pratim Kundu, who describes himself as a wildlife photographer, asked in a post how elderlies, children and birds and animals survived in earlier times when there was no curb on firecrackers.
Another Facebook user, Chayan Mukherjee, who hailed the chief minister’s indulgence on firecrackers, claimed in a post that “most of the Indian environmentalists and human rights activists, as well as professors at various institutions, receive funding from outside to oppose the country’s development.”
Domkal’s CPI(M) MLA Mostafijur Rahaman Rana had urged people to celebrate Diwali as a festival of lights, without noise and loud firecrackers. BJP MLA Tarunjyoti Tiwari gave the issue a communal twist by asking whether the legislator would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’.
State BJP leader Keya Ghosh also criticised Mostafijur Rahaman for advocating a noise-free and smoke-free Diwali.
The lone CPIM MLA of West Bengal had wished smokeless, soundless Diwali.

The political messaging was accompanied by widespread violations on the ground. A large section of the public openly flouted firecracker regulations. Almost all media outlets reported that loud firecrackers were burst throughout the night severely inconveniencing elderlies, children and also pets, birds and stray animals.
Kolkata’s AQI reached 623 around 11 pm on Sunday night, reported The telegraph. At 12.51 am on Monday, IQAir classified the city’s air quality as hazardous, recording an AQI of 532, with PM2.5 at 342 and PM10 at 405. Both particulate matter concentrations were several times higher than the WHO’s recommended limits.
Left with no other option, residents in several localities took matters into their own hands, protesting against the rampant bursting of firecrackers and intervening to stop it. Facebook user Anitesh Chakraborty narrated his experience in a post.
Chakraborty went up to a neighbouring apartment’s rooftop around 1.45 am to ask people bursting firecrackers to stop. While some residents supported his objection, others on nearby rooftops mocked him with gestures and taunts. Nevertheless, the intervention succeeded in stopping the firecrackers. He observed that the rooftops of apartment buildings had become spaces where people felt free to flout restrictions, and argued people to raise their voices against such violations.
According to a report by the Times of India, by 1 am, the West Bengal Pollution Control Board had received 84 noise-related complaints, while Kolkata Police had recorded 434 complaints.
Police rounded up 371 people for bursting illegal firecrackers, arresting 205 of them. Another 387 people were arrested for disorderly conduct. Several commentators pointed out that the most effective way to curb the use of illegal firecrackers was to stop their manufacture and sale. This year, only 238.6 kg of such products were seized, compared to 853 kg last year.
Kolkata’s high-rise buildings were particular hotspots for violations of firecracker and noise restrictions. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari himself acknowledged that the rules could not be enforced in every high-rise apartment building, as the state did not have enough police personnel.
Even hospitals located in silence zones were not spared. According to a report by The Telegraph, areas near hospitals such as B C Roy, R G Kar, M R Bangur and Sishumangal also faced onslaught of loud firecrackers.
To Celebrate Responsibly or Not? Bengal Police in a Fix
Signs of this situation had emerged earlier, when the West Bengal Police deleted a firecracker awareness post within hours of publishing it, as previously reported by Alt News.
Published on the morning of November 5 with the caption, “Please celebrate responsibly. It’s our Diwali too!”, the AI-generated poster featured two stray cats and a dog shivering due to the loud noise of firecrackers. However, it was deleted within three hours.
The post’s comment section was flooded with threatening messages directed at police and familiar Right-wing arguments, including questions about whether the police would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’ and why the police and administration interfered only in Hindu festivals.
Similarly, Delhi Police, too, deleted a firecracker awareness post, while the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a video featuring actor Dia Mirza advocating for a pollution-free Diwali from its social media accounts. Both decisions followed social media outrage from BJP-RSS supporters who claimed that the posts hurt Hindu religious sentiments.
A similar message by AISA leader Neha Bora also faced backlash from the far-right social media ecosystem.
It is that time of the year where our conversations will be accompanied by sore throats and respiratory problems.

BJP MLAs Complain about Noise Levels
Although a section of the Right wing encouraged unrestrained celebrations during Diwali and Kali Puja in the name of upholding Hindu traditions, some voices within the BJP struck a different note.
BJP leader and Sonarpur Dakshin MLA Roopa Ganguly tagged Kolkata Police in a post on Facebook stating she was unable to sleep because of the noise of firecrackers. However, the post is no longer available now.
State urban development minister Agnimitra Paul was seen roaming around the city in a police vehicle, attempting to curb the firecracker menace.
Paul said, “Please think about other people. Consider the condition of the elderly and the sick. The firecrackers are bursting so loudly that my heart is trembling.”
However, these interventions came too little, too late. The ruling dispensation had, through its rhetoric and its reluctance to enforce restrictions, effectively given people a free hand to flout the law, with the environment and public health bearing the consequences.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd
- Published
Warning: This article contains references to suicide
Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".
The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.
But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.
"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.
"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."
The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".
"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.
"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.
"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.
"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."
Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.
But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.
"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.
"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.
"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.
"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.
"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.
"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

The Mundka monitoring station of the Delhi Pollution Control Board recorded a PM2.5 concentration of 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on the Diwali night, which is 60 times the standard measure. AIIMS pulmonologist Vijay Hadda told ANI on November 9, “I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival.”
In any country with a functional government, this would warrant the environment minister to at least make a statement, even if not take direct accountability. Not in India.
Union minister of environment, forest and climate change, Bhupender Yadav, has remained conspicuously silent on the country’s deteriorating air quality before or after Diwali.
From the days preceding Diwali to four days after the festival when this article is being written, Yadav neither issued a single public appeal urging citizens to responsibly engage in celebrations, nor used his social media handles to spread awareness about the environmental consequences of bursting firecrackers or to address the mounting pollution crisis affecting major parts of the country.
Did Bhupender Yadav go Missing from Public Platforms?
Far from it. Yadav remained active on social media throughout this period. Between November 1 and November 12, he made 29 posts on his X account. Not one of them addressed the worsening air pollution, deteriorating air quality across Indian cities, or the need for public awareness and precautionary measures.
The days before Diwali are also crucial because pollution levels skyrocketing on the day of the festival and immediately after has become an annual phenomenon. It is reasonable to expect the minister holding the environment and climate change portfolio to make a public appeal ahead of Diwali, more so because firecracker pollution has been a matter of contention and has reached the Supreme Court in recent years.

Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet
CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.
The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.
Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.
A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.
The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
Iran may be shifting its strategy amid economic pain
Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.
Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.
"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."
U.S. expands its Middle East naval presence
With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.
Iran says it's responding to U.S. attacks
Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.
"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."
Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow?
Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information. Now, a new generation of AI rivals is challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Can Google embrace this disruptive technology without breaking the business that made it rich?
Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was just a scrappy startup, working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined the company back in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science.
" It's pretty wild. When I interviewed at Google, there were just seven people there," Mayer tells Planet Money. By the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee.
That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue. By 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company — by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet — was generating more than $280 billion. That's more than a millionfold increase.
Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results. It monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb. And its search business became like an unstoppable money machine.
In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water. But neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. The company's dominion just kept expanding. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.
For a time, it seemed like the only forces that could cut this juggernaut down to size were politicians or antitrust lawyers.
But the craziest part? The biggest threat to Google was maybe coming from inside the house! From what it was developing in its own labs — and the industrial race it would unleash.
Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI. And, in 2017, a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer, a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible.
Mayer, who is now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and remains a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism about the company's future. "This is not a technology that's happening to Google," she says. "They helped invent this new technology."
Yet, today, Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals. And it's overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links.
Wall Street is getting nervous. In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report. The company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day — the biggest single-day percentage decline since the company went public in 2004.
If this whole AI transition goes sideways for the company, it's a bit like a mother giving birth to a baby and then that baby slapping her in the face and stealing money from her wallet.
Which brings us to… a classic business theory we've been thinking about recently: the innovator's dilemma.
The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail.
Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a "disruptive" technology. He helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary, long before it became a cliché.
The core innovator's dilemma is basically this: embrace a disruptive technology, and risk the profits you're making today. But if you fail to embrace it and let others run with it, you may end up risking your company's health tomorrow.
Today in the Planet Money newsletter we ask: has Google been caught in the innovator's dilemma? And can it pivot to a new technological era without sacrificing its enormous profits?
Did Google squander its AI head start?
Google didn't just invent the transformer. Over the decades, its researchers made computers translate languages, recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go.
The company even developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation.
But they didn't release it.
Then, on Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore.
Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses.
So, first question, why wasn't Google the first out of the gate with something like ChatGPT?
Christensen's theory offers one possible explanation: When you're making tons of money from your existing business in search, why rush to release something that could undermine it? Why disrupt yourself?
His theory wasn't just that companies seek to protect their cash cow. It was that a company can get too focused on the best way to nurture and milk that cash cow. Like, dang, I love this cow. Then when a disruptive technology comes along, they might be like, wait, this won't help me milk my beautiful cow. No thanks.
In other words, a company's focus on its core business can lead it to not see a disruptive technology's market potential. It can create a kind of myopia.
Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, offered an explanation for why Google hadn't released something like ChatGPT sooner— and it suggested the company had fallen victim to the kind of myopia Christensen warned about. Dean told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business. You know, their cow.
"From a search perspective, you want to get the right answer 100% of the time," Dean said. "These models were not near that bar." They were prone to hallucinating and also saying offensive things.
Those were problems ChatGPT had as well. It made tons of mistakes and said racist, sexist, and other incendiary things that made headlines. Yet it took off like a rocket ship when they released it.
And it turned out that people didn't just use ChatGPT as a way to find information or get answers. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text.
Christensen warned about this very trap in The Innovator's Dilemma. Companies that keep disruptive technologies "bottled up in their labs," he wrote, risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be.
Mayer, however, questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI. "The standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer," Mayer says.
We don't know what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first. Would a Google chatbot have taken off in the same way, giving Google a first-mover advantage? Or would its flaws have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect?
Whatever explains Google's initial hesitation, it's now going all in. It's fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich.
The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant — and as profitable — in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search.
Goodbye, Monopoly?
Benedict Evans is a widely read technology analyst who was previously a partner at the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
He says that every 10 or 15 years or so, a revolutionary "platform shift" shakes up the tech industry, giving newcomers a chance to challenge dominant companies. It happened with the rise of personal computers, then the internet, then smartphones. Now, he says, it's happening with AI.
"The whole table gets reset and the things that meant that they had won and you couldn't take them on suddenly don't matter anymore," Evans says.
For Google, the consumer pivot to AI could mean it loses some of the competitive advantages that helped it monopolize search.
The process toward monopolization began with Google building a better search engine than rivals. Then, Evans says, its success became self-reinforcing: more users gave Google more data to improve its results, helping it attract still more users. Economists call this a "network effect," a kind of positive feedback loop that helped Google cement its dominance.
Of course, Google also actively worked to catch and keep customers as well. It, for instance, paid to make its search engine the default in browsers and on devices — deals that a federal judge ruled in 2024 had illegally helped maintain its search monopoly.
Google also cemented its dominance by weaving itself into our lives. It runs the operating system on many of our phones. We use free Google services to send emails, write documents, find directions, and watch a stranger explain how to fix our washing machine. Many of us keep going back to Google search out of sheer habit or because, when we're navigating the Google digital complex, we keep getting nudged to go there.
But a platform shift could loosen Google's grip on us. Why go to Google dotcom to search for information if you're using an AI system made by a rival that can answer your question well enough? And, maybe, those rival AI systems will borrow from Google's playbook and work to intertwine themselves into our lives.
It's still early days in this rapidly transforming market. One big question, Evans says, is whether AI models will develop winner-take-all dynamics like those that helped Google dominate search. So far, it seems like the frontier labs keep catching up with each other. One possibility, he says, is that AI could become increasingly capable of improving itself — what those in the biz call "recursive self-improvement" — allowing whichever company gets there first to build a lead that rivals struggle to overcome. But whether the AI race will end with a dominant leader — and whether Google will be the one that emerges victorious — is still a huge question.
Mayer doesn't expect a single winner. Yes, the mammoth cost of the computing power and energy needed to develop and run frontier models creates a barrier to entry, making it hard for smaller companies to compete. But she believes there's room for several giants. "There will be multiple big players," she says. "I don't think there will be just one."
Google has a really good shot at remaining one of the big players, but it could lose the dominance it has enjoyed in search. As Evans puts it, "Google's share of search has really got only one way to go."
But losing market share doesn't necessarily mean making less money, Mayer argues. She expects AI to attract more people looking for answers and draw more advertising dollars into the market. Sure, she says, Google's share could get smaller, but the pie could get bigger.
Evans points to Microsoft as an example of how a company can lose dominance after a technological disruption but still keep growing. When high-speed internet took the world by storm, it opened up new ways for rivals to compete with Microsoft in software. Companies like, yes, Google developed products like Docs and Sheets that people could use in a web browser, whether or not they were running Windows. Controlling the dominant operating system no longer gave Microsoft the same advantages in the internet era.
But the internet also gave more people a reason to buy computers — and many bought PCs that ran Windows. Microsoft sold more copies of Windows and Office, and its business kept growing because of this and other reasons.
"Well, go look at Microsoft," he says. "Microsoft lost, but at the same time, the market became so much bigger" that "the shareholders got a lot more money."
That said, Microsoft shareholders needed some patience. Its stock price didn't surpass its dotcom-era peak until nearly 17 years later.
Can AI pay Google's mounting bills?
Beyond just the threat to Google's monopoly in search, AI is also challenging the advertising model that made search so lucrative.
Google's historic stock plunge in late October suggested that investors are concerned about this.
On the company's earnings call, executives acknowledged that the growing use of "AI Mode," its chatbot-style search feature, was contributing to slower growth of search advertising revenue because it earned less per query than traditional search. Meanwhile, Alphabet said it expects to spend a whopping $200 billion this year alone on infrastructure, including data centers, largely to support its AI push.
Watching Google's stock price plummet that day, it felt like seeing Google struggle with the innovator's dilemma in real time. Like it was willing to risk cannibalizing its core business to feed its ambitions in the AI age, accepting short-term pain in the hope of long-term gain.
Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google and its parent company Alphabet, has made clear he believes embracing innovation is the only way forward. He was actually asked about the innovator's dilemma on the All-In podcast last year. "I think the dilemma only exists if you treat it as a dilemma," Pichai said. "All along in technology you have these massive periods of innovation and you lean into it as hard as you can. It's the only way to do it."
Mayer is optimistic about Pichai's aggressive approach and Google's position in this new technological era. Google helped pioneer this technology, she says, and using it to answer people's questions draws on what has been its core expertise. She even questions whether there is really any dilemma for Google when it comes to using AI to give consumers better answers.
"They actually aren't doing something new by deploying it," Mayer says. "They're just answering questions differently and arguably better."
She does, however, acknowledge there is a dilemma when it comes to advertisers, who pay most of the company's bills. Google may need to fundamentally revamp its system of clickable ads it has spent decades showing alongside search results.
" So I think that piece of it is hard," Mayer says. "How do I take that advertising spend and move it to a new format that keeps my customers, my advertising customers, as happy?"
But advertisers will follow users, she argues, and AI could provide the basis for an even more lucrative business.
"I don't see why it can't be as profitable," she says. "In fact, I think it probably, in the end, will be more lucrative than it has been in the past."
Who knows what advertising will look like as the AI era advances. Maybe we'll see familiar-looking banner ads or clickable links on chatbot screens. Or maybe we'll be confiding in an AI assistant with a disembodied voice, like Scarlett Johansson in Her, sharing our most intimate thoughts, only to hear a word from our sponsor. Awkward.
Mayer sees other possibilities. Her startup, Dazzle, uses AI to analyze people's photographs. Those photos can help the system learn about you — which brands you like, what products you own, and what you might want to buy next. You can also snap a photo of something you like and ask where to buy it.
"If we can identify the product and send you there," she says, "there's an opportunity for advertisements or lead generation."
The more people share with AI systems, the more those systems learn about them, creating valuable personalized data that could be used to microtarget ads or nudge people to buy things.
For Google, the question is whether AI's new ways of connecting people to products can replace — or exceed — the profits of its existing advertising business.
In a statement to Planet Money, Google said its AI features are already leading to more searches on its platform. "This past quarter, Search queries grew at their fastest year-over-year rate in five years," the company said. It says they're taking a "deliberate approach" to developing ad revenue in this new technological era: "building the best user experience first and then scaling monetization."
Beyond Search
But the AI race is about much more than just building systems that can help people find information and make money from ads along the way. Investors are dreaming of AI models that can do things that once sounded like science fiction, including automating vast amounts of knowledge work. They're betting revolutionary applications will give rise to incredibly profitable businesses.
Evans believes the most exciting market opportunities will be found in entirely new uses for AI — some we haven't even dreamed up yet.
What will those applications be? How profitable will they become? Will they justify the mind-blowing investments Google and other companies are making in this technological revolution?
Evans says the uncertainty around fundamental questions like these helps explain stock market volatility. Investors don't know how much money these companies will ultimately earn — or how long they'll have to wait. And even if AI creates enormous wealth, he says, it's far from clear who will capture it.
One risk Evans sees is that competing AI models become so similar in their capabilities that their developers struggle to charge much for them. The most lucrative businesses could be the products and services other companies build using those models.
He points to cellphone service providers as a cautionary tale. They spent billions to build out the network infrastructure for the mobile internet, allowing people to watch videos, order taxis, and much more on their cellphones.
"All the stuff that they were talking about happened," Evans says, "but it happened 10 years later."
And when that future finally arrived, the service providers weren't the big winners from all that spending. Ouch! Yes, they owned the infrastructure, but it was the companies making smartphones and building apps and services on top of that infrastructure that captured the biggest rewards of the mobile revolution.
Evans suggests that the same risk hangs over the companies building today's AI models. "The point is just because it's amazing and cool and exciting and it's going to change the world doesn't mean that you have value capture or pricing power." In other words, AI could change the world without sending these companies' profits — or stock prices — soaring.
Of course, the fate that befell the cellphone service providers is just one possible scenario. Evans says the AI industry could develop like advanced chip manufacturing, where the rising cost and complexity of making chips left fewer and fewer companies able to compete. Or, he says, it could look like cloud computing, where several big companies make good money supplying the infrastructure that other businesses run on.
Google has a good shot at thriving under more than one of those scenarios. Its empire spans search, AI chatbots and assistants, YouTube, cloud computing, and even driverless cars through Waymo.
Google can make money both from supplying AI infrastructure and building products and services with AI, Evans says. On one side, Google already sells access to its own AI models and supplies computing power to other companies, including Anthropic. Google is also a major investor in Anthropic, and has a stake that could become even more valuable when that company goes public.
But if the business of building and running frontier AI models turns out to be less profitable than so many investors hope, Google could still make money using the technology in its own products. It also has the money and in-house expertise to compete for entirely new AI businesses.
The question is whether it can make enough money from all this to make its huge investments worthwhile — and make up for whatever it might lose in search.
Google helped invent the technology behind this revolution. Now it's betting a fortune that AI can deliver a whole new herd of cash cows — without killing the one that made it rich.
