Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in $4.5m Canada luxury car theft syndicate
- Published
Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.
They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.
Police in Peel, Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports.
The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies.
The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.
The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".
The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.
Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles.
"Together, investigators linked the network to loading sites, container movements and the transportation of stolen re-VINed vehicles," the police said in a statement.
Re-VINing is the illegal practice of altering the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) to conceal its identity and make it harder to trace.
Canadian authorities have described organised vehicle theft as a growing threat, saying it was linked to wider criminal networks.
"Organised auto theft is a predatory business model run by transnational syndicates that terrorise families and fund broader criminal enterprises," Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said.
Last year, Interpol said more than 100 luxury vehicles stolen from Canada and European countries had been recovered, exposing a network involved in trafficking stolen cars to West Africa.
In a separate operation the same year, Ghanaian security authorities recovered 43 luxury vehicles stolen from Europe and North America.
They attributed the success of the operation to improved cooperation between national and international law enforcement agencies.

Trigger Warning: Images of physical injury
A group of around 40 men allegedly ambushed a house church in Rayan village in West Bengal’s Purba Bardhaman district on November 1, and physically assaulted the pastor and several Christian worshippers during a Sunday prayer service. The attackers accused the congregation of converting Hindus by luring them with incentives, and also accused them of running a ‘honey trap’.
Survivors told Alt News that they were forced to chant ‘Jai Sri Ram’, and were told, “This is a Hindu area; worshipping Jesus will not be tolerated”.
Several worshippers sustained severe injuries after the attack. Survivors said they were left traumatised without administrative protection or assurance. A written complaint was submitted at Burdwan police station. However, the survivors alleged that they were forced into withdrawing the complaint as attackers entered the police station and threatened to kill the complainant.
Alt News spoke to pastor Chottu Ruidas, who was leading the Sunday prayer service, and other survivors of the attack. Recounting the incident, Ruidas said the congregation had assembled at Sushanta Majila’s house around 10 am, and the service was nearing its conclusion, with the worshippers participating in communion, when a group of approximately 40 men descended on the house church, raising ‘Jai Sri Ram’ slogans.
According to Ruidas, Bisweshwar Choudhury, an influential and wealthy resident of the village who is known for helping people in need, was part of the group. He approached Ruidas during the prayer service and allegedly slapped him.
“Thereafter, the goons accompanying Choudhury started beating us mercilessly,” Ruidas told Alt News. “They slapped us, kicked us and beat us with the bamboo sticks they were carrying. They even took off their belts and whipped us.”
Ruidas said a 17-year-old boy sustained a severe head injury, leaving him bleeding profusely. “The goons told him, ‘We have treated you. Now go to a doctor and get it fixed,” he recounted.
The attackers allegedly dragged worshippers out of the house and beaten up. Those who attempted to seek refuge in neighbouring homes were pursued and assaulted, Ruidas said.
“After the goons beat us, the other attendees locked me inside a kitchen to keep me safe. But they broke open the door and dragged me out. My elder sister hugged me and fell to the ground while trying to protect me. But they continued kicking us. My sister eventually fell unconscious, and I had to take her to a nearby dispensary,” he said.
Ruidas told Alt News that he had attempted to contact police while hiding inside the kitchen but could not get through. He subsequently informed Pastor Jose Bernard, who then contacted the cops.
Bernard told Alt News that he called the Burdwan police station two to three times, but the police allegedly did not take the matter seriously. He eventually dialled the emergency helpline, 112, following which police personnel reached the village.
Bernard said his wife and minor daughter were also among the worshippers present at the congregation. By the time police reached the location, several miscreants had fled the scene. He claimed that when police entered the premises, the remaining miscreants accused the worshippers of having picked a fight with them.
Then, according to the pastor, instead of taking action against the attackers, police detained 20 women, three minors, and eight men from the Christian congregation.
Bernard categorically denied allegations of forceful conversion or conversion through inducement.
Worshippers Detained, Threatened by Accused inside Police Station
The detainees were first taken to Bardhaman Medical College and Hospital, where a doctor examined them inside the vehicle. Then, they were taken to the police station and kept in two separate rooms.
Pastor Jose Bernard subsequently submitted a written complaint at the police station. However, shortly afterwards, a group of alleged attackers entered the police station, grabbed him by the collar and threatened him with dire consequences unless he withdrew the complaint. He alleged that this happened in the presence of police personnel.
“They entered the police station, grabbed me by the collar, physically intimidated me and threatened to kill me if I did not withdraw my complaint. And all of this happened in front of the police,” Bernard told Alt News.
According to Bernard, police merely told the men, “There are CCTV cameras here; leave the premises’. That’s all.”
Bernard said that the threats and intimidation eventually compelled him to withdraw the complaint. He told Alt News that he had pleaded with the miscreants and police to at least ensure that Christians in Rayan village would not be subjected to further harassment. “This is our government. A Hindu government. A Hindu country. Worshipping Jesus is not allowed. They have to bathe in the Ganga, and we will perform ‘ghar wapsi’,” Bernard recalled them saying.
Bernard further alleged that the inspector in-charge, Debabrata Mukherjee, questioned the congregation about why they had assembled to pray in the first place. When the attendees and Bernard attempted to reason, Mukherjee allegedly asked why they were taking such risks when people were being assaulted for doing so in several places.
Eventually, the women were released from the police station around 11 pm, while the men were released around 1 am.
Speaking to Alt News, Burdwan IC Debabrata Mukherjee denied the allegation that the attackers entered the police station and threatened Pastor Jose Bernard to withdraw the complaint.
He said, “They submitted a complaint and, after some time, retracted it. No one threatened them inside the police station,” adding that “Counter-complaints have been filed against them by locals.”
Asked why the injured were detained at police station for long hours, Mukherjee claimed their families hadn’t turned up to take them home.
The officer refused to answer further questions over phone.
Elderly Woman Assaulted at Home
Another attendee, Sagari Konai, managed to escape the initial attack and returned to her home. However, a group of men allegedly went to her residence and assaulted her. She sustained a fracture in her finger due to the assault, the pastors added.
Ruidas alleged that the men forced Konai to perform sit-ups while holding her ears and apologise for practising Christianity. She was also allegedly coerced into participating in Hindu rituals at a nearby temple.
Konai is an elderly widow who lives with her daughter.
The attack has left the survivors deeply shaken. Ruidas said that he was still in pain from the injuries he sustained and that he was afraid to return to his home in Rayan village. He is currently staying with Bernerd.
Bernerd, meanwhile, said the incident had a profound impact on his young daughter, who witnessed the violence firsthand.
“She has never been exposed to such brutal hatred unfolding before her eyes. I wonder whether these people are animals,” he said.

Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named Dianjunus rex.
The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” D. rex is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. And growing up to 20 inches and weighting nearly five pounds, D. rex’s are huge.
Within the Ascomycetes, the giant fungus constitutes an entirely new biological family (the broader classification of genus and species), meaning that it has no close relatives—at least that we know of. While 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, mycologists believe the province known for its biological diversity could easily harbor 100,000
“The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests,” Indunil C. Senanayake, an associate professor at the Kunming Institute of Botany and the lead author of the paper, said in a press release.
Senanayake and his research team conducted surveys in the Nanban tropical rainforest, where they came across large, whitish fruiting bodies growing in the soil near the roots of dying trees. They documented and collected fungi growing in a wide variety of shapes like cylinders, spindles, and cupped palms. The fruiting bodies appeared to develop finger-like branches upon maturity. They found that the above-ground portions are covered with white, powdery fibers that turn dark yellow as the fungi mature while the portions buried in the soil are black and smooth.
The fruiting bodies dried rapidly when the scientists took samples back to the lab. They found that the interiors were dense and sponge-like, appearing white or yellow with no strong odor or taste. (Don’t try this experiment at home.)
Analyzing the DNA of these fungi, the researchers reconstructed a “molecular clock,” which revealed that D. rex diverged from other species approximately 65 million years ago. This is the end of the Cretaceous period, immediately following the mass extinction that is believed to have wiped out three quarters of all plant and animal species, including the dinosaurs. That means D. rex and T. rex never met, but this era was likely a boon for fungi. Large quantities of dead plant material became available following the die off, which could have provided new ecological opportunities for fungi and other organisms that decompose such matter.
Genomic analyses, however, indicated that D. rex doesn’t have nearly as many decomposition-related genes as the scientists expected. Compared to some of its closest relatives that also feast on plant matter, the huge fungus has only about half the usual number of decomposition-related genes.
Senanayake has a theory about this. Though, so far, they have only found the fruiting bodies around dying plants, the fungus may be leading a “double life”—living inside healthy trees and then feeding on dead plant material when the hosts die. That could perhaps explain how D. rex is able to store enough energy to build the massive fruiting bodies.
This is just a theory for now, but the giant fungi undoubtedly do need a surplus of energy to grow so large. Senanayake hypothesizes that the benefit of these large fruiting bodies is that they tower higher than the surrounding plants and fallen leaves, which could be advantageous for wind-mediated spore dispersal in a dense forest. “However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs.”

The High Court of Karnataka has advised the security and police organisations to prioritise the mental health and well-being of personnel entrusted with firearms while asking the authorities to examine existing policies and take appropriate steps to strengthen the mental health and welfare measures for their personnel.
Justice Suraj Govindaraj passed the order while quashing the criminal proceedings against a 37-year-old CISF Sub-Inspector for attempting to kill herself in 2022 by using her service pistol while on duty in Mangaluru. She had attempted to end her life following years of severe mental distress over her inability to conceive a child due to a blocked fallopian tube.
Allowing her petition, the court set aside the lower court’s order and discharged her from the offence under Section 309 of the IPC (attempt to commit suicide). The court ruled that Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, creates a mandatory presumption of severe stress, placing the burden on the prosecution to prove otherwise. Since no such evidence was produced, the court held that continuing the trial would be an abuse of the judicial process.
‘Grief and anxiety’
“Personnel serving in these forces are also human beings. They have families, relationships, responsibilities and personal problems. They experience grief, anxiety, financial difficulties, marital discord, illness in the family and other difficulties common to human life. Wearing a uniform or undergoing rigorous training does not make them immune to such problems,” the court said.
Further, the court said that “the expectation that they must remain available for duty at all times and discharge their responsibilities, come rain or shine, irrespective of their personal circumstances or mental condition, requires a change in institutional thinking.”
The concerned organisations must ensure that accessible and confidential counselling, professional mental healthcare and timely treatment are available to personnel at all levels, including those posted in remote and difficult locations, the court said.
Signals of distress
Commanding and supervisory officers, the court emphasised, must be sensitised to recognise signs of distress and facilitate appropriate assistance, and personnel who undergo treatment or experience mental health difficulties must also receive suitable support for rehabilitation and return to duty, based on professional assessment.
“The welfare of personnel and the security of the public are not competing considerations. A force which looks after the mental and physical well-being of its personnel is better equipped to maintain discipline, operational readiness and public safety, the court said.

Blackburn boss Mowbray steps down over health issues
- Published
Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role with the Championship club amid health issues.
The 62-year-old returned for a second spell in June having previously spent five years managing Rovers between 2017 and 2022.
Mowbray had previously taken time out of the game during his time as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.
Rovers said Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds would take responsibility for first-team duties "for the time being".
"Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers," Mowbray said in a statement., external
"I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them.
"Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you.
"To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me."
Mowbray has transformed Blackburn this season, after a they hovered around the relegation places for much of last term before eventually finishing 20th in the Championship and five points above the drop zone.
They are currently 13th in the Championship table having won six of their 15 league games and three points outside the play-offs.
'Priority is to support him'
Mowbray has been in management for over two decades and his first spell at Blackburn ended at the conclusion of the 2021-22 season when he was eventually replaced by Jon Dahl Tomasson.
He subsequently held roles with Sunderland, Birmingham and a second spell with West Bromwich Albion before his return to Ewood Park.
In his first spell at Blackburn, he could not halt the club's relegation from the Championship, yet he led them to promotion back from League One at the first attempt and subsequently re-established them in the second tier.
In February 2024, he had been diagnosed with cancer but was eventually given the all-clear following treatment.
He leaves with Blackburn in better shape than they were during a tumultuous 2025-26 campaign, which finished with Michael O'Neill opting not to take the manager's job on a full-time basis and instead choosing to remain as boss of Northern Ireland.
"Tony's passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much," Blackburn chief executive officer Steve Curwood added.
"Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can."

Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
If you want to maintain a healthy weight, you probably know you should watch what you eat and get some exercise, maybe hit the gym. But what about hitting the hay?
There is a lot of evidence linking lack of sleep to overeating and an increased body weight. But does that mean that getting more sleep could also boost efforts to lose weight?
"That's a good question," says Seth Creasy, an associate professor of medicine at the University of Colorado Anschutz who studies the interplay between weight management and lifestyle behaviors like sleep, diet and physical activity. "It's actually still an active area of research."
Creasy says the best evidence so far comes from a randomized clinical trial involving 80 overweight adults who were chronically short on sleep. Researchers randomly assigned half of them to get counseling on how to extend their snooze time.
"They got them to sleep a little over an hour more per night," Creasy says. "And they saw that, without intervening on food, these people started to eat less by about 270 calories per day. So once they were getting adequate sleep, they ate less."
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Other research has found associations between better sleep and weight loss. For example, one study found that people enrolled in a year-long weight loss intervention program who had good sleep health lost more weight and more fat mass compared to poor sleepers.
The poor sleepers in that study were also much more likely to report having trouble sticking to their diet and exercise goals, says Christopher Kline, the study's lead author and an associate professor of health and human development at the University of Pittsburgh.
And good sleep health doesn't just mean how long you sleep, Kline says. He says that factors like sleep timing, regularity and satisfaction also play a role.
"A good analogy I like to make is if you get your eight hours of sleep, but those eight hours are between 4 a.m. and noon, that might not be as healthy as someone who regularly obtains their sleep between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.," says Kline, whose research focuses on how physical activity, sleep and cardiometabolic risks are related.
The links between sleep loss and weight gain
Researchers say right now, the evidence that more sleep can boost weight loss efforts is still scant, but the science is much more consistent when it comes to linking insufficient sleep to weight gain.
When researchers restrict people's sleep, they eat more — by an average of around 300 calories a day if you look across studies, says Creasy, who recently published a review of the research on sleep and weight management.
Most of those studies required participants to severely curtail their sleep, usually to around four or five hours a night. That's much less than the seven to nine hours of sleep that adults are supposed to get.
But Creasy worked on a recent study that found even milder sleep loss can result in weight gain. In that study, people who were assigned to sleep just 90 minutes less than usual gained an average of one pound over six weeks. While that may not sound like much, "over time, it adds up," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, the study's senior author and a sleep and nutrition scientist at Columbia University.
Imaging studies from St-Onge and other researchers have found that, when we're short on sleep, activity ramps up in areas of the brain involved in pleasure and reward. In other words, it becomes harder to make good food choices.
"Our brain is less able to inhibit our desires for those sweet and salty foods" — especially later in the day, Kline says. The result is we end up overeating when short on sleep.
Kline says he experienced this phenomenon first-hand when he was still a doctoral student working the overnight shift in a sleep study lab. Once a week, every week, one of his fellow lab workers would bring in glazed donuts from Krispy Kreme.
"I can tell you there was no chance I was going to end a shift without having at least one or two of those donuts. And I don't even really like glazed donuts," Kline says ruefully.
Skimping on sleep can also disrupt our circadian rhythms and impair our sensitivity to insulin, which may promote fat storage and make it easier to gain weight.
Creasy says early studies suggested poor sleep also affects hormones that regulate appetite, but newer research hasn't always borne that out. "Some studies have shown an effect on them and some have not. So it's just been inconsistent," he says.
Better sleep through food?
St-Onge says the relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. "As we find that how we sleep influences our food intake, we also find that what we eat during the day also influences our sleep at night," she says.
Research from her team and others has linked eating added sugars and saturated fat to more sleep disturbances and less deep slumber. Meanwhile, fruits, vegetables and fiber were associated with better sleep and fewer awakenings at night, she says.
If you want to eat better to sleep better, St-Onge says you can start with small, easy changes. "As a first step, cut out foods that are higher in added sugars and sweetened beverages," she says.
Switching to whole grains instead of refined carbohydrates is also a good idea. Her research has linked added sugars and refined carbs to a greater risk of insomnia.
And she says look for opportunities to eat more fruits and vegetables throughout the day.
"I always put a ton of leafy vegetables in my dishes, like stews and soups and stir fries," St-Onge says.
And of course, don't forget good sleep hygiene, says Philip Cheng, a sleep and circadian rhythms researcher and professor of medicine at Henry Ford Health in Michigan. That means things like keeping your bedroom cool and dark, and sticking to a regular schedule for going to bed and waking up as best as you can.
"That's going to stabilize your sleep in the long run," Cheng says.
But if your poor sleep lasts months or even years, he says it's time to see a medical provider for help.

A rumor spread in November that a "hovering orb" shut down a section of Interstate 80 in southern Wyoming.
For example, a Facebook page called Casper Planet said on Nov. 11 (archived):
A section of Interstate 80 in southern Wyoming has been closed early Wednesday morning following multiple reports of a large unidentified orb hovering above the highway. The first reports began coming into dispatchers at approximately 2:45 a.m.
Several truck drivers traveling east of Rawlins reported seeing a bright spherical object hovering motionless approximately 30 to 40 feet above the interstate. Within minutes, additional motorists began reporting the same object. Authorities initially believed drivers were seeing a drone or possibly equipment suspended from a helicopter.
The post includes two images purportedly showing a large, white orb hovering above a highway.
The claim spread elsewhere on Facebook (archived), and Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
Searches on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo (archived, archived, archived) uncovered no examples of reputable local or national news media outlets reporting on such an incident. If a hovering orb had really closed Interstate 80 in Wyoming, news outlets would have covered it.
The original source of the claim is the Casper Planet Facebook page, which describes its content as satirical. Snopes frequently investigates such claims originating from this account.
Casper Planet first mentioned the rumor on Nov. 11 and subsequently posted two follow-up posts about the same fake incident (archived, archived), both of which jokingly claim agents in black went around convincing people they had seen no such object floating above the highway.
The account's page description reads: "Delivering the Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up."
According to SynthID.com, a Google website that detects digital watermarks in alleged photos, both of the pictures Casper Planet used in its Nov. 11 post were created using OpenAI's image-generation tool.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' descriptions of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

A video showing Akhilesh Yadav speaking to the media is being shared (here, here, here) with the claim that he was drunk while addressing reporters. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows Akhilesh Yadav in an intoxicated state while addressing the media.
Fact: The viral video is altered. The original video shows him speaking normally, and the audio has been altered to make his speech sound unclear. When the original video is heard at 0.75x speed, the audio matches the viral video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same video, uploaded on 19 August 2026, on the official Facebook account of the Samajwadi Party. In this video, Akhilesh Yadav speaks in his normal tone. From the 50-second mark, he makes the same remarks heard in the viral video, but without the slurred tone.
Further, when we listened to the original video at 0.75x speed, we found that the audio matched the viral video. You can watch and listen to our edited video below.
We also found videos of the same interaction uploaded on 19 August 2026 by news agencies Bharat Samachar, IANS, and PTI. The microphones of these news agencies are also visible in the viral video. These videos show Akhilesh Yadav speaking to reporters after attending a Bhagwat Katha in Lucknow. He is seen speaking normally, without the slurred tone heard in the viral clip.
To sum up, this video claiming to show Akhilesh Yadav addressing the media in an intoxicated state is doctored.

Ukraine strikes major Russian bridge with drones and missiles as aerial attacks escalate
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the vital Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, calling it an "unprecedented" operation as Russia reported that its forces downed a record number of Ukrainian drones for the second straight day.
Zelenskyy portrayed the bridge operation as a masterstroke following a weekslong effort by Ukrainian forces to gradually wear down Russian air defenses before bombarding the prized target with a barrage of missiles and drones overnight.
Zelenskyy didn't detail the damage, but the Ukrainian General Staff said that an arch and a span of the bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but with a damaged arch.
Russia's Investigative Committee, the nation's top criminal investigation agency, said the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage but didn't elaborate.
The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and for supporting troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory to Ukrainians.
"The symbol of the occupation has cracked," the Ukrainian General Staff said in a statement.
Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.
A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022.
U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week.
Missiles delivered the final blow in the 7-stage operation
The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said.
Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Precision-guided Flamingo missiles delivered the final blow, he said.
Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military published videos showing what they said were the attacks and subsequent damage to the bridge, with part of the deck in the water and a fallen arch. The Associated Press wasn't able to verify the images.
The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic across the bridge was halted but rail traffic was restored by Tuesday afternoon. He didn't mention any damage.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that "there is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than it was before."
Zelenskyy noted that Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day. There were significant power outages Tuesday in three Ukrainian regions, he said.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said.
U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, meeting at NATO headquarters in Brussels with Ukraine's Western backers, said the Kerch Bridge strike was "another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine's absolute determination to defend itself against Russian aggression."
The United Kingdom announced £240 million ($317 million) in air defense support for Ukraine this winter, including more than 1,000 short-range missiles and more than a dozen radars.
Russian air defenses downed 1,441 drones during a second straight night of major Ukrainian attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
That was a day after Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war.
Ukraine also attacks industrial areas deep inside Russia
Elsewhere, authorities in Bashkortostan, a Russian region in the southern Ural Mountains, said that defenses repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones in the cities of Ufa and Salavat. All plants there worked as usual, officials said.
However, independent news outlet Astra reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refining and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, nearly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of the Ukrainian border. The major petrochemical complex has been attacked a number of times before.
In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 800 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight. Most were downed far away, and 321 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital.
Russia hits bridges in Ukraine's capital
Seven Russian ballistic missiles hit two of Kyiv's main bridges during the night, Zelenskyy said. Both were closed to traffic.
The Pivnichnyi and Pivdennyi bridges are key commuter routes across the Dnipro River connecting Kyiv's two banks. The left bank is largely residential with numerous apartment buildings and shopping malls. The old town and many government offices are on the right bank.
On Tuesday morning, long lines of traffic formed on a third bridge linking the two sides of the city.
Russian attacks damaged other infrastructure and started fires in four districts of the Ukrainian capital, officials said, as Moscow continued its campaign to make life difficult for Ukrainian civilians.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces overnight hit Ukraine's military industrial facilities, energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as vessels used for Ukrainian armed forces.
Russian forces launched a combined attack on industrial facilities in three districts of the southern Ukraine region of Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18 others and leaving a large number of consumers in the region without power, local authorities said.
The possibility of more talks
Meanwhile, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the United States, and European partners held a working video call Monday in which they discussed the results of recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, and the agenda for the next stage of negotiations, said Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service.

A lawyer for the Saudi national accused of bugging OpenAI's San Francisco office is making another attempt to get him released from jail, saying that Justice Department prosecutors haven't dug up any evidence that would support espionage charges.
"Government counsel acknowledged that if there were supporting evidence, new charges would have been brought when Mr. Alfozan was indicted," David Rizk, the attorney for Abdulrahman Alfozan, said in a court filing ahead of his client's Tuesday court appearance.
"Instead, Mr. Alfozan was indicted solely on the Wiretap Act count that was the subject of the Complaint."
Federal prosecutors in San Francisco arrested Alfozan in October, accusing him of planting a listening device in a conference room at OpenAI's office, where he worked as an engineer. The criminal complaint accused him of interception of oral communications.
Prosecutors brought a grand jury indictment against Alfozan later in October, but didn't include more severe charges, such as espionage or theft of trade secrets.
Rizk said prosecutors said in two meetings this month that no evidence emerged to bring additional charges against him.
Rizk asked US District Judge Vince Chhabria, who is overseeing the case, to order the Justice Department to hand over additional information that would enable the defense lawyer to formally request Alfozan's release from jail.
A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in San Francisco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Alfozan has pleaded not guilty to the charges against him. A federal judge ordered him to remain in jail while awaiting trial, ruling there was a high risk he would flee if released because the Saudi government offered to pay his bond and because his wife and son had already flown to Saudi Arabia.
Photos included in the criminal complaint show images of a USB device plugged into the back of a conference room TV and wrapped in toilet paper. The complaint also included what prosecutors said was a photo of Alfozan checking on the device a week after another OpenAI employee found it hidden there.
According to Rizk, the discovery material produced by the federal government so far doesn't indicate that prosecutors took any steps to investigate ties between Alfozan and the government of Saudi Arabia.
Rizk also said Alfozan voluntarily offered to unlock his cellphone, which was seized by the Justice Department, after prosecutors said they lost access to it earlier this month because of a power failure at an FBI facility.
In addition to seeking Alfozan's release from jail, Rizk asked the judge to modify a previous order restricting his use of AI while he prepares to defend himself in court.
"The U.S. Attorney's Office should not be in the business of policing defense counsel's discovery practices," Rizk wrote.

Home services platform Urban Company has opened its QIP, setting a floor price of ₹161.03 per share. The company is issuing equity shares to institutional investors after securing shareholder approval to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr. Urban Company may offer a discount of up to 5% on the floor price. The company’s board approved the fundraise on October 16. Shareholders cleared it through a special resolution by postal ballot, with 99.3% of votes cast in favour. The company’s fundraise committee approved the launch and the preliminary placement document yesterday. Urban Company has set out ₹1,475 Cr in proposed allocations across five uses in its preliminary placement document. It plans to deploy ₹600 Cr to grow InstaHelp, ₹540 Cr for marketing, ₹200 Cr for technology development and cloud infrastructure, ₹85 Cr for office rent, and ₹50 Cr for research and development for its Native products. Urban Company expects to deploy ₹150 Cr for InstaHelp in FY27, ₹300 Cr in FY28, and ₹150 Cr in FY29. InstaHelp competes with Snabbit and Pronto in the instant domestic help market. Urban Company said InstaHelp completed 6.2 Mn orders in Q2 FY27. Snabbit founder Aayush Agarwal said his startup fulfilled 6.45 Mn orders in the same quarter. When it announced the fundraise plan last month, Urban Company said fresh capital would give it room to invest across its businesses, strengthen InstaHelp’s market position, and pursue acquisitions. The company is also expanding into residential air conditioners under Native, which currently sells water purifiers and smart locks. Urban Company has cited its experience servicing millions of residential ACs annually as the driver for this business vertical. InstaHelp Weighs On Earnings On the financial front, Urban Company reported a net loss of ₹182.5 Cr, more than tripling from ₹59.3 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue grew 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 Cr, while total expenses surged 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr. The widening losses were largely driven by investments in InstaHelp, on which the company spent ₹174 Cr during the quarter. Its adjusted EBITDA loss stood at ₹144 Cr, but excluding InstaHelp, the company reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹30 Cr. Notably, its management has maintained that it can achieve its profitability targets without the fundraise and rejected the suggestion that the fundraise is necessary to offset InstaHelp’s impact on its financials. In the past, Urban Company has indicated that the vertical is likely to remain a low-margin business compared with its core operations, adding that it does not expect to make money from the vertical over the next five years. It expects InstaHelp to break even by FY31.

AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”
“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”
While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.
In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.
AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”
AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.
AT&T: Fiber-powered is “literally false”
AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”

- In November, after a string of major outages occurred at government and commercial networks including the nationwide air traffic system, social media posts claimed the conservative Heritage Foundation's blueprint for reshaping the federal government, Project 2025, called for "dismantling" or "destroying" the Federal Aviation Administration.
- There are elements of truth to the claim depending on how it's worded. Project 2025 did propose restructuring the agency (or "dismantling the FAA as we know it," as some phrased it) and moving toward a privatized air traffic system.
- It's inaccurate to say Project 2025 called for the FAA to be "destroyed," much less that its recommendations regarding the agency played some role in the Nov. 13 ground stop that shut down air traffic nationwide.
- According to the FAA, a technical problem caused by data flooding the agency's telecommunications infrastructure network and disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds led to the ground stop.
As officials in the U.S. traded blame for the nationwide flight grounding that took place Nov. 13 — with President Donald Trump's administration pushing Congress for $50 billion to address an aging air traffic control system — a rumor circulated that the Republican-driven Project 2025 called for the dismantling of the Federal Aviation Administration.
Project 2025, a nearly 1,000-page document intended to reshape federal government policies, was created by The Heritage Foundation, a conservative nonprofit organization, and has been directly mirrored in some of the policies Trump has enacted during his second term in office.
According to the FAA, the Nov. 13 ground stop was caused by data flooding the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network, which disrupted the system and made aircraft communications and radar feeds unstable.
"I can't apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can't blame Republicans or Democrats because it's all of them," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on NBC News on Nov. 15.
With an aging communication system and public demand to know what was going to be done to fix it, questions about Project 2025's vision for the future of the FAA gained momentum on social media.
"Pages 632–635 of the Heritage Foundation's Mandate for Leadership call for dismantling the FAA as we know it — starting with splitting the Air Traffic Organization out of the FAA and the Department of Transportation entirely, moving toward a privatized air traffic system funded by user fees," one Facebook post read (archived). "Remember, destroying the FAA is part of Project 2025," the post's image read.
We looked into the claim by parsing Project 2025's section addressing its vision for the future of the FAA. We found that while it did not call for the wholesale "dismantling of the FAA," it did call for drastic changes that would separate the agency from government bodies that imposed regulations the authors deemed limiting to modernization, as well as for the privatization of several aspects of the agency.
So, the claim that Project 2025 called for the "dismantling of the FAA, as we know it" leans heavily on the latter half of the statement. The claim that "destroying the FAA is part of Project 2025" is based on opinion, not factual evidence.
Below is the relevant section of the full Project 2025 text (pages 632-634) detailing the project's proposed changes to the FAA:
As illustrated above, Project 2025 did call for a drastic overhaul of the FAA's structure, including separating the FAA from the Department of Transportation or, at a minimum, separating the Air Traffic Organization from the FAA on the grounds it would result in an overall reduction in oversight and the "constraints imposed" by the annual congressional appropriations process:
The FAA's overly bureaucratic, legalistic, byzantine, and more recently hyperpoliticized way of processing regulations, adopting innovation, publishing rules, and procuring new technologies has been eclipsed by foreign CAAs and ANSPs that are eagerly certifying drones and creating environments in which new technologies and new entrants, such as air taxis, can thrive.
The project called for the FAA to operate more like a business than a government entity, with a shift from funding provided by aviation user taxes to fees for air traffic services paid directly to the Air Traffic Organization, allowing the ATO to issue long-term revenue bonds for major projects.
In sum, there's no truth to claims that Project 2025 proposed "destroying" the FAA. Rather, it outlined several changes that would reorganize its operations and separate it from historic governmental structures and processes.

Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark are seeking to establish a hub for rejected asylum seekers. Here’s what to know about their effort.
Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.
The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.
The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers. With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance.
“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday.
The pilot project is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees. Critics are already worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda.
Why Rwanda?
The country has a history of courting migration-related deals.
Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda.

The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.
Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.
“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”
That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”
Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”
Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.
Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”
Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.
Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”
Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”
Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.
In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.
Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”

Direct-to-consumer (D2C) startups have been facing mounting cost pressures since the US-Iran conflict drove up global crude prices, making it increasingly difficult for them to protect their already-thin margins. Even as higher oil prices push up freight, logistics, packaging and raw material costs for new-age brands and manufacturers, revising price tags does not seem to be a viable option for them for their lack of scale and bargaining power, leaving them grappling for alternatives. Unlike established fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) companies, which can leverage bulk procurement, supplier bargaining power, and diversified portfolios to absorb cost shocks, smaller D2C brands have far fewer buffers. Absorbing the increase depletes their already unsure margins, while passing it on to consumers risks losing them and reacquiring them at a higher cost. It’s a catch-22 situation for them. The pressure is particularly visible in categories such as food, beverages and personal care, for which crude-linked packaging, agricultural commodities and imported ingredients account for a significant share of procurement costs. Higher shipping expenses and volatility in supplier availability have added to the challenge, making it difficult for startups to plan inventory and input requirements. The festive season did offer some respite on the demand side. Online festive sales grew 17% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹1.41 Lakh Cr in 2026, according to Datum Intelligence’s Festive Barometer. Elsewhere, ClickPost’s analysis of more than 80 Mn orders across nearly 400 D2C brands indicated that daily orders increased 27% YoY in the run-up to Diwali, while estimated gross merchandise value (GMV) grew 45%. The problem is that this has not necessarily translated into an easier operating environment for D2Cs. Brands are struggling now to sustain consumer demand beyond the festive period while managing the cost of acquiring customers, fulfilling orders and replenishing inventory. However, there’s some reason for optimism now. Brent crude, which surged to around $118 per barrel in late October, has since cooled to approximately $95 as of November 16, offering a possible reprieve to businesses grappling with rising input costs. For D2C brands, however, the relief may take time to materialise, as the impact of lower oil prices will take a while to filter through to supply chains, freight rates and packaging costs. For D2C startups, the bigger question is no longer whether input costs will ease, but how long they will have to absorb the pressure. How Brands Are Absorbing Cost Spikes The bigger challenge for startups is not necessarily the rise in input costs itself, but the unpredictability of procurement prices, which makes cost planning and margin management very difficult, said the founder of a large D2C beauty brand who preferred not to be named. “What bothers startups most is the variation. If a supplier does not stock one product because the price has gone up, the full production (line) might stop,” he said. For instance, a specialised ingredient may become unavailable because a supplier is unwilling to maintain inventory amid an uncertain price environment. Even if it accounts for a relatively small share of the final product’s cost, its absence can disrupt the manufacturing process altogether. “You cannot make any product with 99% ingredients. That one missing ingredient will hold the thing. Then you scramble and get it from somewhere at any cost,” the founder quoted above added. Brands that rely on imported ingredients or packaging materials feel the pinch harder. Shipping costs can fluctuate sharply, forcing them to choose between paying a premium to avoid production delays and waiting for freight rates to ease. Either way, higher procurement costs and the need to hold extra inventory strain working capital, leaving less money for scaling-up. Bharat Birla, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, said rising commodity and packaging costs have squeezed larger FMCG companies too, particularly in home care, packaged foods and personal care. But for smaller brands, which lack comparable procurement scale, the impact on operating margins can be far more pronounced, he pointed out. Food & Beverage Startups Face Most Cost Exposure The impact of input inflation varies depending on the product category. For several non-food D2C businesses, the cost of goods sold (COGS) may account for around 15-20% of the product price, and at most 30%, according to a large D2C beauty brand founder who did not wish to be named. Food businesses, on the other hand, can have a significantly higher COGS, sometimes reaching 40%. This makes food and beverage brands relatively more vulnerable to fluctuations in agricultural commodities, packaging and transportation costs. Crude oil is particularly relevant for beverage manufacturers because several packaging materials, including plastic bottles, preforms, caps and labels, are linked to petrochemical inputs. Nikhil Doda, cofounder of Lahori Zeera, told Inc42, “Most of our raw materials depend on crude. Our preforms, caps and labels are all affected. That hit was there.” The company did not raise prices specifically to offset the recent inflation, although it implemented selective hikes in April-May 2026 as part of its regular price revision cycle, he added. With Reliance’s Campa expanding and Coca-Cola and PepsiCo sharpening their pricing strategies, further hikes could risk weakening its competitive position. “You cannot increase prices when Coke and Pepsi have decreased their prices from ₹20 to ₹10,” Doda said. So, for emerging consumer brands, the pricing dilemma is sharper: with fewer buffers to absorb cost shocks, they must protect margins without pricing themselves out of the market. Why Cutting Discounts May Be Easier Than Raising Prices Unlike established FMCG players with decades of consumer loyalty, D2C brands rely heavily on digital advertising, promotions and discounts to acquire and retain customers, making price hikes risky in a market where consumers have plenty of alternatives. So, mid-sized and smaller companies are having to look at changes in product mix and pack sizes to manage inflation, Birla said. The room to raise prices, however, is narrowing for all. According to Sandeep Abhange, research analyst – consumer and midcaps at LKP Securities, large FMCG companies have so far absorbed roughly half of the input cost inflation. “HUL faced 8-10% material inflation but took only 2-5% price hikes, while Dabur took 4% against 10% inflation,” he said. Startups, Abhange said, could increasingly resort to calibrated price increases and changes in pack sizes, particularly at lower price points. Smaller packs may see grammage reductions, while larger packs could see more direct price increases. Also, brands should evaluate input inflation alongside marketing expenditure, said the beauty brand founder. “For D2C companies, the cost of goods has a relatively limited impact on overall prices in several categories. If some ingredients become twice as expensive, the cost may go up from, say, 18% to 22%, but marketing costs around 30%.” This means a reduction in marketing expenditure or discounting could sometimes have a greater impact on profitability than a marginal improvement in procurement costs. Brands with healthy gross margins, repeat customers and efficient marketing strategies may therefore be better positioned to absorb inflation. Those dependent on aggressive discounts and paid customer acquisition could face greater pressure. The challenge is particularly relevant after the festive season, when promotional activity begins to moderate and brands have to convert seasonal buyers into repeat customers. Abhange expects another meaningful round of price increases in Q3 and Q4 FY27, particularly across categories such as detergents, soaps, biscuits, noodles and packaged snacks, which remain exposed to crude-linked inputs and agricultural commodities. Crude Prices Have Cooled, But Will Startups See Relief? The softening of crude prices has offered some optimism. However, even as expectations of improved global supply have weighed on prices, geopolitical and shipping-related uncertainties continue to pose risks. For Indian startups, the transmission of lower crude prices into procurement costs is unlikely to be immediate. “Even if crude cools down, the effect on our procurement levels will take at least five to six months. It’s a process, and things should also remain stable,” Doda said. Suppliers may still be working with inventory procured at higher prices, while shipping and conversion costs can take additional time to adjust. Doda added that geopolitical uncertainty makes it difficult to predict when the situation will normalise. If global prices remain stable, he expects the impact to gradually reach procurement costs over the next five to six months. Birla too predicts a similar timeline. This means packaging-intensive businesses may have to wait until the first half of calendar 2027 to see a meaningful reduction in some input costs, provided the decline is sustained. The broader margin outlook, however, remains cautious. Abhange expects gross margins across FMCG companies to remain under pressure through Q3 and Q4 FY27, with stabilisation likely only from Q1 FY28 (April to June 2027) as lower crude prices and easing packaging costs gradually feed through. The timelines are not necessarily interchangeable for every D2C business. The pace of relief will depend on the category, supplier contracts, inventory cycles and the extent to which a brand relies on crude-linked inputs. Next Few Quarters Will Test Unit Economics For D2C startups, the next phase will be about managing growth without allowing higher procurement and marketing expenses to erode profitability. Lower crude prices offer a positive signal, but the relief will take time to reach procurement costs. For packaging-intensive businesses, the five-to-six-month transmission period cited by Doda and Birla suggests that meaningful cost normalisation may take until the first half of 2027, provided global prices remain stable. A broader recovery in FMCG margins could take longer, with Abhange pointing to Q1 FY28 as a possible turning point. In the interim, D2Cs will have to focus on supplier diversification, inventory planning, reducing avoidable marketing expenditure and improving gross margins rather than relying solely on price increases. The current cost cycle may not necessarily become a demand-side problem for the sector, but could reveal the difference between brands that have built resilient operating models and those whose growth depends on continuous discounts and external capital. For emerging consumer businesses, the festive season may have brought more customers through the door, but the bigger test now is whether they can retain those customers, fulfil demand and make money from every additional order.

Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
Japan said it has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian warplanes temporarily entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coast on Tuesday as tensions escalate between the two sides
TOKYO -- Japan said it strongly protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace off its southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft early Tuesday violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes near Fukuoka, long enough for the Air Self-Defense Force to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government has lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.
Separately, South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the military had detected the aircraft before they entered the zone and scrambled fighter jets. The South’s military did not disclose the number of Russian aircraft it detected or what types of planes they were.
Koizumi did not comment on why the violations took place but said Japan continues to closely monitor Russian military activity “with strong interest."
Japan has raised growing concern over growing joint military activity between Russia and China around the Japanese coasts.
The airspace violation was the latest sign of deteriorating relations between the two countries. Tensions have risen since Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Iturup in August, one of four Russian-controlled islands off Japan’s northern coast that Tokyo also claims.
Tensions escalated in mid-October after the arrest of a Japanese journalist in Russia on suspicion of spying. Despite repeated protests and demands for his immediate release, the journalist, who works for the Hokkaido newspaper, remains in custody.
Earlier this month, Russia placed several subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco Inc. under the temporary management of a Russian company following a presidential order issued by Putin. Japan protested and demanded the measure be withdrawn.
The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending hostilities.

Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
- Published
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.
But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.
His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," one woman watching the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.
Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.
There's a sense of injustice that Australia can't escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja was telling the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".
Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Cameron Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.
Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.
But he was also frank - using strong words to reject Khawaja's claims and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."
As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioning Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.
"I don't know what the outcome will be."

Srinagar- PDP MLA Waheed Para on Tuesday said the Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB) should put all upcoming examinations on hold until the truth behind the alleged cheating racket in the finance assistant examination comes out.
Police on Sunday arrested 14 people for allegedly attempting to facilitate cheating in the JKSSB finance assistant examination in Jammu. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) has been constituted to probe the matter.
“Paper leaks, recruitment scams & repeated compromises have turned the aspirations of J&K’s youth into a cycle of uncertainty and betrayal. The FAA cheating racket (as reported by media) is yet another grave indictment of a system that continues to fail those who work tirelessly for a fair opportunity,” Para said in a post on X.
The SIT must expose the entire network, identify every individual involved and fix accountability, said the MLA from south Kashmir’s Pulwama.
“Until the investigation establishes the truth, JKSSB must put the upcoming JKPSI & Police Constable examinations on hold. Our youth cannot be asked to keep trusting a system that repeatedly breaks their trust. Their future is not negotiable,” Para said.

The successful global run of Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana: Part 1, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has turned a quiet, rocky hilltop in Kerala's Kollam district into one of India’s most sought-after travel destinations.
The film's dramatic depiction of the mythical bird Jatayu fighting Ravana to protect Goddess Sita has sparked a renewed cultural interest, drawing thousands of tourists to the Jatayu Earth's Center in Chadayamangalam—home to the world's largest bird sculpture.
At the heart of this architectural marvel is a decade of dedication by a visionary artist, Rajiv Anchal.
Rajiv Anchal is a renowned Malayalam film director and sculptor, best known for directing the 1997 Mohanlal-starrer Guru, which was India's official entry for the Academy Awards.
Anchal is the mastermind and chief sculptor behind the Jatayu Earth's Center. For nearly ten years, he trekked up the massive 1,000-foot-high rock every day to oversee the conceptualisation and construction of the monument. His vision was to create a colossal work of art while preserving the rocky landscape's natural ecology.
The result is a staggering concrete sculpture measuring 200 feet in length, 150 feet in width, and 70 feet in height, built to symbolise women's safety and honour.
Inside the sculpture, Anchal also designed a multi-level audio-visual museum and an immersive theatre.
The recent cinematic retelling of the epic has transformed the site of Chadayamangalam into a bustling tourist hub.
According to media reports, the centre is currently attracting around 3,200 to 4,000 visitors a day, with weekend numbers expected to exceed 5,000.
Local executives note a massive influx of tourists from North India, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka, driven by the emotional resonance of the film's Jatayu narrative.
Acknowledging the trend, Kerala Chief Minister VD Satheesan and the state's tourism department recently invited film enthusiasts to visit the site, positioning it as a prime destination for both spiritual seekers and adventure tourists.
The Jatayu Earth's Center operates daily from 10:00 am to 5:30 pm (timings often extend to 6:00 pm on weekends and holidays).
Visitors can choose from multiple entry packages based on how they wish to ascend the hill:
Note: Adventure sports like rappelling, zip-lining, and paintball incur additional charges, with full-day packages ranging from ₹1,500 to ₹3,500.
Located in Chadayamangalam, the destination is highly accessible for travellers:
By Air: The nearest airport is Thiruvananthapuram (Trivandrum) International Airport, located approximately 50 km away. Taxis and buses are readily available from the airport.
By Train: The nearest major railway station is in Kollam city, roughly 38 km from the site. Varkala railway station is also a convenient transit point.
