How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
- Published
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
Megaspeed is a case in point.
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.
During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.
Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.
"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.
Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.
Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.
But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."
Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft’s report lists the incident’s final status as “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”
Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.
The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft’s incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company’s status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service-health updates.
A perfect storm
Microsoft attributes the outage to three factors. A change deployed to Microsoft’s cloud gateway starting in July created a bug where, under certain conditions, CPU and memory resources could become exhausted and unresponsive. Microsoft contends that the defect was never discovered in pre-release testing because the hardware used was less powerful than some systems already deployed in production, where higher CPU core counts on newer machines apparently contributed to the lockout.
The second factor was server load. Microsoft said that “Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug.” The company keeps two independent gateway systems in place to access Microsoft 365 for resilience. If one system encounters trouble and users can’t get through the front door, the other is opened to keep traffic flowing. According to the report, about 15 hours prior to the outage, traffic from Teams was shifted from the alternate gateway to the primary, where Exchange Online access is maintained. The switchover was a standard fail-safe, but it left the gateway handling more traffic, with a different mix of requests than before. As requests continued to pile up, affected servers exhausted their capacity and refused new connection requests.

The Italianization of Europe
Over more than a quarter-century, I’ve watched Europe’s politics become more like Italy’s, with all the resulting instability, as the far right came in from the cold.
When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.
At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.
As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.
An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.
Back then, I didn’t see the change around me, but now, more than a quarter-century later, after spending decades reporting on Italian politics and changes across Europe, I have come to understand that I was living in the future.
In the time since, I have seen an Italianization of politics all around the continent, with coalitions of small parties resulting in instability, with fed-up voters desperate for new saviors. But more than anything, I have seen — in Britain, France, Germany — countries following the Italian model by allowing the far right into the political mainstream.

Fear, outrage grow as Quebec moves to ban religious symbols for elementary students
Experts say PQ's plan would cause harm, say it's 'misguided' and 'disrespectful'
Mehwaish Raja’s 11 year-old daughter surprised her during a conversation this past summer on the way to day camp.
“She shared with me during the car ride: ‘Mama, I will wear my hijab at the end of the summer,’” Raja said.
Up until that point, her daughter only wore the hijab for special occasions, and Raja had never insisted she wear it regularly.
“I just said, ‘OK.’ And by the end of the summer, it actually happened,” Raja said.
Her daughter now wears the hijab every day in her Grade 5 class in a public school in Montreal’s West Island.
Now, the new Parti Québécois government is proposing a law that would make that practice illegal as part of a series of measures announced on the campaign trail to strengthen secularism.
Raja is struggling to understand why.
“Honestly, I'm out of words. I'm out of words when I hear things like this,” she said.
She doesn’t think the government should be able to decide what her daughter wears to school.
“When we step out of our house, we leave as who we are. What part of us do we leave at home?” she said.
Religious symbols gradually squeezed out of schools
The previous CAQ government already introduced several laws restricting religious symbols in schools, preventing at first teachers, and then all school staff – even parent volunteers – from wearing them.
Generally, religious symbols bans in Quebec have targeted employees of the state considered to be in positions of authority, but the CAQ opened the door to targeting students by introducing a ban on full face coverings at school.
Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is opening that door wider, proposing a blanket ban preventing elementary school students from wearing "conspicuous" religious symbols while at school.
“Separating children through what they wear and through religious beliefs at such a young age is not helping cohesion and integration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in September when announcing the measure, without providing any specific examples.
“We think it's a good policy in terms of letting children just be children, with no connection whatsoever to what their parents believe about religion,” he'd said.
When proposing the religious ban for elementary schools during the election campaign, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the symbols 'interfere with cohesion and integration.' (Ivanoh Demers/CBC/Radio-Canada)
Winning a minority government in the general election did not soften the PQ's resolve, with new Education Minister Joël Arseneau saying the measure was a "non-negotiable."
"It’s on this basis that we were elected, and it’s on this basis that we’re working,” Arseneau told reporters at the National Assembly in late October.
Mother says proposed law based on misconceptions
Asma Qureshi says the PQ's proposal comes from a place of ignorance.
Qureshi, who lives on Montreal’s South Shore, has four children. Her oldest daughter, now in high school, started wearing a hijab to school when she was in Grade 4. Her youngest daughter, currently in kindergarten, wore one to school a couple of times this year just to try it.
Qureshi – who wears a hijab herself – says in both cases, she didn’t ask or order her daughters to wear one.
"I told myself that I would never impose it on my kids," she said.
"There’s this narrative that goes around – and it's been there since I was a young kid – that children and women are being forced to wear the scarf."
Qureshi thinks that misconception is what’s feeding the gradual tightening of restrictions on wearing religious symbols in Quebec, particularly in schools.
She says she hasn’t yet discussed the proposed ban with her daughters.
“How do you tell a child it’s against the law for you to wear something that your mother wears?” she said.
Raja says her daughter's decision to start wearing the hijab regularly this fall convinced her to do the same. (CBC News)
For Raja, who up until now had been reluctant to wear a hijab in Quebec for fear of standing out, says her daughter's decision to wear one at school this fall convinced her to do the same.
“I'm really proud of her because at 11 years old, she decided to wear it, whereas I’m 40 and I hadn't been able to,” she said.
“My daughter truly inspired me."
Ban would cause harm, experts say
Experts in secularism and child development told CBC there is no justification for banning students from wearing religious symbols — and that the measure would be harmful.
Thomas Dee, an economist at Stanford University who specializes in how education policy affects student outcomes, disagreed with the notion of asking children to leave their parents' religious baggage behind.
“Parents are children's first and most impactful teachers, and to sideline their guidance and insights just seems misguided to me and disrespectful,” he said.
Dee testified as an expert witness in the court challenge to Bill 21, Quebec’s first secularism law.
Thomas Dee, an economics professor at Stanford University who studies the effects of education policy on student outcomes, says a policy that marginalizes parents' values in school is misguided and disrespectful. (CBC News)
Sivane Hirsch, a professor in the faculty of education at Université Laval who specializes in cultural and religious diversity in schools, believes the ban is a horrible idea.
“We don’t want children to feel they’re being taught in school against their parents, against their family,” Hirsch said.
Dee said such a conflict would also hurt students’ performance.
“Anything that makes students feel less welcome or less at ease will imply they're not able to bring their full attention and motivation to the realization of their academic potential,” Dee said.
Zeinab Diab, a religious studies researcher at Université de Montréal and author of Au nom de la laïcité, a book about Islamophobia in Quebec, said a secularism law that targets young children is inhumane.
“They are dehumanizing them and limiting their access to school. What kind of society allows that?” she said.
Author and religious studies researcher Zeinab Diab says targeting children for a religious symbols ban is inhumane. (CBC News)
Dee said the presence of religious symbols in the classroom could actually help.
“If you engage with people across difference, you no longer use simple rules of thumb to judge them, but rather you judge them as people,” he said.
Qureshi said that was her daughter’s experience.
She said no other students made negative comments or gave her daughter a hard time when she started wearing the hijab.
“It was just like she was any other regular person,” she said. “That's the beautiful thing – when people can recognize you for who you are rather than what you wear."
PQ needs support of at least 1 other party
In order to adopt the ban, the PQ will need support from at least one other party in the National Assembly.
Charles Milliard, leader of the Quebec Liberals and the Official Opposition, said last week his party wouldn’t support the measure.
“We're talking about children. I'm not going to do politics on the backs of children,” Milliard said.
Québec Solidaire also doesn’t support the measure.
That leaves the Conservative Party of Quebec.
On Monday, leader Éric Duhaime said his party generally supports secularism, but wanted to see more details before deciding whether to support the proposed law.
"I mean, what are we going to do with those kids if they don't respect the rules?" Duhaime told reporters.
"That's the kind of thing that I want to know before we move forward."
Education Minister Joël Arseneau says he's negotiating with other parties about the idea of banning religious symbols for elementary school students, and that their positions may evolve. (CBC News)
Last week, Arseneau said he was in negotiations with other parties about the bill, and that their positions may evolve. He declined CBC’s request for an interview.
Raja says if the ban does become law, her daughter would likely leave her current school.
“If the public system is really asking us not to practise certain values that we strongly believe in, I would choose another way of educating my children,” she said.
For her that would likely be private school, but she said some other parents might choose homeschooling.
Diab said not all families have either the money or the time for those options.
“Maybe they’re going to adapt, but no one should be always in fight and survival mode,” she said.
“This is exhausting.”

EXCLUSIVE: Magenta Edge Films has scooped up the North American rights to the romantic fantasy drama Billy Knight starring Charlie Heaton, Al Pacino, Diana Silvers, and Patrick Schwarzenegger. The pic reps the feature directorial debut of Alec Griffen Roth, who also wrote the screenplay.
A Jan. 8, 2027 nationwide theatrical release is planned.
In the pic, grad school students Alex (Heaton) and Emily (Silvers) traverse their aspiring careers as filmmakers. While Alex grapples with the grief of losing his father, a failed screenwriter, he comes across a handkerchief with the name “Billy Knight” embroidered on it. Consumed with the desire to discover his identity, Alex embarks on a Hollywood adventure to track down this mysterious and reclusive Knight (Al Pacino), all while navigating the line between fiction and reality.
Billy Knight debuts an original song (and appearance) by Beck, as well as special appearances by Diplo, Rick Ross, and Harry Jowsey. The film’s all-star cast also includes Angela Sarafyan, Sara Sampaio, Elsie Hewitt, Aleeha Rogers, Roberta Hanlan, and Savannah Rodin.
Watch on Deadline
“Getting to create this world of make-believe with a slice of reality was unlike anything I ever imagined. It was a dream come true and I am truly blessed to have been given the opportunity to work with such incredible and iconic actors and producers, and the best crew a young filmmaker could ask for. We’re grateful to Bob Yari and Magenta Light Studios/Magenta Edge Films to share our vision in getting this out into the world,” Roth says.
“Billy Knight is a beautiful love letter to Hollywood and the magic of filmmaking,” said Bill Vergos, Head of Digital Film Distribution at Magenta Light Studios, who oversees the company’s Magenta Edge Films label. “Alec has created something truly special, blending fantasy, romance, and heartfelt emotion into a story that celebrates why we fall in love with movies in the first place. With an incredible cast led by Al Pacino, Charlie Heaton, and Diana Silvers, we’re thrilled to champion Alec’s feature directorial debut and bring this film to audiences on the big screen this January.”
The feature was produced by Prominent Productions, Firebrand Media Group, and RNA Pictures. EPs are Tuan Bui, Peter Bortel, Noor Alfallah, Sarah Sarandos, Keyun “Country” Parker, Tony Sarandos, Remi Alfallah and Peter Morgan. Billy Knight was also produced by Autumn Bailey-Ford, Cameron Burnett, Amanda Kiely, Sevier Crespo, Josh Clayton and Kirk Martin.
The distribution deal for Billy Knight was negotiated by C.J. Vranca and Bill Vergos on behalf of Magenta Edge Films, and Josh Clayton on behalf of Elias Film productions. Roth is represented by Keyun ‘Country’ Parker of Parker’s Communication and Entertainment Services.

- The effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth failed in a 211-204 vote on Nov. 10, which many Democrats blamed on 11 of their fellow party members who were absent from the voting chamber.
- Of those 11 Democrats, social media users claimed some of them missed the vote because they were attending an event related to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a powerful pro-Israel lobbying group.
- The event in question was reportedly hosted by Elect Democrat Women. According to the nonprofit OpenSecrets, the top donor to the Elect Democrat Women-affiliated super PAC, EDW Action Fund, was the United Democracy Project — a super PAC affiliate of AIPAC.
- Drop Site News, a nonprofit investigative news outlet, reportedly obtained an RSVP list of the event showing that three of the 11 Democrats who missed the vote were present at the event: Reps. Julia Brownley, D-Calif., Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., and Brittany Pettersen, D-Colo. As of this writing, the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal how it sourced the list.
- Two of the represenatives, Brownley and Pettersen, reportedly acknowledged attending the Elect Democratic Women event. However, none of them had responded to our requests for comment by the time of publication.
- Until we hear directly from the representatives' offices or primary evidence confirming their attendance emerges, we've left this claim unrated.
On Nov. 10, the U.S. House of Representatives voted on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the face of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
The impeachment effort failed in a 211-204 vote, which many Democrats blamed on 11 of their fellow party members who were absent from the voting chamber.
The 11 absent Democrats were Reps. Julia Brownley, Melanie Stansbury, Brittany Pettersen, Laura Gillen, Nancy Pelosi, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland, Frederica Wilson, Jonathan Jackson, Steven Horsford and J. Luis Correa.
Social media users claimed some of those 11 missed the vote because they were attending an event related to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a powerful pro-Israel lobbying group.
The event in question was reportedly hosted by Elect Democrat Women. According to the nonprofit OpenSecrets, the top donor to the Elect Democrat Women-affiliated super PAC, EDW Action Fund, was the United Democracy Project — a super PAC affiliate of AIPAC.
Drop Site News, a nonprofit investigative news outlet, reportedly obtained an RSVP list of the event showing that three of the 11 Democrats who missed the vote were present at the event: Brownley, of California, Stansbury, of New Mexico, and Pettersen, of Colorado. As of this writing, the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal how it sourced the list.
Two of the representatives, Brownley and Pettersen, reportedly acknowledged attending the Elect Democratic Women event. However, none of them had responded to our requests for comment by the time of publication. Until we hear directly from the representatives' offices or primary evidence confirming their attendance emerges, we've left this claim unrated.
On Nov. 11, USA Today reporter Zach Schermele posted that Brownley told him she "left last night's Elect Democratic Women event for the Hegseth vote with plenty of time to spare" and that "when the traffic jam made it clear she might not make it in time, she and other lawmakers started texting each other." He reported that Brownley, 74, then got out of her car and started running, missing the vote by "seconds" (archived).
According to Denver NBC affiliate KUSA, Pettersen acknowledged she attended the event, saying in a statement, "Last night, I was late to the floor and there is no excuse for that. I was at an Electing Democratic Women event."
Stansbury posted a video on Nov. 11 apologizing for her absence, saying, "I know I should've been there at that moment." She blamed rush-hour traffic on Independence Avenue for her absence. She did not mention the EDW event, though her comments were flooded with users accusing her of attending it.
Because the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal where it sourced the list, we are unable to rate this claim. We can, however, break down Drop Site News' findings and any other publicly available information.
The document Drop Site News reportedly obtained also included a "Run of Show" listing the event's schedule, which read:
Run of Show:
- 4:30 pm: Event begins.
  - Mix and mingle
- 5:00 pm: EDW Chairwoman Lois Frankel to give opening remarks.
  - Thank everyone for attending, supporting EDW, and our historic wins.
- 5:10 pm: Acknowledge all new members in attendance and have them answer questions.
- 5:30 pm: Guests resume mingling.
- 6:00 pm: Event ends.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., publicly posted the voting schedule on Nov. 10, which indicated the vote on the impeachment articles he introduced would take place at 5:30 p.m. (archived).
According to Drop Site's reporting, the event took place at Goldfinch Social, a venue in Washington, D.C., about 2 miles from the Capitol.

Instagram is beginning to roll out a “content protection” feature that lets creators see and review copies of their videos posted to the platform.
Instagram is helping creators crack down on copycat videos
Meta will let creators decide to hide copies of their videos flagged by a new ‘content protection’ feature.
“For eligible creators who enroll, content protection is a tool that automatically looks out for visual matches of your original videos, alerts you when we find a match across Instagram and Facebook, and lets you decide what happens next,” Meta says in a blog post. Meta launched a similar tool for Facebook last year to help users “safeguard” their Reels and “maintain control” over their creative work.
When an Instagram creator is notified of a matched video, they can see how many views the match has and decide if they want to track the video, hide it from everyone on Instagram and Facebook, add a credit link, or release their claim on the match.
After a creator enrolls, every “original video” they post on Instagram is protected, and creators can retroactively protect older videos manually. Creators can also put accounts on an allow list that lets them use their videos.
In addition, Instagram will start flagging AI-generated videos that “match the spoken words” in a creator’s original video but have visuals replaced with AI. Initially, Instagram will test this with a “small group of creators” in “the coming weeks.” The platform says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that “use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly.”

On a summer day in 1992, a man dumped a cooler full of a fish called yellow perch into Lake Mary Ronan, in northwest Montana.
Why do people keep dumping buckets of fish into Montana’s lakes?
Guerilla ecology is incredibly easy. It also has disastrous consequences.
We know this because two teenagers saw him do it; they wrote down his license plate number and called in a tip to the Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks department (FWP), which immediately dispatched biologists to capture and kill the perch with nets and poison.
The teenagers got a reward of $500 each for their efforts, while the man was charged with illegally introducing non-native fish into the lake, slapped with a small fine, and sent on his way. The law changed soon after: Now, intentionally introducing a non-native, invasive species to Montana’s waters is a felony punishable by as long as two years in prison or a fine of up to $25,000, or both.
Why I wrote about this
I visited Flathead Lake Biological Station in October, and while I was there I heard from a biologist about this strange, totally avoidable, invisible catastrophe in the making. I was absolutely fascinated — as I looked at the lake, I hardly believed it could lose its signature clarity because of a bucketful of fish — and decided I had no choice but to open this can of worms.
But the perch? The yellow perch — at least two of them — survived, multiplied, and quickly went on to wreak havoc. They established dominance in the lake, wiping out its population of a native fish called the Westslope Cutthroat trout and causing other ecosystem disruptions. This hasn’t only happened here: Montana is filled with thousands of beautiful alpine lakes and rivers, nestled in the sort of rugged territory that sold people on the idea of the West. Yet, across the state, without permission, people keep dumping non-native fish into them.
The reason is simple: The introduced fish, according to some anglers, are more fun to fish than the stuff that’s already swimming around in Montana’s waters. But this guerrilla ecology — or “bucket biology” as some call it — risks upending delicate, longstanding ecosystems, harming not only native fish, but also animals that depend on them, like bald eagles, bears, and otters. It could turn Montana’s pristine waters into murky messes that also require millions of dollars in cleanup and additional maintenance every year.
And it’s not just a problem in Montana. Across the country, states are trying to stop people from filling lakes with fish that don’t belong. It’s a high-stakes issue with ramifications that can reach far beyond the underwater neighborhood of a single lake; efforts to stop illegal fish-dumping have now spawned everything from high-dollar bounties and dedicated fish forensics.
“A decision made by one person can affect an entire interconnected ecosystem,” said Craig Barfoot, Fisheries Program Manager for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes (CSKT), which is based on the Flathead Reservation in northwestern Montana and oversees some of the most pristine aquatic habitats in the state. “It’s like an act of arson.”
The power of a bucket
Flathead Lake, about an hour’s drive south of Glacier National Park, is the sort of place postcards were made for. The 27-mile-long lake, half within the Flathead Reservation (and overseen by the tribes) and half managed by the state, is one of the cleanest, clearest lakes in the populated world — a survey last year found that the lake is clear down to about 36 feet — which draws all sorts of creatures to its shore. During a two-day visit in October, I saw a black bear ambling along the shore and a bald eagle sitting in a tree, tearing into a fish it had scooped out of the water.
This massive glacial lake “was ice about 15,000 years ago,” said Tom Bansak, associate director of the Flathead Lake Bio Station, a research station in the lake that’s run by the University of Montana. “Before western contact, there were maybe eight to 10 species of fish in the lake, which is not very many for a lake of its size.”
That changed starting in the late 1800s, when wildlife managers at the federal and state levels decided to start stocking lakes around the country with fish that were raised in hatcheries and released into the water for recreational fishing. For decades, states mostly made stocking decisions based not on local ecologies but rather on the kinds of fish people wanted to catch, filling them with nonnative fish like trout, bass, walleye, and pike. If you live in the United States, there’s a good chance the closest popular fishing spot is filled with stocked fish; at Flathead Lake, wildlife managers introduced around 30 different kinds of non-native fish, of which about a dozen established spawning populations, and today non-native fish outnumber native ones.
Eventually, state wildlife agencies began to realize that this sort of recreation-driven stocking can harm local ecosystems: In the 1970s, for example, Montana decided to stop stocking non-native fish in most of its streams and rivers. It still stocks plenty of fish, though, including a few non-native species, in some of its lakes and reservoirs, as do most other states.
For some people, however, that’s not enough. Some anglers believe the fish native to Montana, like bull trout, cutthroat trout, and sturgeon, just aren’t as fun to catch or as tasty to eat as, say, northern pike and walleye — both of which have been illegally introduced to the state’s waters in recent years.
Enter the bucket biologists. It can take as little as a bucketful of fish to alter the population of an entire lake, which means that if someone is bored of the fishing options at their local lake, they could unilaterally decide to spice things up with little risk of getting caught. Despite nonnative fish introductions now being a felony in Montana (and at least four other states), not a single person has been charged, let alone convicted there; that man the two teens saw at Lake Mary Ronan more than 30 years ago is the only person to have ever even been reported.
“People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.”
— Sam Bourret, FWP Fisheries biologist
But fish and wildlife officials know it’s still happening because they keep finding non-native fish in the state’s waterways, and the most likely way they got there is by someone illegally dumping them in.
”They’re obviously avid anglers, and we probably know them,” said Sam Bourret, a fisheries biologist at FWP based near Flathead Lake. Investigating illegal fish introductions is Bourret’s speciality: The Great Falls Tribune called him the “fish detective” for pioneering a forensic technique that looks at chemical clues inside otoliths, fishes’ stone-like ear bones, to figure out where they might have come from. He’s also used data modeling based on conditions like elevation and fishing pressure to figure out which lakes might be most vulnerable to future fish introductions, which could help steer resources towards them and stop would-be bucket biologists. From his time on the job, which has included many firsthand interactions with anglers, he can tell many of them are irked that they can’t stock the fish they want wherever they want them. “I do think some of these people are spiteful in their desire to move fish around,” Bourret said. “People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.”
Sometimes the culprit is less intentional. Non-native fish that are kept in ponds on private property (which technically require permits to build and stock but often slip by under the radar) can get into nearby rivers or lakes if the pond overflows during a storm, or by being picked up by a bird and then dropped into another waterbody. Earlier this year, FWP biologists on Bourret’s team removed 4,000 goldfish from a pond at a hotel on the edge of Montana’s Thompson River; the pond had been an attraction for families visiting the hotel with small children, who liked to scoop fish out of the water with nets. But goldfish can be disastrous for freshwater ecosystems, and the FWP wanted to be sure they wouldn’t slip into the adjacent river — and from there into a nearby lake.
But they often don’t get so far ahead of a potential problem. “Introduced fish probably go undetected often,” Bourret said. “We usually find out about them through a needle in a haystack catch. Once a population sets up in a lake, it’s already way too late.”
Fish-shaped dominoes
Monitoring species in the underwater realm of rivers, lakes, and streams is vastly more challenging than it is on land. “It’s a lot more obvious when a terrestrial animal doesn’t belong,” says Andrew Gilham, Fisheries Management Bureau Chief at FWP. “If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird. But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.”
And that may even play into the general public’s understanding of just how much impact a few fish can have. “Some of it may just be that they don’t really understand the consequences that can follow illegal introductions,” he said.
Aquatic ecosystems are delicate balances, and in a healthy lake the populations of fish, predators, and small organisms like zooplankton and phytoplankton typically exist in a hard-won equilibrium. To simplify greatly, there are usually enough zooplankton to eat phytoplankton and prevent algal blooms, enough zooplankton-eating fish to prevent the zooplankton from eating all the phytoplankton, and enough predators to keep those zooplankton-eating fish in check — but not so many that the smaller fish get wiped out.
“If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird. But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.”
— Andrew Gilham, Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks
Bucket biology, especially with voracious carnivores like pike, is a bit like tossing a fish-shaped grenade into the lake. If the newcomers establish a spawning population, they can compete for resources with the native fish or eat them directly, eventually causing something called a trophic cascade: a domino-like series of events that can upend an entire ecosystem.
What happens to fish in a lake can have huge effects on the creatures outside of it, too. In the Yellowstone region, Yellowstone Lake had long been home to a native fish species called the cutthroat trout. These fish would make long, winding spawning migrations through the Yellowstone lake and river system, where some four mammal species and 16 bird species — bears, otters, eagles, and pelicans, among others — would pluck them out of the water for meals. The migrating cutthroat were also important vectors for nutrients, which came from the fish’s poop and were important food sources for plants and algae growing in and along the waterways.
But then, in the 1990s, a non-native species arrived (likely through an illegal introduction): lake trout. Lake trout eat cutthroat, and without any predators of their own, they could feast on the smaller fish without anything to stop them. Once the lake trout appeared in Yellowstone Lake, they decimated cutthroat populations; according to a report from the National Park Service, by 1998, there were some 125,000 lake trout in the lake, and they ate somewhere between 3 and 4 million cutthroat that year.
Zooplankton in the lake, which the cutthroat used to eat, had a population boom, which led to a decline in phytoplankton. And the lake trout just stayed in the lake rather than migrating through the rivers and streams like the cutthroat did, which not only robbed those waters of the additional nutrients they brought, but also took a of a high-impact food source away from bears, otters, and birds. Bear and otter activity alongside the streams declined; while bears are opportunistic feeders and likely found another food source, the otters probably had a harder time finding something to supplement their diets. Bald eagle nests saw a sharp decline in their success rates after cutthroat disappeared, and osprey nest counts fell from 60 in 2001 to 3-5 from 2008-2015.
“We don’t want to just be moving things around willy-nilly,” said Niall Clancy, director of the Fisheries Lab at Salish Kootenai College. “Because one thing we learned is that we are bad at predicting the impacts — and there’s a good chance that something will go wrong that we didn’t think of.”
And, Clancy added, these sorts of introductions can cause financial cascades alongside trophic ones: FWP now spends millions of dollars each year to reduce invasive fish populations in the state’s lakes and boost native fish populations through hatchery programs. This, in turn, diverts money away from other programs.
Can the buckets be stopped?
Stopping illegal fish introductions is a nearly impossible task; catching someone red-handed would require vigilantly monitoring thousands and thousands of miles of shoreline in Montana. Instead, FWP and groups like the CSKT are investing in things like an educational outreach program and signs along popular waterfronts that exhort people not to dump live fish, warning that doing so is a felony.
FWP has also teamed up with groups like Trout Unlimited, a nonprofit that advocates for fish and waterway conservation, to offer massive rewards for information on bucket biologists. In 2017, for example, they offered a reward of over $35,000 for information related to the illegal introduction of walleye in Swan Lake, a lake about eight miles east of Flathead as the crow flies. But even the promise of a big reward hasn’t worked, and nobody has come forward yet. Instead, FWP declared open season on invasive fish like brown trout and walleye, requiring that anyone who catches one of the fish kill it rather than toss it back into the water, and then bring the entire fish into a FWP office so that biologists can study it. Biologists at FWP are also exploring other solutions like following the lead of Washington state in introducing sterile non-native fish to lakes. This would reduce the populations of non-native fish by tricking fertile ones into wasting their mating efforts on fish that will never be able to reproduce.
For the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, the issue goes beyond the science.
“We have stories about the native bull trout and the native West Oak cutthroat going back to before colonization,” said Rich Janssen, head of the CSKT’s department of natural resources. “They’re part of our heritage and our culture, and when they’re gone, they’re gone. It’s like losing our language.”
At Flathead Lake, the lower half of which is in the Flathead Reservation, the fish that were introduced through earlier federal and state stocking programs largely settled into a state of coexistence with the native fish. That doesn’t mean they were completely harmless, however: They competed for resources with the bull trout and cutthroat, which led to a reduction in those fish. Today, the CSKT has placed restrictions on bull trout and cutthroat fishing, banning people from taking those fish except for religious reasons, and has stepped up efforts to proactively monitor for new non-native fish at Flathead Lake. They’ve also removed fishing restrictions for smallmouth bass and northern pike in tribal waters. Both species were illegally introduced to the lake and can not only outcompete the bull trout and cutthroat but eat them outright, so anglers are now welcome to take as many of those non-native fish out of the water as they’d like.
“They’re part of our heritage and our culture, and when they’re gone, they’re gone. It’s like losing our language.”
— Rich Janssen, Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes
When I went for a swim in Flathead Lake this fall, the water was startlingly clear and calm, the surface broken every now and then by ripples from a passing fish or insect. But farther north, where the Flathead River meets the lake, a gauntlet of hungry pike lay in wait for bull trout making their way upriver to spawn. And as cold as the water was — it is a glacial lake, after all — it has also been warming with climate change, creating more pockets of warmer water for smallmouth bass to spawn in and shrinking the cold-water areas that the bull and cutthroat trout like.
I waved at a passing motorboat, which had a fishing pole stuck into a holder on its side. More and more people have been moving to Montana in recent years, attracted by the rugged nature and the allure of the West; new houses and docks have sprung up along Flathead Lake’s shoreline. But much like the pike and bass, their presence has been putting more pressure on the local landscape, and the newcomers could make the problem worse if they decide Montana’s fish aren’t as good as what they have back home. The future of the lake, and many others like it across the country, is murky. What it will look like depends, in large part, on what people decide to do with their buckets.

An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.
Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.
“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.
The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.
The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.
“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.
Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

A video showing people vandalising and fighting inside a restaurant is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows an incident in West Bengal, where RSS workers allegedly created a ruckus and vandalised the restaurant when asked to pay for their food. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS workers vandalising a restaurant in West Bengal after being asked to pay for their food.
Fact: The video shows an incident at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Dhaka, Bangladesh, where a group of people vandalised the premises following a dispute over seating arrangements. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved in the attack. The incident has no connection to RSS workers or West Bengal. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same video. According to these reports, the incident took place at Durbin Bangla Restaurant in Mohakhali, Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 13 November 2026. The incident reportedly began with an argument over seating arrangements between a customer and restaurant staff. According to the restaurant owner, a young man took a seat that a family was already waiting for. When a staff member intervened, the young man left but later returned with others and assaulted an employee named Khalil outside the restaurant. The group then vandalised the restaurant, damaging furniture and other items. The incident caused panic among customers and left several people injured. Police visited the spot and said they were examining CCTV footage to identify those involved and take legal action. The restaurant authorities alleged that students of Government Titumir College were involved, an allegation that police said they were investigating (here, here, and here).
The restaurant is located in the Mohakhali area of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Photos of the restaurant available on Google Maps match the visuals in the viral video, confirming that the incident took place in Bangladesh and not West Bengal.
To sum up, the video of a ruckus at a restaurant in Bangladesh is being shared as RSS workers’ hooliganism at a restaurant in West Bengal.

Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.
This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions.
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.
As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.
Fighting food insecurity
Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.
Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.
Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.
Forward momentum
Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “Eat Real Food.”
But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.
In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually.
Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.
Food is medicine in our local community
Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.
One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.
For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
What other researchers have found
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security.
Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels. This data supports our own previous findings.
However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.
Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.
Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
Meagen Rosenthal, University of Mississippi and Natalie Minton, University of Mississippi

At 2:20 p.m. Eastern time Nov. 17, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and Federal Communications Commission plan to conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, which was announced in September.
According to some posts on social media, however, the test will be followed by a catastrophic 90-day electric and/or Internet blackout, plunging the world into darkness and chaos.
The claim may have felt unusually plausible, given several large failures in digital and physical infrastructure in the days leading up to the test — a Microsoft Outlook outage Nov. 12, a nationwide aircraft ground stop Nov. 13 due to a failure in telecommunication infrastructure, and software outages at several major banks on Nov. 16.
Add to that the curious claim that a 2023 episode of "The Simpsons," the long-running animated TV show somewhat notorious for predicting the future, featured a plot centered around a global blackout that began on Nov. 17. It all seemed to line up.
Snopes readers contacted us ahead of the Nov. 17 emergency alert test, asking for a review of these rumors.
We reached out to FEMA, the FCC and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency for comment on the rumor, asking about the agencies' involvement in the EAS test and the nation's protections against attacks on Internet and electric infrastructure. None of them replied to us by the time of publication.
As with all predictions of cataclysmic events, though, we urge readers to take this one with a grain of salt. There is no evidence indicating that a 90-day blackout will follow the nationwide EAS test, for any of the countless reasons posed online — be it a grand plan from the government, a targeted cybersecurity attack or just because "The Simpsons" said so.
Because Snopes requires substantial evidence to rate a story, however, and we can neither predict nor travel into the future, we're leaving this claim unrated until Nov. 17 has come and gone.
The EAS test
FEMA, in coordination with the FCC, is required by law to conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System at least once every three years, according to its website. The last nationwide test of the EAS, familiar to many Americans as the loud, warbling "beep beep beep" that comes on TV or radio before a severe weather warning or an Amber Alert, occurred Oct. 4, 2023.
In the 2023 test, FEMA and the FCC also sent test emergency alerts to cellphones. However, FEMA's webpage says it will not be testing cellphone alerts this time around. The agency also noted that it may reschedule the test if an actual emergency or severe weather happens Nov. 17. The backup test would be conducted Dec. 3.
No information about the test suggests that any sort of digital blackout will follow, for any reason. If the supposed blackout is supposed to be an act of sabotage by a foreign adversary, why would they have announced the attack beforehand? If the supposed blackout was planned by the United States government, meanwhile, why would it have neglected to warn everyone beforehand through official channels?
The 'Simpsons' episode
As for "The Simpsons" — Snopes has covered many claims implying that the sitcom predicted this or that future event.
The show's oracular reputation grew out of the few times where an absurd plot device ended up being a spot-on prediction, as perhaps most famously happened in a 2000 episode in which Lisa Simpson becomes president and inherits a budget crisis from Donald Trump. (Notably, Trump briefly considered running as the Reform Party's nominee in that year's presidential election.)
We chalk it up to the show's longevity — more than 850 episodes over 38 seasons — above anything else. "The Simpsons" routinely satirizes current real-world events, so given enough opportunities, it's unsurprising the writers occasionally come off as having the gift of prophecy.
In this case, the episode, titled "It's a Blunderful Life," was real, and did feature a plot based around a blackout starting on Nov. 17. Beyond that, the episode's plot bore no resemblance to the claim at hand.
The episode aired Nov. 19, 2023, as the sitcom's Thanksgiving special. It begins decades into the future, as the Simpson family sits down to eat Thanksgiving dinner and Lisa tells everyone to light a candle in remembrance. When asked why by her grandchild, Lisa recounts that a "great blackout" nearly destroyed Springfield. She opens a diary labeled "Apocalyptic Memories" to Nov. 17 (no year is given), and begins explaining as the camera cuts to a shot of the Simpson home "six days before Thanksgiving."
But, there's a problem for the fantasists here — Thanksgiving isn't on the same day each year. In 2023, when the episode aired, Thanksgiving fell on Nov. 23, conveniently, six days after Nov. 17. In 2026, however, Thanksgiving is on Nov. 26, meaning that if the year in the episode truly was 2026, Lisa should have opened the diary to Nov. 20 (i.e., six days before). Sorry to spoil anyone's doomsday prepping.
For more reading, we also previously explained a recent surge in government messaging around emergency preparedness, and a Department of Defense initiative that aims to keep military bases operational for at least 90 days without relying on civilian infrastructure.

The World Health Organisation warned on Friday (November 13, 2026) of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.
“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.
Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza’s population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the “Yellow Line” — a demarcation established under October’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire.
“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where of course the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Ms. Van De Weerdt explained.
The Israeli military told Reuters the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law, and are not intended to harm the civilian population.
“The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs launched the winterisation plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.
Last week COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organisations.
Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.
“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come,” Ms. Van De Weerdt said.
Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.
The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mould and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.
While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.
“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today, so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.“
COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organisations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators, and other equipment have entered Gaza.

In Europe, an Emboldened Iran Contributes to a Sense of Anxiety
Prosecutors and government officials believe Iran or its proxies are behind a series of security breaches and threats in Britain and Europe, unsettling the region.
On Veterans Day this past week, President Trump declared that his decision to go to war with Iran had been a complete success.
“When this conflict is over, and it will be soon,” he said, speaking on a blustery morning from Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington, “the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place.”
That is not how it feels in Europe.
A growing number of attempted terrorist attacks across the continent and in Britain, including a foiled plot against a major American military base, arson attacks on Jewish community sites and cyberattacks that raised temperatures in refrigerators and blood banks are rattling national security officials and unnerving the public. Many have been attributed to Iran or to proxies acting on its behalf.
The sense of global unease was heightened when the U.S. government grounded all air travel for hours on Friday in what officials later said was a technical issue.
European residents had already grown frustrated before the most recent round of turmoil. The economic consequences of the war that Mr. Trump and the Israeli government started against Iran in February have piled up: Gas prices are higher because of disruptions of oil deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz. Groceries cost more. Heating homes in winter has become far less affordable.
And in recent weeks, the effect has grown darker as security officials have accused Iran or its proxies of conducting a series of terrorism-related plots. In September, U.S. prosecutors say, an Iraqi man, an Iranian operative and a senior operative for an Iran proxy group in a New York jail plotted to attack R.A.F. Fairford, an air base in England used by American bombers. They did not succeed, but the effort prompted a major security incident.
