Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
- Published
Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.
But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".
This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.
"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.
"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."
But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.
Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.
Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.
Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.
He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.
He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.
"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."
Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."
"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."
He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.
"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."
But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".
"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.
Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.
Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.
"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."
During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.
Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.
But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.
"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."
Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.
Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.
The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.
Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.
Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.
One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".
He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.
"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.
"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."
He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.
Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.
"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.
There are difficult moments too.
Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.
"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."
The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.
"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."
Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.
One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.
Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.
He acknowledges these criticisms.
"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."
Of course, there is no guarantee.
Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.
"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."
According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.
But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says.
"They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.
Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “number one terrorist” in protests held on Monday.
Demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.
Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon, and public holidays instituted for the Asean summit.
Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The backlash against Trump follows the ouster of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include businessman Elon Musk.
Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said.
“Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 120km from Manila.
Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 25 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty Philippines said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” director Ritz Lee Santos III said.
“Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

The US Supreme Court dealt President Donald Trump a setback in his drive to cancel billions of dollars in federal grants, leaving intact a ruling that the administration was probably acting illegally by targeting research projects he said were “DEI programs.”
With no noted dissents on Monday, the justices rejected an appeal by the administration in a clash with faculty members and researchers at the University of California.
The rebuff keeps in place a federal appeals court ruling that for now requires the National Science Foundation and National Endowment for the Humanities to continue funding $59 million in grants. The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals said Trump probably violated the Constitution’s free speech clause by discriminating against the grantees because of their viewpoints.
“It means that the 9th Circuit ruling stands and all of the grants that were cut off based on the perceived viewpoint of the research must continue to be restored,” said Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the University of California’s Berkeley Law and the lead lawyer for the researchers. He said the appeals court ruling would also serve as an “important precedent” for other court’s around around the country.
Even so, the high court’s sidestepping of the case leaves unanswered questions about a controversy that raged during Trump’s first months in office last year. Trump directed agencies to terminate grants that involved diversity, equity and inclusion, as well as “gender ideology” and “environmental justice.”
The Justice Department said it will “continue to advocate for the executive branch’s lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives.”
In its appeal, the Trump administration contended that the Constitution lets the government choose to fund only those projects that align with its perspective. US Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the ruling by the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals would “hamstring every future administration” if not reversed.
“The First Amendment provides the government significant flexibility when it acts as patron to subsidize speech,” argued Sauer, the administration’s top courtroom lawyer. “The government may itself promote favored viewpoints, including by disbursing public funds to private entities.”
In rejecting the government, the 9th Circuit said the Supreme Court has distinguished between a decision not to fund a program at all and a rejection of particular applicants because of their views.
“Because the agencies’ termination of grants is aimed at the suppression of viewpoints with which the government disagrees, it likely violates the First Amendment,” the appeals court said in a 3-0 decision.
The University of California group urged the Supreme Court not to take up the case, saying the 9th Circuit applied “clearly established law.” The researchers said the blitz of terminations upended cutting-edge studies in science, medicine and other areas.
“The stakes for the researchers, and for the public that benefits from their work, could not be higher,” the group told the high court.
Much of the grant cancellation occurred under the direction of the Department of Government Efficiency, the Elon Musk-led effort that tore through the federal government last year, firing workers, dismantling agencies and canceling billions of dollars in spending. DOGE, as the office is known, claimed to have canceled $110 billion in grants and contracts, though the actual savings to the government might have been far less than that.
The administration drew criticism for the wholesale, and in at least some cases erratic, nature of the terminations. The New York Times reported in March that DOGE officials relied on ChatGPT to select which National Endowment for the Humanities grants to target.
In the University of California case, the researchers faulted the administration for relying on keywords, including “diversity,” to determine which grants were problematic. They say the approach scooped in projects with titles mentioning “Leaf Diversity” and “Diversity Within the Legume Rhizobia Mutualism.”
The case is Trump v. Thakur, 26-210.

Mangaluru/Bengaluru, Nov 17: An IndiGo flight from Mangaluru to Bengaluru aborted its take-off due to a technical issue, after which the aircraft returned to the bay and was later declared Aircraft on Ground (AOG), sources at the airport said on Tuesday.
All 229 passengers and seven crew members on board were safely deplaned, with no injuries reported.
The incident occurred around 6.05 pm at Mangaluru International Airport on Monday.
A replacement aircraft was arranged and only 34 of the 229 passengers travelled on the relief flight, which departed Mangaluru at 12.10 am on Tuesday.
According to an IndiGo spokesperson, a technical issue was detected shortly before take-off on flight 6E 388 on November 16.
Following standard operating procedures, the pilots returned the aircraft to the parking bay for necessary checks.
The aircraft had not become airborne. Some local reports stated that sparks were noticed beneath the aircraft during the take-off roll and that one tyre burst, prompting the pilot to apply brakes and halt the aircraft on the runway.
The airline's statement described the cause only as a technical issue under probe and did not independently confirm details of sparks or a tyre burst.
After a detailed technical inspection by the airline's engineering team, the aircraft was declared AOG, meaning it would remain grounded until repairs and certification were completed. Passengers were disembarked.
IndiGo arranged meals, refreshments, hotel accommodation, alternate connections and refunds as applicable. A replacement aircraft was arranged, the sources said.
According to sources at the airport, the aircraft had taxied normally and gained speed, but several tens of metres from the threshold, the pilot had brought the flight to a halt.
Former MP Nalin Kumar Kateel was among the passengers.
Local reports also named MLA Manjula S Aravind Limbavali and a judge among those on board. Several passengers were travelling via Bengaluru for connecting international flights.
In a press statement, IndiGo said a technical issue was detected, shortly before takeoff, on IndiGo flight 6E 388 operating from Mangaluru to Bengaluru on 16 November 2026.
"Following standard operating procedures, the pilots returned the aircraft to the parking bay for necessary checks. The aircraft will return to service after required maintenance and clearances. The relevant authorities were promptly informed," it said.
It added that customers were safely deplaned, and their teams did their best to minimise inconvenience by offering meals and refreshments.
"We also offered alternate connections, hotel accommodation, and full refunds to customers who opted for it, as applicable. We thank our customers for their patience and cooperation. As always, the safety of our customers, crew and aircraft is of the utmost importance to us," the Indigo spokesperson said.

Triumph or flop? The Rugby League World Cup that split opinion
- Published
Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not?
It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are.
The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear,, external to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement.
But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers.
For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final.
Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world.
England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early.
And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit.
"This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo.
"Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding.
"I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow."
That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.
Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though.
The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022.
That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.
For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant.
While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams., external
Viewer access to the World Cup has varied too. While Australia had free-to-air live television coverage, fans in the UK only got it for the wheelchair final, shown on BBC iPlayer. For all other games, they needed a Premier Sports subscription, which was also the only way to watch the tournament in North America.
With many matches staged at times when British and American viewers were likely to be in bed, it feels as if a chance to spread the game's gospel has been missed.
Festival feel or competitive balance? Or neither?
Many of the players at this World Cup were Australia-based, as they play club rugby in either the NRL's men's competition or its Women's Premiership.
That helped the International Rugby League - the world governing body - to keep costs down, after it spent a vast sum transporting players from the southern hemisphere to England four years ago.
Paring back the men's competition also helped on the costs front, though another supposed benefit - cutting out the lopsided group-stage scorelines of four years ago - has not been evident.
France and the Cook Islands both conceded more than 180 points in the group stage, while scoring a combined 58.
Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live earlier this month that the men's World Cup had suffered for being slimmed down - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy and Wales also missing out.
"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.
"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.
"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.
"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."
A format that contained no quarter-finals came in for widespread criticism from pundits, external before a ball was kicked.
The men's tournament featured one group of four and another of six. But two teams went through from both groups, and not everyone in the six-team pool played each other.
In the words of Castleford Tigers head coach Paul Rowley, the former England hooker: "It's trying to make a square with five sides." England captain George Williams, during the build-up, called the format "weird".
And England turned out to be the major losers. The draw left them with no margin for error as an underprepared and jet-lagged squad faced a dangerous Tonga side first up, and lost 30-12.
And ultimately, McDermott's side paid the price. Of the 26 teams across the three World Cups, only one side won two out of three group games and still failed to make the semi-finals: England's men.
- 'We got disrespected' - Walsh and Australia make World Cup point 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup 
  - Published11 hours ago
- Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup 
  - Published2 days ago
A growing audience?
An October and November tournament brings a different vibe depending on where you are. The last World Cup, in the UK, was staged as the temperatures dropped. This time around, it was held with co-hosts Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea heading towards summer.
Fans have gone to games in T-shirts and shorts instead of thick winter garments - and tellingly, average footfall increased.
That is despite the fact that the capacity 52,000 crowd in Brisbane for finals night was lower than the 67,000 at Old Trafford four years ago.
In 2022, the men's group stage - spanning 24 games - was watched by an average crowd of 9,811, itself down on the 14,345 figure from 2013, when England and Wales played hosts.
This time around, the average crowd rose to 21,360. It probably helped that there were fewer group games. It certainly helped that every Australia match was well attended, and that there was strong backing for New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga and Papua New Guinea, who played twice in their capital Port Moresby.
Lessons have also clearly been learned from 2022's heavily criticised ticket pricing structure.
Instead of adults paying more than £20 to attend matches, it has been a more friendly A$19, which equates to £9.74 per ticket.
But while attendances at this year's tournament are up, there is still work to be done around the women's game.
The sight of more empty seats than supporters in grounds for a number of double-headers is hardly a good look for the organisers or broadcasters.
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner notably raised the issue after her team defeated Samoa 40-0 in their Pool A opener at the home of Parramatta Eels on 16 October.
That match had followed Samoa's men thrashing France 78-4 - but in a stadium with a capacity of 30,000, many of the recorded 13,174 crowd had dispersed before the women's game got under way, with the stands appearing barely 20% full.
"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that.
"Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt."
Sadly for Skinner and her peerless team, it was a pattern that was repeated in Sunday's final, with the stands in Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium only filling as kick-off time for the men's game approached.
Northern hemisphere indifference?
Four years ago, the Rugby League World Cup was shown free-to-air in the UK by the BBC, with record-breaking viewing figures.
Almost 30 million people tuned in to watch the five-week extravaganza.
This time, the action has largely been behind a paywall. Premier Sports has shown all the World Cup matches live. The BBC showed the wheelchair final live, plus online highlights of selected games from all three tournaments.
In addition, it provided live radio coverage of all men's matches and some women's games, plus live text commentaries on selected games.
Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League - and not the Rugby Football League. Last month, IRL chair Troy Grant told the iPaper that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money - though no other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer either.
Former England international Jon Wilkin highlighted the issue during a BBC Radio 5 Live discussion at the start of this month, saying: "The World Cup should have been on the BBC.
"There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."
In response, a BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."
And therein lies a problem for the sport in the northern hemisphere, where more backing, more financial support and more coverage is needed to reverse the fortunes of the Super League and international teams largely bound to that competition.
The financial gulf to southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television deal over seven years in July.
Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around £21.5m per year.
Even with the pending announcement of a deal to bring NRL investment into Super League, that particular playing field is a long way from being levelled.
And it means that when the next World Cup comes around, Australia can expect to be favourites to win the men's and women's tournaments again.

Updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the new year.
The Best Planners
If you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.
The undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.
The covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.
If you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.
Hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.
I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.
I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely new planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.
I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and important things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the plan for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.
You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.
I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.
I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the new year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most important to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”
Academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the new year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.
Honorable Mentions
Like I said, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.
More Planners I’ve Tried
Agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.
Ban.do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) and the 2027 12-Month designs are now available.
Happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $33: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.
Laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners, at least for the Nancy design I tested previously. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did. I'm currently testing the 2027 Luna ($62) and Scout ($62) planners from Laurel Denise to see if I still feel the same way compared to the original design.
Leuchtturm1917 12-Month Ruled Planner for $29: This is a solid, minimalist planner that has a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple of lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.
Muji Undated Weekly Planner for $7: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.
Papier Hardcover 2027 Planner for $40: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid-year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style), but the academic one ($29) has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover academic planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid-year and academic layout options.
Passion Planner 2027 Planner for $50: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to plan out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.
Some Planner Accessories
Looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.
Passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.
Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson
Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!
Planner Alternatives
Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.
Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.
One of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.
FAQs
Why Choose a Paper Planner?
Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.
What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?
Paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to plan out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.
What Sizes Do Planners Come In?
Here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.
- A5 (5.8 by 8.3 inches)
- Regular/Medium / B5 (7 by 9 inches)
- Large/Letter (8.5 by 11 inches)
- Personal/Pocket (3.5 by 5.5 inches)

Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
- Published
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.
In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.
Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".
Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.
The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.
The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.
"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.
Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.
In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.
"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."
"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."
The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."
Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.
The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin.
Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.
For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.
Lost status
With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

After Decades of Blood and Mistrust, Doubts Over Who’s to Blame for an Israeli Hostage
Israeli spies kidnapped and killed Iranians. They were convinced that Tehran was to blame for a fallen airman. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.
Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.
As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.
He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.
As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.
What did he know about Ron Arad?
Mr. Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago, and the Israeli military says he is the only service member classified as missing in action. The government’s long search for him has captivated the public and has come to symbolize Israel’s commitment, rooted in Jewish tradition, to bringing its soldiers home, dead or alive. Articles, books and documentaries have been produced about the hunt for Mr. Arad.
The Israeli government was so determined to find him that, even four decades after his disappearance, it took the risk of kidnapping General Saberi in the shadow of his own embassy.

Manila, Nov 17: Amid the geopolitical tension, what the world needs today is peace, stability and predictability, Prime Minister Narendra Modi underlined at the ASEAN-India Summit, the East Asia Summit and the Quad Summit in Philippines, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri said on Tuesday.
Misri, in a briefing, said the prime minister has just completed a short but very intense visit to Manila, where he participated in the 23rd India-ASEAN Summit, the 21st East Asia Summit and the 7th Quad Leaders Summit.
At each of the three meetings, the prime minister underlined that in a world that has seen a great deal of geopolitical tension, flux and stresses and strains, what the world really needs today is peace, stability and predictability, Misri said.
Calling the Quad Summit a “very substantive and forward-looking meeting”, he said it reaffirmed the commitment of all four partners to a free and open Indo-Pacific and reaffirmed their commitment to advancing practical cooperation between themselves.

“The summit was also consistent with ASEAN centrality being held on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit and its outcomes build on the progress of the five Quad foreign ministers meetings that have taken place in the last roughly 20 months and the three foreign ministers’ meetings that have been held this year alone in Delhi, in Manila and in Atlanta,” he said.

“This is an exercise and an initiative that will take forward the existing cooperation between the Quad countries on maritime domain awareness. It will address shared challenges such as illegal fishing and trafficking,” Misri said.
The Quad leaders also announced a partnership for cable connectivity and resilience and emphasis was also placed on cyber cooperation between the Quad countries, Misri said.
The summit this time resulted in new practical tools that the leaders hoped would advance peace, stability and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific and for the benefit of the four Quad countries, Misri said.
“The mechanisms under the Quad will continue with meetings of the foreign ministers in the coming months as well as the other mechanisms under this leadership structure,” Misri said.

- The claim that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth awarded a commendation medal to a different person than the soldier who reprimanded his group Nov. 11 at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is unfounded.
- The rumor stems from social media users comparing a blurry image of one side of the soldier's face with a sharper frame from a video showing the other side of the soldier's face. Aside from the apparent asymmetricality, no evidence has been offered that the images — which differ greatly in angle, lighting and distance — show different men.
- A Pentagon spokesperson told Snopes, "As shown in the photos, Secretary Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."
On Nov. 11, video footage captured a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Virginia reprimanding Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his entourage after one of them talked and laughed out loud on the steps of the monument. The next day, Hegseth was photographed ostensibly awarding that same soldier a commendation medal in a Pentagon ceremony. 
Almost immediately, posts (archived) on X and Facebook popped up comparing images of the soldier taken at the tomb with one of Hegseth awarding him the medal in an apparent attempt to sow doubts it was the same person.
People claimed the sentinel's ears looked completely different in the two images and suggested the medal recipient was a body double. Several Snopes readers asked us if it was true Hegseth gave the medal to a doppelganger instead of the actual soldier.
(X user @JamesTate121)
The argument, as summarized in one post, went as follows:
Even though it's not the same side ears, most pairs of ears are pretty symmetrical. The details of the ear of the guy he gave the comm medal to, claiming it was the soldier who reprimanded his group, is totally different shape and physical attributes.
If it were true that most pairs of human ears are symmetrical, the argument might stand, but researchers say perfectly symmetrical facial features are the exception, not the rule. When you add to that the differences contributed by angle, lighting and distance in photographs, arguing that the appearance of asymmetricality, especially in photographs, is definitive proof that a pair of ears don't belong to the same person is bound to fail.
In the above collage, a blurry image of one side of a soldier's face is contrasted with a sharper frame from a video showing the other side of a soldier's face, and it's true they don't seem very symmetrical. Does that mean both ears can't belong to the same person? Not at all. Nor has any other evidence been offered to support the claim it isn't the same man in both photographs. The claim is therefore unfounded.
Snopes contacted the Department of Defense to confirm the identity of the soldier. A spokesperson responded, "As shown in the photos, Secretary Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."
As Snopes has previously reported, soldiers have guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington since March 1926. The Arlington National Cemetery website states that the guards initially "discouraged visitors from climbing or stepping on the Tomb." The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment has guarded the monument since April 6, 1948. Barbara Starr, CNN's former Pentagon correspondent, told the network (at 11:24) on Nov. 11 that sentinels correct any visitors who do not act with "respect and silence" at the tomb.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated numerous claims about Hegseth. Snopes has also covered many "body double" claims over the years.

The meme appeared to have used outdated census estimates for the population of Texas, which increased by nearly 2.5 million people between 2020 and 2025. Even still, Snopes could not replicate the meme's alleged findings.
After Democrats in Texas flipped control of the state House of Representatives and won the governorship during the 2026 midterm elections, a meme circulated suggesting there may have been election fraud in the historically Republican stronghold.
According to the meme, the number of registered voters exceeded the number of voting-age citizens in counties across the state. Several social media posts relayed the image, which showed a map of Texas' 254 counties, including on Instagram and Facebook. Some posts on X also shared the meme, including one that said "97 counties are over the adult-citizen count" (archived):
The meme claimed the counties in red had more registered voters than adult citizens, and the ones in yellow had at least 10% more registered voters than adult citizens. The image gave numbers for only six counties as evidence of its claim — Collin, Denton, Fort Bend, Montgomery, Parker and Williamson — saying that in each of them, the number of registered voters exceeded the number of adult citizens.
The meme cited as its sources the Texas secretary of state's November voter registration figures and Census 2020-24 adult citizen estimates.
We could find no evidence for the meme's claim. Using the most recent U.S. Census' adult citizen estimates (2024) in these counties and comparing them with the Texas secretary of state's numbers on voter registration per county, we could not replicate the image's alleged findings. For this reason, we rate the claim false.
The meme carried a watermark for the X account @_Patriot1776Q_. We reached out to the account asking for more information about the numbers and we will update this report should we receive a response.
It should be noted that Texas' population was the fastest-growing in the country between 2024 and 2026, and our calculations do not account for this growth due to the fact that the U.S. Census' most recent estimate for adult citizens is for 2024. (This also means that comparing the number of registered voters in 2026 to an older, smaller population estimate, as the meme claims to do, would be a flawed comparison.)
An attempt to replicate the meme's calculations
In January, the Redistricting and Voting Rights Data Office of the U.S. Census published its estimates for citizens of voting age by race and ethnicity for 2024. Snopes uploaded that data into a spreadsheet organized by state and county, with the six counties the meme mentioned highlighted them in yellow.
Next, we pulled data about registered voters and actual voters in each county in Texas. (To reflect population changes, we included July 2025 U.S. Census data and calculated the estimated number of adults, citizens and noncitizens combined, per county.)
We compiled the data for the six counties used in the meme and six more among those marked yellow — that is, counties where there were supposedly at least 10% more registered voters than adult citizens. Our calculations did not demonstrate the map's claim.
In an attempt to replicate the meme's numbers, we used the 2024 estimated number of adult citizens against the 2026 number of registered voters. For these numbers to be accurate and definitive, we would need to have 2026 actual numbers of adult citizens in these counties, as opposed to estimates.
For example, the meme said there were 34,319 more registered voters in 2026 in Montgomery County than there were registered adults based on 2020-2024 estimates. We found there were in fact 20,076 fewer adult citizens (based on the 2024 estimate) than there were registered adults in 2026.
The meme also said Parker County counted 111% registered voters relative to the number of estimated number of adult citizens. Our calculation found 108%. Once again, this number did not reflect the updated number of adult citizens in the county in 2026; Parker County is reportedly one of the fastest-growing counties in the nation.
Texas also places voters "in suspense" before removing them from the voter rolls when election officials believe a registered voter may have moved. This means that the number of registered voters reported for a county includes people who may no longer live in that county. Parker County, for example, had just under 9,000 voters in suspense in November, according to the state.
It also should be noted that voter turnout across Texas was roughly 50% in the 2026 midterms, and no county had more votes than adult citizens.
For further reading, Snopes also debunked the claim that Texas "found" 20 million votes to flip it to a Democratic majority.

Jeremiah Fears recorded his first career triple-double as the New Orleans Pelicans avenged a blowout loss in San Francisco last week with a 115-94 shellacking of the visiting Golden State Warriors on Monday.
Saddiq Bey tallied 10 of his team-high 23 points in a 23-2 game-opening run for the Pelicans, who had lost six in a row, including three straight to open a five-game homestand.

Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg put up 28 points and grabbed eight boards for the Warriors, who took their third loss in a row.

Apple's most expensive smartphone—the iPhone Duo—lacks one of the company's hallmark features: Face ID. The folding phone is already jam-packed with a hinge and multiple display layers, leaving no room for the TrueDepth sensor required for biometric face authentication. The Duo relies on Touch ID instead.
That's changing now in a software update. On Monday, Apple announced that it's bringing facial recognition to the iPhone Duo as part of the iOS 27.3 developer beta update. But since it can't rely on the tried-and-true Face ID system without those crucial components, it's borrowing the feature from the company's recently launched smart display, the HomeView.
The HomeView personalizes the display content for up to six people in a household, with its camera recognizing people who step in front of it. (It also uses voice data for recognition when someone asks Siri a command.) This “person recognition” technology is protected by the Secure Exclave—different from the Secure Enclave chip that houses Face ID data—a memory-protected space in Apple's A20 Pro processor. As WIRED's Lily Hay Newman writes, it's still not as comprehensive as Face ID, and could be more susceptible to attacks.
Rumors abound that Apple is racing to add proper Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo. Still, tight development cycles might mean the feature may not arrive until the third generation in 2028. That also points to limitations in the Duo's new face recognition tech.
You cannot use it to authenticate payments or unlock sensitive content, like your banking app. You'll still need your thumbprint or passcode to approve Apple Wallet purchases. Instead, it's designed to unlock the foldable without tapping a finger on the Touch ID sensor. There is also a time-based limitation. For face recognition to work, it needs a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication within a 45-minute window. This capability is also restricted to the front screen and camera—it doesn't work if the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Also in iOS 27.3, Apple has a new toggle that lets you lock your iPhone Duo when you close it.
Google's newer Pixel folding phones are the only ones on the US market with secure facial authentication, though it's not as effective in the dark as Apple's Face ID. Samsung's facial biometrics on its Galaxy phones aren't strong enough to protect sensitive content and are largely used to unlock the device.
Apple’s willingness to roll out a watered-down version of Face ID is a rare compromise for the company—and shows just how much of a friction point Touch ID has become for Duo owners.

Waymo self-driving taxis are no longer driving on highways after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its vehicles from state freeway operations. The ban, which the DMV says began on November 11, comes after the department determined that Waymo’s freeway driving poses “an imminent hazard to public safety.”
In response, Waymo says it has stopped highway driving in all of its markets. The company may continue testing its vehicles on non-California highways with safety operators behind the wheels.
The ban follows two recent concerning incidents, California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote in a statement. In one, three Waymos entered an active highway construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula. The other was captured in a viral video showing a Waymo vehicle interfering with California Highway Patrol cars on a San Francisco highway as they tried to enforce a “traffic break” as workers cleared debris from the crash.
Groveman said the California ban will remain in place until Waymo has proved that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies" that led to the incidents. It’s unclear how long that process will take.
In a written statement to WIRED, Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher said the company is “working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Waymo vehicles will continue to operate on surface streets in the 15 metros where it offers taxi service, including portions of Los Angeles, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.
This is the second time Waymo has publicly restricted its freeway operations after beginning to transport passengers on them last year. In June, the company recalled its software after federal regulators found that its system failed to recognize highway construction zones. Regulators with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) cited several incidents in April and May in which Waymo cars drove past ramp closure signs and into active lane closures. The events did not lead to collisions or injuries.
The NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Last week, the agency said it was examining whether another Waymo recall software fix had actually solved its robotaxis’ safety issues. This recall, which occurred last December, was tied to incidents in which Waymo cars repeatedly drove by stopped school buses with their lights on and/or stop arms extended.
Self-driving cars have struggled with construction zones for at least a decade. The zones can look and be arranged differently based on what sort of construction is being done, and where. While humans can easily understand bollards, placards, and blinking arrows, the lack of hard-and-fast rules has proven difficult to reliably program into driving software. The issue is especially hazardous at high freeway speeds, where workers exist alongside fast-moving car traffic.

War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
Environmentalists have long puzzled over a wide network of water projects lacking any obvious justification. Then their areas were targeted in airstrikes.
Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.
Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.
Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.
Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.
“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”
In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.
His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”
