A widespread outage at iPhone maker Apple has brought many of its services to a standstill for thousands of users globally. According to DownDetector, users began to experience issues with some of Apple’s services at 9:51 PM IST on November 17. As per the outage tracking website, many of the big tech giant’s online services were reporting issues, including Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music and Apple Support. Confirming the development, Apple’s systems update page noted that iCloud Mail, ‘Apple Care on Device’, and Apple School Manager were facing outages. Many users online also reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones. Apple has not publicly commented on the development so far. However, the company told Bloomberg the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement reportedly read. This follows a string of major outages at big tech giants. On November 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams went offline worldwide for more than 30 hours after several of Microsoft's servers became unexpectedly unavailable, placing additional pressure on the remaining infrastructure. Prior to this in April, AI giant OpenAI also faced a partial outage which has impacted operations of its chatbot, ChatGPT, and agentic coding platform Codex and API platform. In March too, the Sam Altman-led company was also hit by an outage that left ChatGPT unavailable for thousands of users. The outages have renewed concerns over enterprise dependence on a handful of providers, with experts flagging the need for stronger business continuity plans and multi-vendor redundancy. Given the recent surge in AI-driven cyberattacks, social media users continue to speculate the reason behind the outages. So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.

Opening its ₹2,500 Cr qualified institutional placement (QIP) for subscription today, Urban Company has outlined a ₹600 Cr investment plan to strengthen its 10-minute house help service, InstaHelp. The funds will be deployed in the quick household service arm in tranches over the next three years, majorly to fuel service professional minimum guarantee payments, service professional referral payouts, training and onboarding spends. The company expects to deploy ₹150 Cr in InstaHelp through FY27, ₹300 Cr in FY28, and ₹150 Cr in FY29. Rest of the QIP amount is set to be deployed as follows: ₹540 Cr for marketing ₹200 Cr for technology development and cloud infrastructure ₹85 Cr for office rent ₹50 Cr for R&D for its Native products. “Unorganised providers served approximately 90% of home-services spend in Fiscal Year 2026, organised offline players approximately 9% and online full-stack platforms approximately 0.9%. The online home-services industry is projected to grow at a CAGR of 19-25% to ₹12,000-15,000 Cr ($1.3-1.7 Bn) by Fiscal Year 2031,” the filing added. On the InstaHelp investment plans, the company outlined several risk factors on pouring in more cash in the bleed-heavy segment, where it locks horns with emerging players like Pronto and Snabbit. The segment recorded an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹174 Cr in the second quarter of FY27, up from ₹132 Cr in the preceding quarter. This is despite InstaHelp delivering over 1 Cr orders in the first half of the ongoing fiscal, generating about ₹124 Cr in net transaction value and just ₹31.8 Cr in revenue. Excluding InstaHelp, Urban Company’s adjusted EBITDA was ₹97.07 Cr in H1 FY27, while InstaHelp alone lost ₹305.96 Cr, up from ₹54.13 Cr a year ago. This is already above its ₹234.76 Cr loss for all of FY26. That puts InstaHelp’s loss at roughly three times the profit earned by everything else, leaving the company with a consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss of about ₹209 Cr for the half. Its average order value has gone down to ₹123 in the first half of FY27 from ₹165 in H1 FY26, highlighting reduction in the amount customers are paying per order. The company highlighted two major reasons— lower introductory prices and competitive intensity. In a gist, here are the key challenges Urban Company faces in scaling InstaHelp - Sustained losses: The consumer services giant expects InstaHelp to remain loss-making for some time as it continues to spend on acquiring service professionals, training, technology and marketing. It has also cautioned that there is no assurance of profitability within a specific timeframe. Uncertain path to profitability: The combination of high investments, operational challenges, competition and regulatory risks could affect InstaHelp's ability to scale and achieve profitability. Thus, expected returns from the company's investment in the segment. Scaling service supply: The company needs to build a large pool of service professionals and train them adequately to maintain consistent service quality. Amid this, supply may not scale at pace with consumer demand. Limited differentiation: InstaHelp offers relatively generic house-help services, which can also be provided by online and offline competitors. The market it is trying to crack has long been dominated by unorganised players. The segment has limited barriers to entry, making it difficult for the company to differentiate its offering in the short term. Safety and conduct risks: Service professionals enter consumers' homes daily, exposing the business to risks such as theft, property damage and inappropriate conduct. If any of such incidents occurs, Urban Company stands to lose out on brand marketability apart from litigation or regulatory scrutiny. Regulatory uncertainty: The Code on Social Security, 2020 and other regulations governing gig and platform workers, including state-level laws, could increase compliance costs or force Urban Company to change InstaHelp's business model. InstaHelp is directly competing with quick household help startups Snabbit and Pronto, who are also bidding to establish their names in the rapidly expanding market. Snabbit claims to fulfill over 35,000 daily orders and crossed 4 Mn home-help jobs during Q1 FY27. However, its FY26 financials underline the steep cost of building an instant home-services business. The startup reported operating revenue of ₹12.2 Cr, against total expenses of ₹194.8 Cr, translating into a net loss of ₹167.8 Cr. On the other hand, Pronto is exploring opportunities in the physical AI space after raising $45 Mn in a Series B funding round in May 2026. At the time, founder Anjali Sardana said the platform was processing 26,000 bookings a day but remained constrained by the availability of trained professionals. Meanwhile, Pronto founder Anjali Sardana has also launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based venture focused on building data, evaluation and deployment infrastructure for physical AI systems. As part of its effort towards it, Pronto launched Pronto Verified — an opt-in service where domestic workers wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras while performing tasks such as cleaning and dishwashing. Overall, the nascent quick home services offerings are gaining size in a $59 Bn home service market in India, as per an IBEF report. Shares of Urban Company ended today’s trading session 5.80% lower at ₹161.65 apiece on the BSE.

5 European countries want to start deporting migrants to Rwanda, despite concerns from human rights groups
Countries working with Rwanda to set up 'return hub' for migrants who don't have legal right to remain in EU
In one of his first acts as Britain's prime minister, Keir Starmer in 2024 quashed the U.K. government's controversial plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, saying it was "dead and buried before it started."
Now, five European countries are trying to resurrect a similar scheme.
Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced Monday that they are working with Rwanda to set up a "return hub" for migrants who do not have the legal right to remain in the European Union.
"We need to take back control of our borders," said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen during a joint news conference in Vienna. "What we are pushing for is a more sustainable and, I will also say, a more orderly asylum and migration system."
Those sent to Rwanda will be given the chance to integrate and settle there or another nation that grants them the legal right to stay — or return to their home country.
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at a joint news conference that the EU countries' Rwanda deportation hub plan would be a 'game changer' for illegal migration. (Helmut Fohringer/APA/AFP/Getty Images)
Mounting political pressure
The plan, which some EU officials have dubbed a "game changer," is part of a hardening stance toward asylum seekers. It comes as many European governments face growing pressure from voters and rival far-right political parties to show they can control migration.
In September, a regional election victory by Germany’s far-right, anti-immigration party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), was widely seen as a symbol of changing public sentiment toward migration.
Over the past few years, asylum claims in Europe have been dropping, and experts point to a combination of factors, including changes in government policy and the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in Syria in 2024. In 2023, there were more than a million first-time asylum applications. Last year, the annual figure dropped to just under 670,000, according to data from the European Union.
Migrants board a coast guard boat from a Frontex vessel, to be transferred to the port of Kaloi Limenes, following a rescue operation on the island of Crete, Greece, on Nov. 9. (Stefanos Rapanis/Reuters)
Britain's failed experiment
When Britain first unveiled its Rwanda partnership in 2022, then-prime minister Boris Johnson pitched it as necessary to stop boats full of asylum seekers from crossing the English Channel.
The year prior, there were nearly 50,000 asylum claims in the U.K.
Under the British plan, people could be sent to Rwanda while British authorities processed their asylum claims. Under the proposed European arrangement, the east-central African nation would only take in those whose asylum applications have already been rejected and who cannot be sent back to their home countries because of a lack of co-operation.
For Rwanda, proponents argue that the agreement presents an economic opportunity, and European officials are framing the country as an ideal place for a "second chance." Critics dispute that characterization, arguing Rwanda has a track record of repression. Amnesty International said that without scrutiny the Rwanda deal could become a "black hole for human rights."
Britain's then-home secretary Suella Braverman, left, and Rwanda's then-minister of infrastructure Ernest Nsabimana, right, lay bricks at a housing development for migrants in the Rwandan capital Kigali on March 19, 2023. Britain eventually scrapped a controversial plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda. (The Associated Press)
In a joint statement, 47 organizations urged the countries to scrap the Rwanda plan, arguing there are insufficient legal safeguards and no monitoring system to eliminate the risk of rights abuses.
In 2025 — two years after Britain's Supreme Court ruled the U.K.'s Rwanda plan unlawful — the U.S. struck its own deal with the country to accept up to 250 migrants.
No hard numbers
When European officials unveiled their agreement during Monday's news conference in Vienna, they said they hope to send the first people to Rwanda by the end of 2027, though they did not specify how many people in total would be sent there.
The five countries are billing the plan as a pilot project, insisting it will act as a deterrent to prevent people from travelling — sometimes thousands of kilometres — to reach Europe in the first place.
"As everybody knows, criminal organizations are making billions of euros on human smuggling, and too many lives are lost at sea," said Frederiksen. "We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders."
In her speech, Frederiksen said some European leaders have been working toward this kind of initiative for "eight or nine years."
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta says he believes that under the 'return hub' plan, asylum seekers in Europe may opt to return to their countries of origin without going through Rwanda at all. He added that Kigali was not planning for 'thousands' of people to stay in the east-central African nation. (Helmut Fohringer/APA/AFP/Getty Images)
New EU rule
The announcement of the Rwanda hub comes a month and a half after the Council of the European Union greenlit a new policy, the EU Return Regulation, which opened the door to setting up migrant hubs outside Europe.
The rules stipulate that unaccompanied minors cannot be deported and that hubs can only be created in countries that respect "international human rights and the principles of international law."
Clémentine de Montjoye, a senior researcher in the Africa division at Human Rights Watch, called the plan "utterly deplorable," in part because of what she calls a stunning contradiction.
Europe has repeatedly voiced concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record and its support for M23, an armed group accused of committing war crimes in the eastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
De Montjoye pointed out that Germany even reduced its aid to Rwanda last year because of its role in the conflict, which has displaced hundreds of thousands of people.
A bicycle taxi driver looks on while waiting for customers at a busy junction near a market in Kigali, on July 16, 2024. The east African nation is set to host a deportation hub for failed asylum seekers from five European countries. (Luis Tato/AFP/Getty Images)
Now, Germany and four other countries are trying to frame Rwanda as a land of opportunity.
"The question is: What kind of due diligence has been done by these five countries?" De Montjoye told CBC News from Nairobi, Kenya. "It's very concerning that the risk of human rights harms are being kind of swept under the carpet in order to present an image of coming up with solutions."
'Fig leaf' of deterrence
Outlining the motivations for creating the hub, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said European countries are hampered because countries of origin often do not co-operate when it comes to taking back rejected asylum seekers.
According to statistics from the Mixed Migration Centre, which operates under the Danish Refugee Council, only one in five people ordered to leave Europe actually do so.
A demonstrator holds a placard reading 'Stop EU-Rwanda-deal,' on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development on Monday in Vienna. (Radek Mica/AFP/Getty Images)
Roberto Forin, the centre's deputy director, says there is a need to manage migration in a more orderly way, but believes the Rwanda deal will act only as a "fig leaf" rather than a real deterrent.
He says smugglers will adapt, and asylum seekers who feel they have no alternative will continue to make risky journeys, even if the odds of being allowed to stay are lower.
"This is more about politics than migration policy," he told CBC News from Vienna. "Governments, actually across the political spectrum, have made a tough border as part of their promises to voters."

A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a six-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been sacked following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition -- which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on February 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity", the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was sacked and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui, a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies.

The much-anticipated crime thriller OM: Operation Mole, starring Dhanush and Mammootty, has completed its censor formalities ahead of its theatrical release. The film has been awarded a U/A certificate by the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), with its final runtime approved at 178 minutes, or 2 hours and 58 minutes. The film is scheduled to release worldwide on Friday, November 20, 2026.
Dhanush, Mammootty starrer OM: Operation Mole gets U/A certificate; runtime locked at 2 hours 58 minutes
Directed by Rajkumar Periasamy, best known for Amaran, the film marks Dhanush’s 55th outing as a lead actor. It was initially announced under the working title D55 and subsequently carried the title OM Chapter 1: Udhiram – The Blood Wood. The makers later unveiled its final title, OM: Operation Mole, along with the theatrical trailer earlier this month. With the certification process now complete, the film is gearing up for its release across Tamil, Telugu and Hindi markets.
Set in the dense forest regions of Andhra Pradesh, OM: Operation Mole revolves around a red sandalwood smuggling syndicate and an undercover police operation aimed at dismantling the network. Dhanush plays an undercover police officer who infiltrates the cartel, while Sai Pallavi portrays IPS officer Nithya Reddy, who leads the mission. Mammootty essays a pivotal role within the smuggling network, bringing the two leading actors together in a dramatic confrontation.
The film also features Sreeleela as Roja, Dhanush’s wife, alongside veteran actor Naseeruddin Shah and Malayalam actor Indrans. The project marks Naseeruddin Shah’s return to Tamil cinema after more than two decades.
Produced by Shraddha Agrawal, Dhanush and Azmat Jagmag under RTake Studios and Wunderbar Films, the film has music composed by Sai Abhyankkar. Ezhil Arasu K has handled cinematography, while R. Kalaivanan is credited with editing.
Initially planned for an October release, the film was moved to November 20. The revised date places OM: Operation Mole in theatres this weekend, with the makers having adjusted the release calendar to avoid clashes with major festive releases such as Jailer 2 and Scene.

Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
- Published
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there have been multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.
"Due to the threat of repeated shelling, emergency workers are constantly forced to periodically suspend work and retreat to a safe place," it added.
The DSNS said the death toll had risen to at least 72 people making it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".
He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.
BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.
Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.
A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.
While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Fears of second strike heard on police radios
Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.
The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.
Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.
Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.
His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.
Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.
International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.
Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".
Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.
Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

Do school cellphone bans work? New study says yes – but it's complicated
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students' reading and math achievement. Now, new research suggests putting students' phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses.
"Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year," says Harvard University's Tom Kane, one of the new study's co-authors. "It's been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak."
Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That's a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement.
"That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did," adds Dartmouth College's Douglas Staiger, another co-author.
The study's authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. It was a joint effort between Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth and NWEA, a K-12 testing and research organization.
Kane, Staiger and their teams analyzed a nationwide sample of more than 3 million elementary-, middle- and high-school students over the past five school years, comparing the test scores in schools that adopted phone pouches to the scores at similar schools that did not.
Not only did strict cellphone bans appear to trigger small learning gains, the researchers say, those gains didn't seem to fade out after the first year of implementation. Instead, Kane says, the gains appeared to continue, year after year – at least up to three years after adoption.
Research on phone bans is mix
Tuesday's headline finding, that locking phones during the school day led to small but statistically significant improvements in math and reading scores, comes with an important caveat:
A separate study, from April, found that these pouches had "close to zero" impact on student test scores – and if there was a benefit, it was not statistically significant.
"Overall, we didn't find evidence of meaningful achievement gains," says Brian Jacob, a co-author of that April study and a professor of education policy at the University of Michigan.
What should we make of these seemingly contradictory results?
Both are large-scale studies by well-respected teams of researchers. The April study has been peer-reviewed; the more recent study has not.
Both studies similarly focused on schools' adoption of lockable pouches made by the for-profit company Yondr. According to Tuesday's paper, more than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the '19-'20 and '25-'26 school years. Typically, schools that use the pouches require that students put their phones in them at the beginning of the day and don't get them back until the end of the school day, when the pouches are unlocked by a school administrator with a special magnetic device.
But the two studies also differ in key ways. The April study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while Tuesday's study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.
Simply put, the study released Tuesday had more fine-grain, student-level data, but the study released in April was able to examine a much larger sample of schools.
But the two studies' findings also aren't as different as they may seem. Jacob and his co-authors did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math. It's just that those gains were offset by ban-related learning losses in middle school.
Overall, Jacob says, the new study "is encouraging. And if [the benefit] really persists and accumulates over time, it really could be a meaningful benefit. I think we'll just have to wait and see if that happens."
Another co-author of that April study, Tom Dee, a professor at Stanford University's Graduate School of Education, says of Tuesday's findings, "I hope they are right that these very small test score gains will aggregate and add up over time. However, I'm not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans."
Taken together, Dee says, he considers the results from these early studies into cellphone bans "largely disappointing," and insists "we need continued study on this topic."
Kane sees the results differently. Even if the benefit is small, he argues, relative to the cost – roughly $25 per student – these pouches still make financial sense for schools. "That's still a lot less than having to pay teachers for an extra week or two of instruction."
When it all went wrong
For nearly a quarter-century, from 1990 to 2013, math achievement among fourth- and eighth-graders rose steadily. Reading scores also improved.
Then around 2013, student test scores began a sustained tumble that continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and has only recently begun to slow. For years, politicians and pundits blamed pandemic-era school closures for the losses, but the data tells a different story.
"Particularly in reading, test scores were going down for four to six years before the pandemic," Stanford University researcher Sean Reardon told NPR earlier this year. "In fact, you wouldn't really know there was a pandemic effect if you just looked at the last 10 or 12 years of test scores. There's been just a steady kind of decline regardless of the pandemic."
Which raises the question: What happened around 2013?
Possible explanations abound. The federal government began stepping back from holding schools accountable for low test scores. Many schools also saw funding cuts in the wake of the Great Recession.
This new study is the latest to make the case that the mass adoption of cell phones by children and teens also helped fuel those test score declines.
The researchers note that, in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did. And similar rates in other industrialized countries coincided with similar student achievement declines.
Now, Kane says, he wants to study students' smartphone and social media use outside of school.

Ronaldo, Maradona, Baggio - what happened to the World XI?
- Published
Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.
Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.
The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.
It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.
This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.
"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.
Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.
"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.
"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"
Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair were whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.
"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.
"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"
Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.
The 21-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.
"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.
"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'
"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.
"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"
Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.
"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.
"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"
When Maradona came to Wembley
This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.
They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.
But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.
Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around £250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.
"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.
"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.
"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."
Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.
"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"
'It wouldn't happen now'
One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.
Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.
Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.
But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.
"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning £100k a week.
"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.
"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."
Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.
"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.
"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.
"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.
"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."
In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.
"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.
"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.
"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

Following a terrorist attack on November 11 at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district, a video went viral on social media with the claim that retired Indian Army officer and journalist Pravin Sawhney described Indian military and counter-terrorism drives in the valley as “false flag operations”.
Social media users claimed that Sawhney said that operations against the Kulgam attack, the Balakot airstrikes, and Operation Sindoor were orchestrated for political gains.
X user @RedDeFactoIND (Red Vanguard) shared the viral clip, which shows an interview conducted by The Wire. (Archive)
𝗘𝘅-𝗔𝗿𝗺𝘆 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗕𝗼𝗺𝗯𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹🚨: Pravin Sawhney in Recent Interview for Wire said, “Another false flag, just like Pulwama and Pahalgam,This is a pattern”
Indian journalists and influencers are now openly questioning the government’s narrative.
The voices from within are getting louder.
#CRPFSoldiers #CRPFCampAttack #kulgamattack #Kulgam #KulgamTerrorAttack
— Red Vanguard (@RedDeFactoIND) November 12, 2026
In the viral clip, the interviewer can first be heard saying (translated from Hindi): “Sushant, I want to know from you…the theme of your latest essay is the politicisation of army…During the false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, the way the Bharatiya Janata Party used the military for political gains. My second question is that today while there is a war-like situation in the world…is testing the Pralay missile is an indication of a new false flag operation?”
“On one side China is occupying [Indian land], on the other there are CJP protests…Rahul Gandhi…,” the interviewer goes on to say before his voice is abruptly cut off.
The interviewee then seems to respond with, “Two things are very clear. One, for false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, Operation Sindoor was launched but the Indian army failed. Second, my answers are within your questions.”
Several other users on X and Facebook also circulated the same video with identical claims. Among them were X handles @KaurUdhoke3 and @HinduReformer, along with multiple public Facebook pages focusing on South Asian geopolitics. [Archives: 1, 2]
Fact Check
A closer look at the viral video reveals noticeable lip-sync discrepancies and an unnatural, monotonous cadence in the voices of both men in the interview, which are salient features of AI-generated audio manipulation.
Further, columnist and strategic affairs expert Sushant Singh has been misidentified in the viral video as Pravin Sawhney. In the viral video itself, the interviewer refers to the interviewee as Sushant, and not Pravin. Below is an image of Sawhney, who does not appear in the viral clip.
On November 13, Singh himself took to X to debunk the clip, clarifying that the video was AI-generated, and highlighting that users had also misidentified him.
This is AI generated video of an old interview, which completely fabricates my conversation with @ashubh. This Pakistan-made AI video clip not only gets my identity wrong but creates what was never said.
The original full interview of March 2025 is here: https://t.co/Y6teNLJDfg
— Sushant Singh (@SushantSin) November 13, 2026
In his post, Singh also attached a link to the original YouTube interview from which the visuals were taken. Alt News examined the original video uploaded on The Wire’s official YouTube channel in March 2025.
Comparing the viral clip with the March 2025 interview confirms that the visual frames, including Singh’s attire, the background setting, and lighting, are identical. However, the audio track in the viral clip has been changed using AI.
In the original interview, Singh makes no mention of Kulgam, Pulwama, Balakot, or any ‘false flag operations’. Instead, he is heard discussing civil-military relations and institutional oversight.
To sum up, a manipulated video of journalist and strategic affairs analyst Sushant Singh is circulating on social media with users misidentifying him as journalist and FORCE editor Pravin Sawhney. The claim that the speaker in the video termed India’s counter-terrorism measures in Kulgam and Pulwama ‘false flag operations’ is false as well.

The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved a new breast cancer drug from Roche, teeing up the launch of a medicine that the Swiss company has said could become its top-selling product ever.
The approval of Wilserdly, also known as giredestrant, was one of the most important regulatory decisions Roche had been awaiting. It also gives the company another foothold in breast cancer treatments, a field in which it has a storied history with the drug Herceptin through its subsidiary Genentech, though in recent years it’s fallen behind rival pharma companies in oncology.
The approval is specifically for patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that has picked up a mutation in the ESR1 gene, a sign that the tumor is developing resistance to standard treatments. The evERA trial showed that the drug, an oral treatment known as a selective estrogen receptor degrader, or SERD, extended the time period before patients’ tumors progressed.

Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
When doctors operated on Pope Leo XIV’s lung in October, some wondered if he’d postpone a long-planned trip to South America. It’s gone well so far.
Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss.
They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru.
Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap?
“It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.”
It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency.
The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members.

LED lights have become an everyday reality in homes, offices, public places and significantly, our screens. And while their energy efficiency is welcome, for many people, their increased use has led to eye discomfort: this includes sleep issues, a blinding sensation while driving at night, redness and watering. Ophthalmologists say this problem is on the rise and point to multiple factors behind it, including brightness levels, positioning of the light, its temperature, colour-tone, and flickering effects.
Apart from lighting up our homes and workplaces, LED lights are now in every gadget, including mobile phones, laptops as well as television sets. Constant exposure can cause mild to extreme visual discomfort, glare, eye strain, and even headaches for some people. This is a genuine visual concern experienced by many people, says Sugato Paul, consultant, ophthalmology at Manipal Hospital, Broadway, Kolkata. Dr Paul explains that discomfort is primarily associated with high luminance and excessive brightness. “Many cool-white LEDs have a relatively higher proportion of short-wavelength (blue) light, generally in the 400–500 nm range. This can increase the perception of brightness, contribute to visual discomfort and make certain individuals more susceptible to glare under specific circumstances,” he says.

‘Constructive and trusted’: PM Modi on Quad partnership at Manila Summit
The Quad leaders - PM Modi, US President Trump, Australian and Japanese PMs Anthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi - met in Manila on Tuesday.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday hailed the Quad grouping as a constructive and trusted partnership, saying that the four countries — Australia, India, Japan and United States — provides trusted solutions for the entire Indo-Pacific.
The Quad leaders, PM Modi, US President Donald Trump, Australian and Japanese Prime Ministers Anthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi, met in Manila on Tuesday.
The engagement marked the first Quad leaders-level meeting of Trump's current presidential term and comes amid efforts by the four countries to strengthen cooperation across the Indo-Pacific region.
..It gives me immense pleasure to meet you all. Manila and Quad have shared an age-old and special bond. In 2007, officials of the four countries met for the first time right here. 10 years after that in 2017, it was here in this city that we started our dialogue once again. Today, holding a Quad meeting once again in this historic city, marks an important milestone. Since January last year till date, our foreign ministers have met five times. This bears testimony to our political will and shared commitment towards our partnership...," PM Modi said in his statement at the Quad Summit in Manila, where US President Donald Trump was also present.
“From Maritime security to trusted supply chains, new technology to disaster response - it has been our endeavour that Quad provides trusted solutions for the entire Indo-Pacific,” he said.
'Modi very tough': Trump
PM Modi delivered his statement shortly after receiving a praise from US President Trump while posing for the leaders' group photo.
“We have a great relationship with these people, and these countries, and we have right from the beginning, I've been with all three of them for a long time, and they're phenomenal people, and they're friends of mine, so that helps. By the way, he's (PM Modi) a very tough man, just in case,” Trump told reporters.
The meeting is the first Quad leaders’ meeting since Donald Trump began his current presidential term. It comes as the four countries look to strengthen their cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region.
The meeting is being held in Manila alongside the ASEAN-related summits, which leaders from across the region are attending. The White House had listed it as the “Quad Leaders’ Meeting” in Trump’s official schedule.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had confirmed ahead of the meeting that Trump would attend the Quad engagement, along with the ASEAN and Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meetings.
“The fact that President Trump will be at ASEAN as well as at APEC, and that we’ll have a Quad Leaders’ Meeting as well,” Albanese had said.
He also spoke about Australia’s interest in reducing global conflicts and pointed to the economic impact of the war in Iran on countries across the region.
The meeting follows talks between Quad foreign ministers in Atlanta on October 31. At the meeting, the four countries agreed to step up cooperation in emerging technologies, critical minerals, maritime security and investment.
The ministers also announced plans to provide more than $85 million in technical and financial assistance to improve access to trusted artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific.
They also welcomed a $10 million commitment from the US to build facilities in India and ASEAN countries to recover critical minerals from waste.
On maritime security, the four countries stressed the need to keep key shipping routes, including the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, open for navigation. They also underlined the importance of ensuring the safe passage of commercial ships and their crews.
The last in-person Quad leaders’ summit was held in Wilmington, Delaware, on September 21, 2024, under former US President Joe Biden. The declaration issued after the meeting had said India would host the next leaders’ summit in 2025. It also reaffirmed the group’s commitment with the words, “The Quad is here to stay”.

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a new passport this week.
Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.
Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.
Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.
Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.
On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.
“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.
Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.
Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.
This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.
Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.
Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.
Despite the abuses and oppression that mired her 15 years in power and subsequent conviction for crimes against humanity, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.
Analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.
Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.
“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is based in India.
Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.
Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.
Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

My wife and I were driving back from a date night. She was talking about a friend's very expensive utility bill, but I had missed the beginning of what she said (I was driving, after all).
Then I remembered: Wait, I can ask Siri to remind me! At a traffic light, I double-tapped the digital crown on the Apple Watch, and Siri's new Live Rewind feature spun back the clock 15 seconds and showed me a transcript of what my wife said.
I sheepishly interrupted her to show her the transcript. “Look!” Her reply? “Why wouldn't you just ask me to repeat myself?” She shrugged at this new Apple Watch capability and continued talking.
A few days later, I was chatting with my brother on my stoop. Once again, I lost focus for a few seconds and remembered to ask Siri to help me recall what my brother said moments ago. But this time, before I excitedly showed my brother the Apple Watch screen, I preemptively said, “Yeah, I know I could just ask you to repeat yourself.” I got a perplexed look back.
Live Rewind, one of Apple's new Audio Intelligence features on its latest Apple Watches, is designed to give you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. It's in public beta in watchOS 27.3, but is expected to launch officially before the year's end.
Coming alongside it is another new capability called Siri Recap: Give the assistant permission to listen to your environment—you can set schedules or have it trigger when you reach the office—and you'll see a “Recap” in the Siri app at the end of the day. It’ll show you summaries of conversations and list out important details that people said. It's very similar to AI notetakers, many of which run on dedicated hardware devices.
The power here is that it all happens on your Apple Watch, the same device you wear everywhere to track your fitness, monitor health, and check notifications. That ubiquity is exactly what makes privacy advocates uneasy—they say features like these normalize ambient surveillance, much like smart glasses, undermining the privacy of bystanders who don't consent to being recorded.
“One of the concerns that we have with things like the Apple Watch is we don't know what the watch is picking up on,” Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at the nonprofit digital rights advocacy group Fight for the Future, tells WIRED. “Just because the device wearer is the one opting in to use the feature, you're not getting consent from everybody who you walk around.”
Apple has spent a great deal of effort explaining how the system works and how the company plans to maintain the privacy of its users and the people around them. First, these features are opt-in, and they are limited to the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4. They also require an iPhone 16 or newer with iOS 27 and Apple Intelligence. These features are not available for users under 18, and they currently work only in English.
For Live Rewind, the audio is processed on-device and cannot be accessed. When you activate it, a small chime plays from the Apple Watch that serves as a warning for folks nearby. Text disappears unless you choose to save it to Siri. For Recaps, Siri keeps them factual, doesn't identify speakers, and also omits content the system deems sensitive. If you don't save a Recap, it'll self-delete in seven days. Apple uses its Private Cloud Compute processing system for the data, which is never stored or logged on its servers. Data stored in the Siri app is end-to-end encrypted when syncing with iCloud.
Even if you're happy with Apple's privacy focus, I haven't found these capabilities tremendously useful over the past week. Live Rewind works well in moderately quiet environments, but the transcript can quickly turn into inaccurate gibberish when there's a lot of background noise.
Activating it in front of the person you're chatting with feels awkward. It comes across like pulling out your smartphone when someone's trying to talk to you—a little rude and distracting. Instead of keeping screens out of sight—a big digital detox trend—you're introducing one in the middle of a human conversation. I brought the topic up with my wife again, and she echoed some of those feelings, saying it felt like a feature that would stunt a person's social skills. Instead of asking someone to repeat themself, they're bringing an Apple Watch into the mix to fill in the gaps.
I am not saying it can't be helpful. When it works, it feels like a superpower. Maybe there are certain situations where you don't want to interrupt a group conversation and ask someone to repeat themself. Right now, though, there's the problem of remembering that this feature exists and remembering to use it. I have also found the 15-second rule a little too short, and it resulted in me missing parts of the conversation.
Recap has been a little more helpful. For testing purposes, I've set Siri to capture recaps all day, every day, but I like that you can create a custom schedule or have it trigger when you arrive at a specific location, like the office. You can manually turn Siri Recap on or off in the Apple Watch's Control Center. Most impressive is that, despite having Recap enabled constantly, I haven't seen a meaningful dip in battery life. I've continued charging the Apple Watch Series 12 after a day and a half.
One of the more perplexing things was opening the Siri app to look at my recaps and finding a bunch of conversations I had no recollection of having. Turns out, Siri was recording media I was watching, like on YouTube or Instagram. This is a problem I encountered with AI notetakers, like the Amazon-owned Bee AI wearable, which claimed to be working on “liveness detection” to solve it. Its latest hardware shipped with a feature where it doesn't record a conversation if it doesn't detect the wearer's voice within a set period. Hopefully, Apple can figure out a solution. For now, you can edit or delete these recaps.
One day, I forgot to record an interview (though I took notes), and I knew the person said something that I hadn't written down. I headed over to Siri and found exactly what I was looking for—paraphrased, but there. That said, the Recaps aren't designed to be detailed summaries and action plans from your meetings or conversations, unlike dedicated AI notetakers. They're meant to jog your memory. At times, I wish Siri were more detailed, but if that's what you're after, you'll have to invest in a third-party device.
Recap can be helpful for work meetings, but I haven't personally found it all that compelling in my personal life. Looking back at what it has picked up over conversations with friends and family, the only thing I feel is: Yep, those conversations happened. A friend was talking about their woodworking hobby—they can't use oil-based polyurethane as a finish in the winter months as it stays tacky. Siri logged this in such a matter-of-fact way, but when I revisited the conversation in the recap, I didn't find it helpful, useful, or interesting. (No offense, friend!) It's just nuggets of life.
Apple has pulled off impressive feats with these features, capturing these moments in a way that feels a little more privacy-preserving than competitors, without tanking the already limited battery life of its smartwatches. But socially, we're still figuring out what it means to walk around with always-on passive recorders. For now, I'm happy to stick with my wife's advice and ask: “Come again?”

GTA 6 takes players across the streets of Vice City and the wider Leonida region, so you will want your TV settings to do the game’s visuals justice. Whether you are playing on a PS5 or Xbox Series X, a few adjustments can improve picture quality, HDR accuracy, and controller response. So, go check out the best TV settings to play GTA 6.
- TV Settings to Change Before You Play GTA 6
- Best TV Settings for GTA 6 on PS5
- Best TV Settings for GTA 6 on Xbox
TV Settings to Change Before You Play GTA 6
Before launching GTA 6, you should adjust these settings on your Sony, LG, Samsung, or other TVs. These options help reduce input lag and improve color accuracy, shadows, and highlights.
With GTA 6 locations in Leonida being vibrant and colorful, you wouldn’t want things to look bland or over-tuned. Also, modern TVs come with multiple gaming features, so why not use them all?
Enable Game Mode
Game Mode is the first setting you should enable on your Smart TV. It reduces background image processing, which helps lower input lag and makes controller inputs feel more responsive.
Depending on your TV manufacturer, this option may have a different name:
- LG: Game Optimizer
- Samsung: Game Mode
- Sony: Game Mode
- TCL: Game Mode
If your TV supports Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), enable it or set it to Automatic. This allows your console to automatically switch the TV to low-latency mode when you start playing a video game.
You will find the Game Mode option under your TV settings. Remember, on most TVs, ALLM and Game Mode are only available when you are using the HDMI 1 port.
Turn Off Motion Smoothing
Turn off motion smoothing and frame interpolation features on your television. These settings create artificial frames between existing ones to make movement look smoother.
While motion can work well for movies and TV shows, it can add input lag when gaming. They can also make fast movements look unnatural. And with GTA 6 not releasing at 60 FPS, you wouldn’t want to force it to run at higher frame rates.
Here are some common motion smoothing options you should disable in your TV settings for a better GTA 6 experience:
- LG: TruMotion
- Samsung: Picture Clarity/ Motion Plus
- Sony: Motionflow
- Hisense: Motion Enhancement
- TCL: Motion Clarity/ Action Smoothing
Enable HGiG and Adjust HDR
HDR plays an important role in improving how the bright highlights and dark scenes look. This is especially useful for GTA 6 visuals, where you will travel between sunny Leonida Keys streets, neon-lit Vice City buildings, and dark interiors.
If your television supports HGiG (HDR Gaming Interest Group), enable it in the HDR picture settings. HGiG prevents the TV from applying additional dynamic tone mapping on top of the HDR calibration handled by your console.
You should also disable Dynamic Tone Mapping (DTM) if HGiG is available. Once you adjust these settings, use your console’s built-in HDR calibration tool to match the output to your television.
Adjust Color Temperature and Sharpness
For more natural-looking colors, set your TV’s color temperature to Warm or Warm 2. On some LG televisions, this option is available as Warm 50.
This setting provides a more accurate white balance and avoids the overly blue appearance that some default picture presets produce. If you want your GTA 6 map to look more vibrant, you can turn the tone a bit warmer, but it will make the overall look artificial.
As for sharpness, keep it at its neutral setting. Avoid adding extra sharpening, as it can introduce unwanted outlines around objects and buildings.
Turn Off Energy Saving
One of the best ways to make your TV run at full power is by turning off energy saver modes of any kind. Disable Energy Saving, Eco Mode, and automatic brightness adjustment features on your television.
These options can reduce screen brightness depending on the room’s lighting conditions. This can make it difficult to see details in darker scenes or maintain consistent HDR brightness.
You can adjust the brightness manually based on your room and TV panel instead.
Enable VRR and 120Hz Output
Thre Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) setting allows your TV to synchronize its refresh rate with the frames produced by your console. This helps reduce screen tearing and stuttering when a game’s frame rate fluctuates.
Set VRR to Automatic if your television supports it. You should also enable 120Hz Output to make sure your console can use these features when supported.
Best TV Settings for GTA 6 on PS5
After adjusting your TV, you should also optimize your PS5 settings for GTA 6 to make the most of its display features. Here are the recommended settings:
| PS5 Setting | Recommended Option | 
|---|---|
| Resolution | Automatic | 
| 120 Hz Output | Automatic | 
| VRR | Automatic | 
| Apply to Unsupported Games | Off | 
| HDR | On When Supported | 
| RGB Range | Automatic | 
| ALLM | Automatic | 
Best TV Settings for GTA 6 on Xbox
If you are playing not a PlayStation gamer, here are the Xbox settings for GTA 6 you must use to get better results on your TV:
| Xbox Setting | Recommended Option | 
|---|---|
| Resolution | 4K UHD | 
| Refresh Rate | 120Hz (if supported) | 
| Allow 4K | Enabled | 
| Allow HDR10 | Enabled | 
| Allow Variable Refresh Rate | Enabled, if supported | 
| Allow Auto Low Latency Mode | Enabled, if supported | 
| Color Space | Standard | 
These are all the TV settings you must utilize to get the best visuals and performance on GTA 6. What TV are you using to play the game? Let us know in the comments.
What are the best TV settings to play GTA 6?
Enable Game Mode, use an HDMI 2.1 port, turn off motion smoothing, and enable HGiG if your TV supports it. You should also calibrate HDR through your console for accurate brightness and contrast.
Is GTA 6 better on a TV or monitor?
A TV is a good choice if you prefer playing from a couch on a larger screen, while a gaming monitor is better suited to a desk setup.
Do you need an HDMI 2.1 TV to play GTA 6?
No, you can play GTA 6 on a television with HDMI 2.0 or any supported connections on PS5, PS5 Pro, and Xbox Series X|S.
Should you enable HDR for GTA 6?
Yes, if your television supports HDR properly. Enable HDR on your console, calibrate it using the built-in tool, and use HGiG if available to avoid double tone mapping.

Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.
Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms.
"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.
Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.
In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.
The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.
Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.
Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.
Following widespread complaints about the rising cost of living, he recently said he would work to reduce the cost of fuel but denied that this was a return to the subsidy. For decades, many Nigerians have seen cheap fuel as one of the few perks of living in Africa's largest oil producer.
His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.
Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.
"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.
However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.
"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.
While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.
Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.
"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.
To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.
But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.
Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.
"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."
To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.
"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.
