The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.
Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.
He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.
"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.
Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.
"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.
Another huge challenge facing Nigeria is the power sector, which has suffered from years of underinvestment.
The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.
Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.
The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.
"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.
Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.
The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.
For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.
"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.
"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.
Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.
"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.
As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge - building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.
"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.
"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

Following a week of disruption, cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase has partially resumed processing INR withdrawals for users in India. In a post on social media platform X, the platform said that the outage at one of its banking partners disrupted payouts for all of its clients. Coinbase India further noted that it has now begun processing all failed INR withdrawals, pending since November 9, in batches through an alternative banking route. The crypto exchange noted that the first batch has been processed, adding that the remaining batches will follow soon. However, the platform is yet to fully resume withdrawals. Coinbase India said that the INR withdrawal option on its app will still remain unavailable, citing outage issues at its banking partner. The company has directed users to contact its support team for withdrawals in the interim. “In light of this banking failure, we are strengthening our banking setup in India and will share more on this soon,” said Coinbase India. The exchange also assured users that their funds remain safe. It also said that customers will receive push notifications and email confirmations once their withdrawals have been initiated. This comes a week after Coinbase India, on November 9, said that it was temporarily suspending INR withdrawals due to an outage at its banking partner. The move had prompted public outcry from its customers online, with many seeking more clarity on the timeline for disbursals. The development comes barely five months after the crypto exchange relaunched its platform in India after a two year-long hiatus. The platform had exited India in 2023 after Indian authorities tightened its scrutiny around the unregulated asset class. Subsequently, it secured the requisite licensing to operate as a cryptocurrency exchange from the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) in March last year, paving the way for its return to one of the top cryptocurrency markets globally. It is important to mention that Coinbase is one of the largest cryptocurrency exchanges globally, and is also listed on the Nasdaq. At the heart of all this is the Indian cryptocurrency market, which is projected to become a $14 Bn opportunity by 2034. However, Indian authorities continue to be wary of the crypto ecosystem. Just last year, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra said that cryptos may affect the country’s financial stability. On top of this, a Parliamentary standing committee on finance recently termed the asset class as “high risk” citing rampant money laundering, trafficking, radicalisation and suspicious crypto transactions.

When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion.
Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become.
Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it."
This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor.
Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate.
With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range.
Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.”
With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring, now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest, which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.”
After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.
In April, Tiberius announced it had successfully fired one of its Sceptre projectiles from a NATO-standard 155-mm howitzer for the first time. It is now working with the US Army to mature the system, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license, and distribute the munition. It is also developing a missile, which it expects to start generating revenue next year.
Tiberius has turned the AI system it initially built into a product called GRAIL (Generative Real-Time Artificial Intelligence for Lethality). Steelberg says he is “most excited about” this. He hopes the platform can enable continuous upgrades to the weapon designs Tiberius licenses by decentralizing manufacturing. Steelberg says that, as well as automating supply chain management and compliance, the software simulates weapons against different targets in a range of environments and weather conditions, such as an Arctic peninsula. In addition to open-sourced data, the team is trying to get hold of much sought-after active combat data from around the world, including Ukraine. The idea is that this all enables users to test, iterate, and design weapons for specific uses much quicker.
“In the world of AI and design and development getting faster and faster, what is it that the West or the group of allied nations have an undeniable advantage on?” Baynes asks. “If you can weaponize all of the spare capacity and precision manufacturing across the UK, France, Germany, the Nordic countries, the US,” he says, “that's something that our adversaries today can never ever match.” Tiberius aims to achieve this by copying “the Apple model,” continues Baynes, who reported to Steve Jobs for four years. He says outsourcing manufacturing to many third-party subcontractors can accelerate development and deployment and keeps expensive production costs off Tiberius’ balance sheet during peacetime.
“We're taking the approach of Silicon Valley,” says Steelberg. “When you run into a big, hard, hairy problem, you not only cross that, but you turn around, you build a bridge—it’s a toll bridge, obviously—so the entire industry can cross that hurdle faster, better, stronger. They might pay a small fee, but it's better than dying in the ditch and not making it across it.”

In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

Lupus patients struggling with the debilitating disease are lining up to try experimental CAR-T therapies even after the recent deaths of four patients in clinical trials for a variety of autoimmune diseases, according to doctors who treat the life-threatening condition.
The trials remain halted and full details of the deaths — three linked to Novartis and one to Bristol Myers Squibb — have not been released.
Still, patients are willing to take the risk, compelled by accounts of people with advanced disease who were able to stop all medications and reclaim normal lives.
“I have patients that are literally waiting to get in,” said Dr. Anca Askanase, chief of rheumatology at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York, who has enrolled patients in the Bristol Myers CAR-T trials.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, the most common and severe form of lupus, causes agonising joint pain and raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease. Current treatments, which range from steroids to immunosuppressants and targeted biologics, often fail to control the disease. Some 10% to 15% of people with lupus die prematurely.
Brittan Kopittke, 27, who works for the University of North Carolina helping to counsel patients considering CAR-T, was diagnosed with lupus at age 22. SLE, which affects about 300,000 people in the US, typically develops between the ages of 15 and 44.
What began as a rash on her chest rapidly progressed to crippling joint pain, mouth sores and crushing fatigue. Steroids to reduce inflammation and the antimalarial drug hydroxychloroquine to tamp down antibodies attacking her healthy cells and tissues failed.
“My mouth sores were rampant. I was struggling to eat. I was struggling to drink. I was just very, very miserable,” she said.
Despite trying a cocktail of medicines, her disease advanced, attacking her kidneys, heart and lungs.
“I had reached the end of the line with treatments,” she said.
In June 2024, Kopittke went to UNC-Chapel Hill for a trial testing CAR-T, a personalised immunotherapy successfully used to treat blood cancers. It involves removing blood cells called T cells, genetically reengineering them to attack rogue immune cells, and reinfusing them with the aim of growing new, healthy immune cells.
Kopittke developed two dangerous reactions: cytokine release syndrome, which causes systemic inflammation, and a life-threatening, high-grade neurological complication called ICANS that left her unresponsive for three days.
Now, some two years into remission, Kopittke said she does not “sugarcoat” the risks when advising patients. “But I do say that I would do this again.”
150 trials underway
Novartis, Bristol Myers, and other companies with approved CAR-T cancer therapies, such as Johnson & Johnson and Gilead, are currently testing the technology against other hard-to-treat diseases.
There are about 150 trials underway pursuing CAR-T for lupus, as well as many others for myasthenia gravis, scleroderma, myositis, multiple sclerosis and stiff-person syndrome.
“There’s billions and billions of dollars pouring into this space,” said P.J. Utz, a Stanford Medicine autoimmunity researcher.
The risks became clear when Novartis in late August said it halted eight trials of its experimental rap-cel CAR-T therapy in autoimmune and neurological disorders after three patients died from a rare but known hyperinflammatory complication called IEC-HS.
Novartis, in an emailed statement, said it is working with multiple investigators and external academic experts to understand the root cause of the deaths and will share its findings “once the analysis is completed and the results can contribute to furthering patient care.”
Bristol also paused enrollment in its CAR-T autoimmune trials, citing temporary inflammatory events in patients. On October 23, it announced the death of a multiple sclerosis patient in one of the trials but said it had identified the cause of the safety issue and hopes to resume testing in 2027.
Piecing together what happened
The revelation of deaths in the Novartis trials surprised doctors eager to try CAR-T, buoyed by the success of Georg Schett of the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. In 2022, Schett published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine showing five lupus patients achieved remission with CAR-T. Subsequent studies showed lasting remission.
The Novartis deaths have left doctors in the dark, Schett said. The company needs to disclose what diseases the patients had, how well controlled their diseases were and what emergency treatments they received, Schett added.
Without those details, he said, doctors enrolling patients in other trials are left to speculate. “This is very sad for the community.”
Schett said he and CAR-T inventor Carl June of the University of Pennsylvania have tried to piece together what happened in the Novartis trials for an article they have submitted to NEJM.
He attributes the rare hyperinflammatory events in part to Novartis’ compressed manufacturing process, which reduces the time it takes to produce the cells from more than 10 days to fewer than two.
With this process, patients receive cells in an immature form, which Schett suggests is triggering a severe inflammatory response as cells expand in patients’ bodies. “We don’t see that in other programs,” he said.
He and others were less concerned about the more familiar side effects reported by Bristol Myers.
“We have treated high-grade inflammatory events that have been reversible with treatment,” said Kopittke’s doctor, Saira Sheikh, of the University of North Carolina, who chairs a network of nearly 70 lupus clinical trial centres.
Dr. Cuoghi Edens, a rheumatologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, which treats more than 100 paediatric lupus patients, said her hospital has had great success with a CAR-T therapy from Cabaletta Bio, which uses a more traditional manufacturing process.
Cabaletta has started testing its treatment in patients as young as 12. Edens said she walked through the informed consent process with a 15-year-old late last month.
“When the potential long-term impact of your diagnosis is death,” Edens said, “I don’t know if (treatment risks are) going to make that big of a difference to these patients.

Tetanus and diphtheria are two preventable diseases. And still, they surface years after childhood vaccinations. As antibody levels decline over time, especially against diphtheria, could the introduction of the Td vaccine signal a crucial point in closing this long-overlooked gap in adult vaccination and protection?
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), maternal and neonatal tetanus has declined significantly over the past two decades. But thousands of people still die from the disease each year, with newborns being especially at risk, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Diphtheria also continues to cause outbreaks in areas where immunity wanes or vaccine coverage is insufficient.

US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
- Published
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.
No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.
As it turns out, Belonging does not read as incendiary. It errs, rather, towards discretion and legacy-building. It is also, at its best, a heartbreaking story of love and loss.
Gandhi’s voice is measured and generally frill-free. Flourishes do accompany the meet-cute at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge in the mid-1960s that sets off the story. “That January Sunday, which was to change my life,” she writes, “the sky [was] a beautiful azure dotted with puffy white clouds as in a Tiepolo fresco.” The introduction to fellow student Rajiv Gandhi was “a bolt of lightning”.
And, as in a film, there is parental resistance. Sonia’s father, a businessman who worked in construction in a small Italian town, is a second world war veteran, nicknamed Maino the Lion. A 1998 New Yorker profile by Patrick French, briefly a collaborator on Belonging, had him down as “an unrepentant fascist” until his death. Well, was he? We don’t get to find out. Wherever expedient, Gandhi maintains her strategic silence.
Stefano Maino, at any rate, is “padre padrone” – literally, “father master”. When he hears about his middle daughter’s love interest, he brings “his fist down on his writing table” with a shout of “Basta!” And yet, he buys her a ticket to India the moment she turns 21.
On the boy’s side is the person who would come to be described as the world’s most powerful woman, Indira Gandhi, the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Barely has Sonia landed in Delhi than Indira decides the pair must wed (the news reaches the Mainos via radio; Signor Maino stays away). Indira then manages Sonia’s first pregnancy, directs the name-giving ceremony – you get the picture. Gandhi refers to her, factually, as “my mother-in-law”, but, subverting the stereotype, she becomes a devoted daughter. Walking us through her induction into elite Indian family life, she draws an affectionate portrait of this formidable 20th-century figure.
But family and party allegiance are a distorting lens through which to view history. Charged events, such as Indira’s crushing of a huge railway strike, acquire a benign gloss. The 21 tumultuous months of the 1975 Emergency – which saw members of the opposition arrested, civil liberties curtailed, the press censored, while a despotic nepo-baby (Sanjay, Indira’s younger son) ran amok – are rendered with a brisk calm. Tenderness is reserved for the repercussions on the family in its subsequent period out of power.
Sanjay’s death at 33, just after Indira’s return to power in 1980, leaves the matriarch broken. “In her eyes [Rajiv] was the only one who could come to her rescue.” Gandhi does not interrogate the hereditary approach to democratic politics, but she does recount, affectingly, the fight to protect herself and Rajiv – a commercial pilot with no greater ambitions – and their two children from the inferno.
In the book’s strongest scene, she waits disoriented in a crowded hospital in 1984, “shivering under my dressing gown”, having ferried her mother-in-law’s bullet-ridden body there. Indira was slain by her Sikh bodyguards in revenge for ordering the army into the Golden Temple, Sikhism’s holiest site. As Rajiv embraces her with the words “they want me to be sworn in as prime minister”, Gandhi feels “a rage welling up deep inside me”. “They will kill you too!” she says. “They will kill me anyway,” he replies. The “they” is unspecified, and gives these pages an air of foretold tragedy.
Rajiv’s eventful term plays out under this death cloud. It starts with a pogrom against Sikhs, spearheaded by Congress leaders. Gandhi goes some length to eulogise her husband’s tenure: in reality, it was a troubled and contradictory record. Rajiv was 40, severely underqualified, and grieving. Miscalculations abounded, among them clumsy religious manoeuvring that played into the Hindu-nationalist BJP’s hands, and a military entanglement in Sri Lanka designed to end the civil war with Tamil separatists.
And that death cloud never blows way. The children are withdrawn from school; Gandhi, perpetually anxious, finds her hands trembling in public; Rajiv is once shot at. When he loses the election his successor vindictively withdraws his special security cover. Their son Rahul (the current leader of the opposition) predicts the worst. At a rally in Tamil Nadu in 1991, a Tamil Tiger operative makes to place a garland around Rajiv, then 46, with explosives strapped around her body.
The graphic photograph of the aftermath of that scene is seared into Indian memory. Thanks to the vigilance of her children, Gandhi has never seen it. “I had become the child to be protected, they the parents,” she writes, in a wrenching section. Years later, when she collapses in Japan, a nurse is startled to find her grown children lying on either side of her on the small hospital bed.
Gandhi’s first reaction on hearing the news about Rajiv? “I wanted to die.” Gradually though, she picks up the smithereens of her life. As the remaining Gandhi elder, she picks up the pieces of the splintering Congress party, too.There are few parallels to a life as singular as this. A century ago, Congress had its first foreign-born female president, the British theosophist Annie Besant; farther afield, Janet Jagan, the American-born Jewish wife of Cheddi Jagan herself became president of Guyana – but both women were political activists to begin with. Gandhi, in her words, “had no right – except for the fact that I carried the family name”.
The exhortations to Gandhi to take over the party reveal plenty about Congress culture, and they are eventually successful: the spectator becomes the player. We watch her bone up on her Hindi, lead campaigns, stitch up alliances (including with a party sympathetic to the Tamil Tigers), and combat the BJP, which brands her, among other things, a “Monica Lewinsky” who would establish a “Rome Raj”. In 2004, she leads an alliance of parties to victory.
To her children’s horror, Gandhi is badgered into nearly accepting the post of prime minister. Instead she handpicks a candidate, Manmohan Singh, while keeping charge of the party (eventually leading it for a staggering 22 years) and chairing the ruling coalition as well as an advisory council that keeps a hand on policy levers.
“It had been my choice to become Indian,” she reflects after the long night of the soul that leads her to decline the premiership – a source of fascinated speculation over the years. “I made it out of love for a man, but that love came to encompass his family and his country. And it was this love for India that had demanded the most from me.”
Belonging comes into its own when unpacking those demands, and showing the transition from grief to its successor emotion, resilience.

Live Updates: Trump’s Whirlwind Asia Trip Starts in the Philippines
President Trump’s 48-hour trip will begin with a meeting with Southeast Asian leaders in Manila. He will later meet Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia in Shenzhen, a Chinese economic hub.
Latest
President Trump on Tuesday began a whirlwind Asia trip in which he will meet Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control and U.S. restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips.
Mr. Trump landed in Manila, where he is scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours there, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where all eyes will be on his expected meeting with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind. Each leader will arrive at the session, planned for Thursday, with a different agenda, and some analysts have compared it to Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union divided up postwar Europe in 1945.
That analogy has limits: No one thinks these three leaders, powerful as they are, are there to redefine the borders of any continent. But their very presence at one table would underscore they have major sway over the shape of the next world order. And for Mr. Trump, who loves the symbolism of a dramatic photo op, that may be enough.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump will catch the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
He isn’t just any latecomer: He is the one who issued tariffs on countries across the region, even on allies — bolstering the feeling in Asia that the United States is not a reliable partner, but rather one that treasures its commercial interests over its security interests. Southeast Asian leaders will be looking for any signs that the Republican defeat in the midterm elections may have humbled Mr. Trump or made him reconsider his policies.
Mr. Trump will also meet with leaders from the so-called “Quad” — the United States, India, Japan and Australia. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.
Before leaving for China on Wednesday, Mr. Trump will be hosted by Mr. Marcos, who has been contending with Chinese challenges to islands that both Beijing and Manila claim.
In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and A.I. industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.
Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.
“We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes,’’ Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington, referring to the agenda of the trilateral meeting. “We will talk about Iran a little,” he said, insisting the situation was in “very good shape.”
Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.
On nuclear weapons, Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one. And on the Iran war, analysts say it seems unlikely that the three-way meeting would make any progress — at a moment when Russia is happy to see energy prices remain high, and China is eager to see them rapidly decline.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
- A counter to China: Last December, the United States launched an initiative called Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce. Read more ›
- Philippine leader: President Trump’s well-known affinity for autocratic leaders was on display the last time he met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines. Read more ›
President Vladimir V. Putin could meet with Kim Jong Un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit this week, Russian state news agencies reported, citing Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesman. Before his departure for China, Putin met on Monday with a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. It was not yet clear whether the North Korean leader would attend the summit.
President Trump has landed in Manila, lingering on the tarmac for a welcome ceremony before walking alone to Marine One. He has several events tonight, but he will not leave his hotel for them. A meeting with quad leaders, a U.S.-Thailand trade deal signing and a dinner will all be held at the resort where the president is staying. In other words, he showed up late to this summit, and the summit will be coming to him.
Thousands of protesters have assembled in downtown Manila, chanting in Tagalog, “Trump leave the Philippines.” They are opposed to his Pax Silica A.I. supply chain initiative.
President Trump’s stopover at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is part of a state visit to the Philippines, where he will be received with a 21-gun salute.
The last time he met President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, was full of praise for the Filipino leader.
“Great family, great family legacy and highly respected in his country,” Mr. Trump said while hosting Mr. Marcos at the White House last year.
But that legacy was long considered an obstacle to Mr. Marcos’s political ambitions. He is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986 by a nonviolent uprising. The elder Marcos died in exile in Hawaii, without facing trial on U.S. criminal charges that he had plundered the Philippine Treasury. Years later, a court found his estate liable for torture, summary executions and disappearances.
The younger Marcos spent years rehabilitating his family’s image and won election in 2022. He is hosting Mr. Trump at his official residence, Malacañang Palace, which was also his childhood home.
Mr. Marcos and his wife, Liza Marcos, will receive Mr. Trump on Wednesday with a 21-gun salute. Mr. Trump is expected to sign the palace guest book, hold closed-door meetings, pose for a handshake, then attend a state luncheon held in his honor.
It is not clear whether Mr. Trump, who has a well-known affinity for autocratic leaders, will meet with Mr. Marcos’s mother, Imelda, 97, with whom he has socialized in New York. Ms. Marcos wielded immense power when her husband was president and later came to be known for her flamboyant lifestyle, shoe collection and unexplained wealth.
Mr. Marcos has said that when he called to congratulate Mr. Trump on his election victory in November 2024, Mr. Trump asked about Imelda Marcos.
“My mother is really his friend, he knows my mother very well,” Mr. Marcos said, relaying the conversation. “He was asking about her, ‘How’s Imelda?’ I told him she sends her congratulations.”
After the pomp and circumstance at Malacañang, which traces its roots to the Spanish colonial era in the Philippines, Mr. Trump is headed to Shenzhen, China. The highlight of that leg of his trip will be a trilateral meeting with two strongmen: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
For the second year in a row, President Trump is attending the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders, a show of alliance to a region that the United States sees as a strategic and maritime counterweight to China.
But Mr. Trump will reach the gathering, held this year in Manila, only on Tuesday, just as the summit wraps up, and he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.
Mixed signals like this — to say nothing of Mr. Trump’s punishing tariffs — are adding to a widespread belief within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. That leaves the bloc balancing between Washington and Beijing, with which many of its members have deep trade partnerships.
“They’ve learned that the United States is not reliable, so a lot of the hedging has been away from the United States,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.
The Philippines, America’s oldest security ally in Asia, provides a window into this balancing act.
After taking office three years ago, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reversed his predecessor’s tilt toward China and pivoted back toward the United States. That stance contributed to many tense encounters between Filipino and Chinese vessels in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing territorial claims.
As U.S. patrols in the South China Sea have dropped, Mr. Marcos has appeared to be more conciliatory toward Beijing. In August, he said that there was a “distinct possibility” that the Philippines and China could partner on oil and gas exploration in those waters despite their territorial feud.
“Marcos Jr. already has begun a shift toward China, one that a single visit by Trump is unlikely to stop,” Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote last week.
On Sunday, China and ASEAN failed to agree on a code of conduct in the South China Sea — something the Philippines, which has some of the biggest stakes in the dispute, had vowed to secure while chairing the bloc this year.
Chester Cabalza, president of International Development and Security Cooperation, a Philippine think tank, said, “Strategically, Manila opens its doors for conciliation with Beijing to stabilize normal ties. But on the ground, the real battle has yet to subside.”
Domestically, Mr. Marcos has to walk a tightrope, too.
“For Filipino fishermen and coastal communities, the South China Sea is not simply about a geopolitical dispute. It concerns livelihoods, access to maritime resources and national dignity,” said Arnaud Leveau, president of the Asia Centre, a Paris-based think tank. Any diplomatic accommodation perceived as sacrificing Filipino interests, he said, would therefore be politically risky.
The wider region has been battered by the consequences of another Trump policy: the war in Iran. Southeast Asia depends heavily on oil and gas imports from the Middle East and was roiled by soaring prices of fuel. In the Philippines, crops rotted in fields because farmers could not afford to transport them to markets. In Thailand, public servants were asked to use stairs instead of elevators to reduce energy expenses.
ASEAN comprises 11 nations — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, and, since last year, East Timor — with vastly different degrees of freedom and wealth. The bloc represents almost 700 million people, or almost 10 percent of the global population.
Making decisions on a consensus-basis and pledging not to interfere in one other’s internal affairs, the bloc has often been criticized as slow and ineffective, with the situation in Myanmar often cited as an example. A coup in that country in 2021 unleashed a civil war that ranks among the world’s most violent conflicts.
Myanmar’s leaders remain barred from ASEAN summits, under an agreement that was extended on Monday. Still, almost half of the bloc’s member states have had bilateral engagements with Myanmar since the coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, used stage-managed elections to take the post of president this year. Washington has also recently re-engaged in direct talks with Myanmar.
Mr. Trump’s attendance at the summit, which concludes with an ASEAN-U.S. meeting, is part of a state visit to the Philippines. He is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before heading to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Mr. Marcos has said little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump; but earlier this year, he described Washington as a “steadfast partner.” His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.
In recent days, hundreds of demonstrators have gathered in Manila to protest Mr. Trump’s visit. They oppose his “Pax Silica” initiative, a move to build a supply chain for the artificial intelligence industry that bypasses China, saying it would exploit Philippine natural resources.
Renato Reyes, who led one of the protest groups on Sunday afternoon, said, “Marcos is so desperate to welcome Donald Trump that he will roll out the red carpet, even if Trump arrives late for the summit.”
Aie Balagtas See contributed reporting from Manila and Damien Cave from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.
President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.
Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence.
For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports.
Echoes of Yalta
The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China.
The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe.
The White House has said that Mr. Trump wants to discuss the threat of nuclear proliferation. U.S. officials have expressed concerns about China’s accelerating nuclear buildup, expected to reach 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030.
The last nuclear arms control treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February. Trump administration officials have said that any new agreement on nuclear arms control must include China, but Beijing has shown no interest in the topic. China has an estimated 620 nuclear warheads, compared with the more than 5,000 that Russia and the United States have each, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
U.S. administration officials said they did not expect a deal out of the meeting, which they characterized as a starting point for discussions.
The gathering has prompted concern in Ukraine that Mr. Putin might push for a deal, deciding Ukraine’s fate without Kyiv’s involvement. A U.S. administration official said Ukraine was not expected to be part of the discussion between the three leaders.
U.S. Partners Look for Reassurance
Mr. Trump will start his trip in the Philippines, the oldest American treaty ally in the Asia-Pacific region, as the United States faces questions about its support for its partners in a region where China’s military and economic might continues to grow.
In Manila, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. plans to discuss with Mr. Trump the South China Sea, where the Philippines and China have competing claims. Philippine officials have said that they hope Mr. Trump’s visit might result in more American military assistance.
Mr. Trump is also expected to meet with leaders of ASEAN, a Southeast Asian grouping of 11 nations, as well as a gathering of the so-called Quad grouping of the United States, India, Australia and Japan.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia said on Sunday that he expected “lots of engagement” with Mr. Trump during the meetings.
“Obviously, that’s our most important ally,” he said. “But we want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts that are around the world.”
Chinese analysts described the meeting of the Quad group, formed in part to counter China, as an effort by Mr. Trump to project power after his party’s defeat in the midterms. “Its symbolic value outweighs its practical value,” Xu Liping, a senior scholar at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, told Shanghai Observer, a state-run outlet.
The Spy Scandal
After Manila, Mr. Trump will travel to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, where he will meet Mr. Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.
Jensen Huang, a key adviser who accompanied Mr. Trump on his last trip to China, will not be by his side. Mr. Huang helped shape the president’s views about technological competition with China and persuaded him to loosen restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.
Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was collecting intelligence on Mr. Huang for Beijing. China has rejected the allegations, calling them “smears.” Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.
So far, the president has not raised the issue with Mr. Xi and is not expected to during their meeting on Thursday. But the saga is likely to cause unease in China about whether Washington will impose tighter controls on the export of technology to the country.
As a result, U.S.-based analysts speculated that Mr. Xi might try to use his personal relationship with Mr. Trump to forestall such restrictions.
Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, said Mr. Huang’s downfall would likely mean “there is going to be more anxiety on the Chinese side about their access to American chips.” She expects Mr. Xi to emphasize the importance of easing U.S. controls on chip exports to China during their meeting.
Cooperation between China and the United States on artificial intelligence may be more difficult after the Nvidia scandal.
Still, there may be progress on the creation of a notification system that would allow the countries to alert each other about national security issues related to artificial intelligence, which the two sides agreed to in September.
“There’s some shared concern on both sides that U.S. or Chinese models might be misused by bad actors and cause damage to the U.S., China, or other countries,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution focusing on China’s technology development.
Xi May Have a New Calculus
When Mr. Xi sits down with Mr. Trump in Shenzhen, he will be dealing with a president who will soon face a new constraint at home: a Democrat-controlled Congress.
Lawmakers may pressure Mr. Trump to tighten export controls against China or accelerate weapons sales to Taiwan, according to Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser focusing on U.S.-China relations at the International Crisis Group. That means that “Xi will have to work much harder to keep Trump on side,” Mr. Wyne said.
Mr. Trump will be the first American president to visit China twice in one calendar year.
Analysts say the leaders’ summits, which have included state visits in Beijing and then in Washington, have been the only thing holding together a fragile détente between the two countries as they clash over A.I., export controls, Taiwan and other issues.
The two sides declared a trade truce last year when they met in Busan, South Korea. That deal, which was to expire this month, has been extended until January.
China’s restrictions on the export of crucial rare-earth metals and rare-earth magnets, which are needed to manufacture most modern technology, remain one of the most difficult unresolved issues.
Mr. Trump is likely to raise this with Mr. Xi, according to a senior U.S. administration official who said that China’s continued restrictions is one reason Washington only agreed to a two-month extension of the trade truce.
Ana Swanson contributed reporting from Washington, Aie Balagtas See from Manila, and Laura Chung from Sydney, Australia.

The acting director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, John Powers III, will become the permanent director, the agency announced Monday.
NIAID has been without a permanent director since March 2025, when the Trump administration ousted Jeanne Marrazzo. Powers has been serving in an acting capacity since June. A physician-scientist, Powers has worked with NIAID since 1999 in several roles focused on clinical research.
The second Trump administration has brought a renewed spotlight to the infectious disease institute, in large part because of the president’s ire for former director Anthony Fauci, and because of unsubstantiated accusations that research funded by an institute in China played a role in creating the SARS-CoV-2 virus. It has also seen tumult in its leadership. After Marrazzo was ousted, Jeffery Taubenberger was appointed acting director. He unexpectedly stepped down, and several other leaders at NIAID were reassigned to other institutes or asked to resign.

Hooked by design: How gambling apps keep 'losers' spending more cash
Design features, inducements keep vulnerable gamblers addicted to play
This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
After three years of compulsive online betting, Robin Koczerginski tried to quit in 2025.
He stopped using his favourite sports gambling apps: Bet365, DraftKings and BetMGM.
He says that after installing special software on his devices to prevent him from accessing the apps, almost immediately his phone lit up with email notifications and special offers luring him back.
"Bonuses, free bets, all this stuff. I honestly felt like it escalated even more after I stopped playing," the Toronto father, writer and communications strategist told CBC News.
It was all to "entice [me] to come back in," he said.
It worked. He relapsed and started gambling again.
A CBC News investigation has found Koczerginski's relapse is indicative of a larger problem fuelled by a sophisticated, multibillion-dollar online gambling industry that routinely uses automated inducements and design features to try to keep users hooked.
This despite rules in most jurisdictions, including Ontario and Alberta, that require online casinos to monitor player behaviour and intervene when players show signs of addiction or high-risk play.
'Dark patterns' make cashing out difficult
Casino and sports betting apps welcome users into an online experience purposely built to keep people playing and losing money, experts told CBC News.
Beyond attractive colours, flashing animations and a rapid pace of play, experts say companies employ design features known as "dark patterns" crafted to trick users into playing for longer or not notice their losses.
CBC spoke to a former designer from Bally's Corporation in the U.K., a mid-sized global casino, sports betting and online company, who said they installed features to discourage users from setting up spending limits and added colourful pop-ups to distract them from the feeling of losing.
- More people are seeking emergency care for gambling, a new study says — and it's mostly men and boys
"Everything on the screen is playing with your psychological feelings," the former Baily's designer said, noting this is true of the designs of many popular social media apps and consumer websites.
CBC agreed not to identify the designer, as they fear repercussions for speaking about trade practices.
They also said the company used dark patterns to delay the process of closing an account to allow time for users to change their minds.
Bally's declined to answer questions about its design features but instead offered a statement that reads in part: "We take our responsibility to our players seriously and work closely with our regulatory partners to ensure responsible gaming principles and safeguards are reflected throughout our products and offerings."
Experts who study online gambling apps say these features are common.
"On any gambling site that you go to there will be a large deposit button at the top of the screen, but the withdrawal button will be more than likely hidden," said Jack McGarrigle, a PhD candidate in psychology at Swansea University in Wales who is studying the phenomenon.
Jack McGarrigle, a PhD candidate in psychology at Swansea University in Wales, says gambling apps often make it difficult to withdraw money, cancel accounts or access safer gambling tools in a bid to keep gamblers hooked. (Mat Heywood/CBC)
It works to discourage withdrawals, according to Koczerginski.
"Deposit, it takes 10 seconds. You just click a couple of buttons and your money's in your account," he said. "When you withdraw, it is different. There's a period of time that you have to wait, and it's super easy to cancel that withdrawal, which I've done before, too."
McGarrigle says apps also often obscure the "responsible gambling" features that allow players to set daily or weekly spending limits.
He likens these features that keep gamblers playing to ones used by social media and online shopping platforms that keep users scrolling as long as possible.
But the stakes are different.
"If you spend too much time on TikTok, you're not going to go bankrupt or lose your house," McGarrigle said.
CBC looked into these features by setting up accounts on multiple popular gambling apps and found that cashing out took several extra steps and required waiting eight to 10 days to receive a physical cheque in the mail.
It's also common for gambling apps to de-emphasize the loss of cash.
T.S., a 22-year-old recent university graduate from Ontario, quit gambling in 2025 after losing $14,000 in one night on blackjack.
"When you played blackjack on FanDuel, for example, they wouldn't even say that you'd lost money," he recounted.
"But if you won, you get a big pop-up on your screen that says you won … It's obvious that they're trying to make it fun to win and easy to ignore when you lose."
CBC has agreed not to name him as he fears being stigmatized by prospective employers.
T.S., 22, says the design of gambling apps makes it easier to ignore losses and celebrate wins. (YanJun Li/CBC)
In a statement to CBC News, FanDuel said the company "is committed to providing customers with a clear and transparent entertainment experience."
"Responsible gaming tools are built directly into our apps and are easily accessible to every customer. These include reality checks, deposit and time limits, and the My FanDuel Spend dashboard, which gives customers visibility into their spending and activity so they can make informed decisions about their play."
'Targeting losers'
A former data analyst at DraftKings has been speaking out about his time at the company, which is one of North America's biggest online gambling companies.
Jayden Butts told CBC and The New York Times that his work between 2022 and 2024 involved identifying and targeting potentially vulnerable gamblers.
Butts says he was tasked with studying DraftKings player data to identify the most profitable customers to target with bonuses.
Jayden Butts, a former data analyst at Draftkings, says the company was using player data to send promotions to potentially high-risk gamblers. (Submitted by Jayden Butts)
"What I was asked to do is, given all the immense amounts of data that we had on customers — where they're from, how they play, what they like to play, you name it — with all of these features, can we create something that tells us who we should be sending our promotional offers to?"
But he became uncomfortable as he concluded the most profitable customers might also be high-risk problem gamblers.
DraftKings told CBC in a statement, "We do not market to customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming."
Butts, however, felt he was exploiting vulnerable players.
"I'm making their lives harder and their financial situations worse, the better I do at my job," he said.
"It's targeting losers. I don't want it to sound like, ‘Oh, they're targeting the suckers.' It's literally like they are targeting people who are most likely to lose money."

- CBC Investigates MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada amid mounting harms
Butts says he was dismissed in late 2024 for performance issues. He says he'd become disillusioned.
DraftKings told CBC News in an email that it uses "basic marketing practices" such as data science and analytics — and not AI — to customize its promotional targeting toward "customer groups, not individual customers."
"Statements by Mr. Butts only reflect his views, as a single junior-level business analyst at DraftKings who was employed at the company for less than two years."
"The premise that a problem gambler would be 'the best investment' is patently false. Our long-term success depends on customers who engage responsibly."
DraftKings also rejected the characterization that withdrawals are more difficult to make than deposits.
“Withdrawals and deposits involve different processing requirements. DraftKings approves and sends 97 per cent of withdrawal requests within five minutes,” a spokesperson wrote in an email Monday.
Calls for stricter regulation
After Butts's initial allegations were published by The New York Times in September, politicians and gaming regulators in the U.S. launched inquiries into whether DraftKings and other companies are misusing data and AI to target problem gamblers.
Ontario's regulator, the Alcohol and Gaming Commission, did not respond to CBC's questions about whether it is investigating DraftKings.
The AGCO issued a detailed statement citing Ontario's regulatory standards, which set requirements for game design, player information, advertising, inducements and player protections.
CBC looked into design features of gambling apps by setting up accounts on popular apps, and found that cashing out took several extra steps and required waiting 8-10 days to receive a physical cheque in the mail. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
"Operators must monitor for indicators of gambling-related harm and intervene appropriately …. Player data or analytical tools cannot be used to target high-risk players with marketing or inducements," the AGCO wrote.
T.S. and Robin Koczerginski have both quit gambling, sought addictions treatment and are now in recovery. Koczerginski has enrolled in a program called BetGuard, which excludes him from all regulated gambling sites in Ontario, making a relapse near impossible.
They both say that when they were gambling, erratically and at all hours, they felt highly targeted despite showing classic signs of problem gambling.
- Sharp rise in young men contacting Ontario gambling helpline, researchers find
- CBC Investigates 'We often try suicide': The hidden cost of problem gambling in Canada
"They're really trying to pinpoint exactly who you are, what you like, what is, like, your particular flavour of bets that you like to place, and trying to use that to keep you going, especially as you are fighting really hard [to stop] when you're addicted," Koczerginski said.
T.S. believes governments need to step in with stricter controls on gambling companies.
"[The companies are] not going to do it on their own," he said.
"They're never gonna stop targeting problem gamblers. That's where their money comes from."

A 29-year-old woman from Manuguru, who was rushed to hospital after suddenly losing movement in her right arm and leg, regained significant mobility within hours after doctors at two government hospitals coordinated to administer emergency stroke treatment within the critical window.
Rajani’s ordeal began on an ordinary morning when she suddenly developed slurred speech and complete weakness on her right side. Recognising the signs of an acute stroke, doctors acted swiftly to prevent permanent brain damage.
She was first taken to Area Hospital, Manuguru, where Sai Kumar, a General Medicine specialist, identified the symptoms and arranged an urgent referral to Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, nearly 60 km away, for emergency treatment.
Recognising the narrow window for intervention, M. Ramakrishna, medical superintendent of Area Hospital, Manuguru, coordinated directly with Tejaswi Gadde, physician at Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, to facilitate her transfer.
At Bhadrachalam, doctors immediately conducted a CT scan to rule out bleeding in the brain before administering clot-dissolving medication. With Rajani still within the recommended 4.5-hour treatment window, doctors administered intravenous Tenecteplase at 2 p.m., around 3.5 hours after the symptoms began, said G. Ravi Babu, District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS), Bhadradri Kothagudem.
The response to treatment was encouraging. Before the intervention, Rajani had no detectable movement in her right arm or leg, with her muscle power recorded at 0/5. Following thrombolysis, her muscle strength improved, and she regained the ability to move the affected limbs against resistance, though full strength is yet to return.
She remains under close neurological observation. The case also highlights the availability of advanced emergency treatment in government hospitals serving remote and tribal areas. The thrombolytic medication, which costs around ₹45,000 in the market, was administered to Rajani free of cost.
Dr. Ravi Babu appreciated the doctors, nurses and supporting staff at both hospitals for their prompt decisions and coordination. “Such interventions demonstrate how teamwork between government healthcare institutions can help deliver advanced, life-saving treatment even in geographically remote areas,” he said.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."
