Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.
The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific.
The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen.
The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit.
Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila.
The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days.
Trilateral meeting
For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together.
"The Chinese strongly disagree with the idea that they should be involved in any kind of trilateral discussions with the United States and Russia on nuclear weapons," Kagan said.
"China wants to avoid this because they don't want to be locked into a subservient position. And they also don't want to create a precedent. I think the main thing for the Chinese is they know if they do a meeting and nuclear issues are discussed, it becomes much harder for them to refuse to do it in the future," he said.
A White House official said they do not expect any agreement to come out of the meeting on denuclearization.
"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said, calling the trilateral an "entry point" for the three countries to talk about reducing nuclear weapons stock.
Another U.S. official not authorized to speak on the record acknowledged that denuclearization is a "difficult" topic for China.
"But we do think it's time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said.
Putin, for his part, stands to benefit from a meeting with Trump and Xi, as Russia's war with Ukraine nears its five-year mark. Trump has made friendlier moves toward Russia in recent months, siding with Putin and striking a deal to release more Russian oil into the market ahead of the midterm elections.
Trump said last month that he was fine with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not being present at a potential meeting with Putin about the war.
"Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said.
A White House official said Ukraine is not intended to come up in the meeting with Xi and Putin. And there is no plan for Putin and Trump to have a separate meeting.
Kagan said the meeting with Xi, Trump and Putin could end up being on the shorter side if there isn't much all parties are willing to discuss. But at the same time, "I could see this going longer because President Trump likes dealing with Putin and Xi. He sees them as his peers. He sees them as important world leaders," Kagan said.
Either way, a photo of the three leaders meeting together is enough to make headlines.
"That picture alone is going to be worth well over a thousand words," Kagan said.
Busan Agreement
This is the second time Trump and Xi are meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit – but this year's meeting is notably different from last year's in Busan, South Korea, when tensions between the US and China were fraught amid the escalating trade war.
The meeting in Busan established a sort-of truce between the two countries. The U.S. immediately lowered some tariffs on Chinese goods and China agreed to loosen exports on rare earths. But the execution of the agreement has been spotty.
"There's friction in this truce. It's not smooth, but it's basically functional," Kurt Tong, Managing Partner at The Asia Group, said.
A White House official said the U.S. isn't getting rare earths from China at the pace or level they'd like.
"We really want to focus minds among our counterparts in China on compliance with this," they said.
Still, Tong expects the agreement to be renewed past its January expiration. The two sides will likely agree to the renewal either in Shenzhen or later this year at the G20 summit Trump is hosting in Miami, according to Tong.
Meetings in Manila
Before the president arrives in China, he's holding meetings with several allies in Manila, including a meeting with the other leaders of the Quad nations: India, Japan and Australia.
"I think it's quite significant symbolically and politically that the U.S., Australia, Japan and India, the major democracies of Asia and the Pacific, get together… it's especially significant that they're doing it just before the meetings in China," Tong said.
The White House said Trump will also sign a trade deal with Thailand while in the Philippines.
The opportunity in Manila for Trump is to repair and reinforce relationships with countries like Japan and India, and the host country the Philippines. The ASEAN summit is also the region's first look at the president since his party lost control of Congress and on a global stage, a chance to see what the last two years of Trump's presidency may look like.
"I think the real thing that people will be looking at first is, how does he present himself?" Kagan said. "How does his behaviour towards Modi and towards India change? Those are things people will be looking at very, very closely for clues for what the next two years are likely to be like."
Nvidia fallout
A White House official said they don't expect Trump to raise the issue of Huang's affair and resignation with Xi. The focus of the meeting is about trade, the official said.
Huang resigned last week after admitting the extramarital affair with Alice Huang. Trump administration officials are now facing scrutiny and questions about how much they knew about Huang's affair and how much Huang had access to Trump and his orbit.
"I think the main impact is here in the United States, where there are calls for accountability with respect to Mr. Huang's activities with the U.S. government and questions about what happened… the net result of that is to provide a tailwind to persons who are interested in tightening up the technology denial regime toward China," Tong said.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed last week to appear in front of the Senate Banking Committee to answer further questions. Trump, for his part, has continued to defend Huang and called him an honorable person.

The Madras High Court has barred Eternal-owned quick commerce platform Blinkit from using the likeness of Chennai Super Kings (CSK) superfan Saravanan Hari without his written consent. The interim order came in a suit in which Saravanan has sought ₹1.1 Cr in damages, alleging that a Blinkit newspaper advertisement used his likeness and gave readers the impression that he endorsed the platform. Justice P B Balaji observed that the Constitution protects the rights of every individual and that personality rights can extend to people who have built a distinct public identity. “This is an interesting case, where a diehard fan of the Chennai Super Kings (CSK) has filed the present suit, seeking to protect his individual personality rights,” the court observed. Inc42 has reached out to Blinkit for comment. This story will be updated on receiving a response. What Sparked The Dispute? The dispute stems from a full-page Blinkit ad published in the Chennai edition of The Sunday Times of India on March 23, 2025. The ad promoted a match-ticket voucher offer with the slogan “The men in yellow always deliver”. In the bottom-right corner was a cartoon of a yellow-painted cricket fan with curly hair, a moustache, and “THALA 7” on his torso, giving a double thumbs-up. According to the plaint, Saravanan developed his match-day look around 2013. It includes yellow face and body paint, lettering across his torso, red lipstick, a curly wig, a thick moustache, dark eyebrows, and his signature double thumbs-up pose. Saravanan said he has travelled with CSK and attended matches in India and overseas. He cited television appearances, newspaper coverage, brand collaborations, and public engagements, along with his association with CSK, recognition from CSK veteran MS Dhoni, and an appearance in the Tamil film GOAT, as evidence that his look had become recognisable. Saravanan alleged that the advertisement created a false impression that he endorsed Blinkit. According to him, friends, fans and acquaintances contacted him to ask whether he had formally associated with the company. Some customers dissatisfied with Blinkit's services even expected him to resolve their complaints, he alleged. What The Court Ordered Blink Commerce, which operates Blinkit, said in its reply to Saravanan’s legal notice that the characters in the ad were fictional and bore no connection to him. It also said it would refrain from using the character in future ads as a gesture of goodwill. Justice Balaji found a prima facie resemblance between the cartoon and Saravanan, pointing to TV and newspaper coverage showing the same pose. The court said the ad could lead readers to believe that Saravanan had appeared in it or consented to the use of his likeness. It granted an interim injunction against Blink Commerce, finding that Saravanan had made out a preliminary case for protection against commercial use of his persona. Bennett, Coleman & Company Limited, the publisher of The Times of India, denied liability, saying its role was limited to providing ad space and that the advertiser supplied the material. The court said the publisher’s liability would be examined at trial. The court directed Blink Commerce and the publisher to preserve materials relating to the ad, including artwork, samples, design records, emails, and correspondence with designers and external vendors. It deferred consideration of Saravanan’s separate request to preserve and produce the defendants’ books of accounts until they appear and file their replies. Besides damages, Saravanan has sought a declaration recognising his distinctive persona as his property and protection against unauthorised commercial use by unknown parties. The matter is listed for December 14.

They’re Young, Frustrated and Want France to Change. They Disagree on How.
One is a left-wing student leader, the other a young far-right activist. Together, Soumaya Sarré and Louise Montangon reflect the polarization of France, where more protests were set for Tuesday.
Soumaya Sarré, 18, is a history and Arabic studies undergraduate who grew up in a working-class district on the edge of Paris. She is a voice of the youth-led protests that have spurred unrest across France since September. “I can carry our voices, the voices of young people from working-class neighborhoods,” she told me.
Louise Montangon, 22, is a philosophy undergraduate from rural France. As the student protests gained momentum, she became one of their leading critics, regularly condemning the young demonstrators on television panels and social media. “The majority of university and high school students actually want to attend their classes,” she said in an interview.
Unknown to the public until this fall, these two women from opposite ends of the political spectrum have surfaced as emblems of the combustible French moment, which was set to intensify again on Tuesday with more strikes and protests.
Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon aren’t formal leaders of their political camps, and their sudden prominence partly reflects society’s tendency to search for avatars for leaderless movements. Their simultaneous rise, and their divergent politics, nevertheless reflect the polarization of French society, and particularly its youth — five months from a presidential election dominated by candidates from the far-left and the far-right.
Polls of people under 25 suggest that more than 40 percent support the main far-left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, while more than 20 percent back his far-right opponent, Marine Le Pen. In legislative elections in 2024, nearly half of voters from that age group voted for Mr. Mélenchon’s party, and a third voted for Ms. Le Pen’s.
Support for moderate solutions has plummeted after years of centrist governance under Emmanuel Macron, France’s term-limited president.

Only between a quarter and a third of people currently diagnosed with obesity should be considered as in poor health, according to a new study that joins calls to overhaul how the condition is diagnosed.
The study, published in Nature on Wednesday, follows a proposal last year from experts and medical organisations to move obesity diagnosis beyond just body mass index (BMI), based on a person’s weight and height, to include body fat and broader health.
The study attempts to show what this new definition could mean for diagnosis levels, prevalence, and ultimately, treatment, for a condition the World Health Organization currently estimates affects more than one billion people globally.
Obesity can be a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, liver and kidney disease and cancer. The study suggests defining it as pre-clinical, when the condition is largely a risk factor, and clinical, when it is causing ill health.
Waist circumference should be part of diagnosis, study says
Using data from almost 850,000 adults from China, Britain, the US and Spain, the study estimates that under the new framework, 1% to 3% of those defined as obese using BMI alone would not be, while another 5% to 9%, with higher body fat for example, would be diagnosed with the condition. Across a population, this could affect tens of millions of people.
The study’s senior author Francesco Rubino, professor and chair of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London, said the inaccuracy of BMI measurements was well-known.
“But we haven’t so far got a better system,” he said. That is what the new framework aims to do, he added, saying it could “provide a meaningful clinical characterisation of obesity that can inform care and policy.”
The new framework proposes measuring body fat, including by waist circumference, as well as BMI, and considering if a patient has any organ dysfunction linked to weight, like heart or liver problems, before making a diagnosis.
This means some people with high BMI alone would not be classed as having obesity. Those who have high body fat and high BMI would be diagnosed with “pre-clinical obesity”, and those who also have organ dysfunction would have “clinical obesity” – considered an active disease that would usually require more urgent treatment.
Under these criteria, only on average roughly 27% of people with obesity across the four studied countries have clinical obesity, the study estimated – representing around 8.5% of all adults.
The majority of those with “pre-clinical obesity” – around 82% on average across the four countries studied – did not progress to clinical obesity, although progression rates were higher in China and Spain, the study found.

Swabbing public transport to identify urban microbiomes, a city’s microbial signature

A team of researchers from IIT Madras swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains on Chennai Metro’s Blue and Green Lines in December 2021 and January 2022, targeting four high-touch surfaces: station handrails (bannisters), ticket-vending kiosks, train handrails (rods), and ticket counters. Photograph used for representational purposes only

From waste-water surveillance to public transport surfaces, mankind is constantly on the lookout for diverse microbial sources to test, to understand anti-microbial resistance patterns in a particular society. The latest in the urban transport systems sweep, performed at Chennai Metro Rail stations, showed that Chennai had a distinctive ‘transit biome’ - influenced by the city’s coastal climate, humidity, urban density and relatively nearby agricultural activity.
A team of researchers from IIT Madras swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains on Chennai Metro’s Blue and Green Lines in December 2021 and January 2022, targeting four high-touch surfaces: station handrails (bannisters), ticket-vending kiosks, train handrails (rods), and ticket counters. The team swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains and after quality control, 47 samples were sequenced using whole-genome metagenomic sequencing. Metagenomics is defined as the direct genetic analysis of genomes contained with an environmental sample.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths in 2021, highlighting the need for coordinated action across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, experts said at the sixth Global Media Forum on AMR.
Speaking ahead of World AMR Awareness Week (November 18-24), Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, Director ai-AMR Department, World Health Organization (WHO), and Director, Quadripartite Joint Secretariat on AMR, said gaps in financing, surveillance, and coordination continued to hamper global efforts. “Behind these numbers are patients, families, farmers, and communities,” he said, stressing that global commitments should translate into results on the ground.
The updated Global Action Plan on AMR for 2026-2036 seeks to strengthen prevention, surveillance, responsible antimicrobial use and sustainable financing. World leaders have committed to reducing bacterial AMR-associated deaths by 10% by 2030.
Junxia Song, deputy chief veterinarian and chief of the One Health and Disease Control Branch, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), said antibiotic use in livestock could increase by nearly 30% by 2040 without intervention. Better animal health and farm management practices could reduce use by up to 57%.
Aitziber Echeverria, AMR coordinator, Chemicals and Health Branch, United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), called for action against environmental pollution, including antimicrobial residues in wastewater.
Kefas Samson, senior technical officer and lead of multisectoral coordination, AMR Department, WHO headquarters, highlighted gaps in diagnostics, surveillance and access to quality-assured antimicrobials. Jane Lwoyero, programme officer, World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), stressed the importance of vaccination and farm biosecurity.
Shobha Shukla, chairperson, Global AMR Media Alliance (GAMA), and host of the forum, called for a person-centred, rights-based and gender-transformative approach to tackling AMR.
The forum also recognised 56 journalists and media professionals as Global AMR Media Awardees 2026 for their contributions to reporting on antimicrobial resistance.

On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”
Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “horrible idea.” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.
Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported.
If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.
Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements.
“Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’”
Trump officials accused of “corruption”
What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who plan to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.”
“I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.”
Yoon noted that evidencesuggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground.
The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D–Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported. He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang.
Other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom.
“It is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal said. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.”
Trump officials profit off Nvidia policies
Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio.
Other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.”
“The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth said. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said.
“White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were protecting their own fortunes rather than looking out for Americans,” Haworth said.
If the US fails to hold them accountable for alleged conflicts of interest, “it would send a signal that powerful men once again cannot be held to account and that powerful men are protecting powerful men,” Haworth said.
Nvidia “lucky” to have Sacks
Detailing Sacks’ alleged conflicts, the group cited New York Times reporting that the former AI Czar had long supported Huang’s stance that allowing Nvidia to sell more chips in China would help the US stay ahead in the AI race. After Sacks became Trump’s key AI advisor, Huang quickly forged a “tight bond” with him, and “both stood to benefit” from their push to sell chips to China, TOP reported.
Also notably, while advising the White House, Sacks opposed policies such as the Trump administration’s recent move to cut off China’s remote access to US-made chips through now-restricted Southeast Asian data centers. Citing Sacks’ alignment with Huang, TOP reported that after just one meeting with the two men, Trump decided to allow Nvidia to sell AI chips to China that the Biden administration had previously blocked.
Huang valued his alliance with Sacks, TOP noted, citing reporting that showed Huang declaring last year that Nvidia was “lucky” to have Sacks advising Trump. But TOP is concerned that the alliance was built on mutual financial interest and that Sacks took a part-time role in the Trump administration to avoid divestments or disclosure requirements that might have revealed the extent of his possible conflicts of interest.
TOP flagged two areas it believes warrant Congressional investigation. While advising Trump to embrace AI deregulation, Sacks and his firm, Craft Ventures, continued investing substantially in AI. Sacks also stood to benefit from pushing Trump to integrate AI into warfare and national security tools, TOP’s report said. Craft Ventures has invested in Palantir, “a Peter Thiel-founded government contractor seen as a ‘rising star’ in the US Defense Tech World and holding hundreds of millions in US government defense contracts,” TOP said.
Lutnick “benefited greatly”
Even within the Trump administration, officials have turned on Commerce Secretary Lutnick, seemingly looking to blame him for mishandling the Nvidia spying investigation and allowing Trump to maintain close ties with Huang despite apparent intelligence risks.
Lutnick has bragged publicly that he promised Huang “really easy access to the President” after joining the administration, TOP reported. That alliance helped push Trump to approve the sale of Nvidia H200s to China, TOP said. And that seemed to directly benefit Lutnick, TOP said, because before he was confirmed as secretary, he was CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, which held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock.
“In his role as Secretary, Lutnick is responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals, like China,” TOP reported. “Lutnick and the company he controls benefited greatly from opening sales of Nvidia chips to China.”
After Lutnick was required to hand that company over to his son, Cantor Fitzgerald “maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives,” TOP noted.
Those investments shifted substantially around the same time that Lutnick began facing pressure to “crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China,” TOP reported. Cantor Fitzgerald “reduced its Nvidia holdings by nearly 50 percent between September 2025 and March 2026,” TOP said.
However, when Trump was reportedly first told of the spying allegations this spring, Cantor Fitzgerald again continued to boost Nvidia. Most prominently, the company helped “finance the expansion of one of Nvidia’s newest business partners, IREN,” facilitating a five-year, $3.4 billion deal between Nvidia and the Australia-based cloud computing provider.
Among those now criticizing Lutnick for weak enforcement of export controls that appeared designed to protect Huang’s bottom line is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But even with scrutiny coming from within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that Lutnick did anything wrong. Yoon suggested that, given Lutnick’s long career, there may be normal explanations for potential financial conflicts.
“Maybe a separate question is ‘should people with a long storied history in business and industry be working in government at this level?’” Yoon said.
Probes may delay Huang’s return
Haworth said the next 48 hours will be critical in determining whether Huang succeeds in returning to Nvidia.
“I think it’s going to be incumbent on the incoming Democratic leadership to insist that whether or not he returns, investigations will follow,” Haworth said.
But Yoon thinks Nvidia is unlikely to bring Huang back any time soon, despite current evidence suggesting that “Nvidia’s actions here have been perfectly legal” and that “influencing a political system for your financial interests is very much legal in the United States.”
It seems “untenable for Nvidia to continue doing what they’re doing,” Yoon said. Zooming out even more, he suggested the scandal showed that the entire AI industry can no longer afford to operate under a profit motive alone, so long as governments continue positioning the technology as a strategic asset.
If US investigations expose corruption, bribery, treason, or other crimes, Nvidia risks losing some of its dominant stake in the GPU market. On Tuesday, the Information reported that some Nvidia customers had already lost trust and were looking to Google and AMD for more stability.
Nvidia has also been accused of intervening in a Commerce investigation, which Yoon said could also be “pretty consequential” if any evidence bears that out.
“I think it’s pretty unlikely that Huang makes it back to Nvidia any time soon,” Yoon said. “Maybe he goes on a redemption tour and comes back in five years or something, but I’m not really seeing a path forward for him right now.”

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden downfall is in a sense shocking, considering his wealth, global fame, and role leading what was until recently the world’s most valuable company.
Why the left and right are both cheering Jensen Huang’s downfall
The deposed Nvidia CEO’s diverse coalition of haters could reshape AI policy.
But Huang’s immense influence in Washington — and particularly in President Donald Trump’s Washington — has long been intensely controversial among a surprisingly diverse cross-section of the political, business, and tech advocacy world. And his ouster not only drives a wedge through Trump’s second-term coalition, it could usher in a major change in how the US steers the AI revolution.
Huang — who resigned this week after allegations he’d had affairs with two Nvidia employees and one Chinese businesswoman who some US officials claim was spying on him for the Chinese government — has been crucial in helping shape the Trump administration’s AI policies. That’s perhaps no surprise, given that Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial to the AI revolution.
His many critics, however, say Huang’s influence has been deeply harmful. Their main objection? They believe the Trump administration hasn’t been doing enough to stop China from getting or accessing advanced AI chips — in part because of Huang’s lobbying and sway with the president.
This coalition of Huang critics spans the political spectrum. It includes right-wing China hawks and the bipartisan foreign policy establishment, who want to win an AI race against China. It includes economic populists in both parties, who resent China’s economic sway. It even includes some leading members of the Trump administration itself — Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have reportedly pushed for tighter chip restrictions.
It also contains some even odder bedfellows. The coalition includes people who want to slow down the AI race, like the tech safety advocates who warn that advanced AI could cause human extinction. Yet it also includes two major US frontier AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, who hope to impede the growth of Chinese competitors by limiting their access to chips.
All of these disparate groups come together around the core idea that the US urgently needs to do more to stop advanced chips from getting to China. Selling AI chips to China is like “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said.
Standing against them all — and often getting his way with Trump — has been Jensen Huang.
Beyond the obvious — Nvidia’s business is selling chips, and Huang wants to be able to sell more chips in more places — Huang is associated with a camp in the AI policy debate that some have dubbed with “let it rip.” Along with former White House AI czar David Sacks, Huang has scoffed at warnings that AI could cause human extinction, calling them “irresponsible” and “doomsday narratives.” He’s also dismissed some national security concerns, saying that being a “China hawk” was a “badge of shame” and said that the bigger risk to American influence over AI would be US companies losing market share around the world.
So Huang’s ouster and the claims of Chinese espionage around it have opened up an opportunity for a shakeup in US policy — and a rare chance for those China hawks to potentially investigate, undermine, and push out their rivals, while seizing the policy reins around chip exports.
Trump administration officials who want tougher restrictions have their knives out for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a frequent ally of Huang’s. There’s a bipartisan push in Congress for new export controls legislation before the end of the year. Congressional Republican committee chairs are demanding Huang and Lutnick come in and testify in the coming weeks, before Democrats take over Congress.
Plus, there are the partisan incentives for Democrats to dig into the question of what Trump knew about all this (he was reportedly briefed on the spy concerns last fall). And there are political incentives for ambitious Republicans to find an issue on which they can distance themselves from an unpopular administration without antagonizing their conservative base.
With so many different forces invested in the outcome, you can bet this topic will continue to dominate headlines for months to come — with unpredictable results for both the new Democratic Congress, the future of the GOP, and the AI boom.
The many critics of Jensen Huang’s influence on the Trump administration
In Washington itself, the most influential faction opposed to Huang is the bipartisan national security establishment, most of whom strongly believe in the necessity of competing with China for global influence.
These “China hawks” were influential in the Biden administration and have historically been dominant in GOP administrations and on GOP-controlled congressional committees. And many of them have been flabbergasted at Trump’s policies toward China and Chips this term.
“I don’t think we should be using any American technology to uplift China’s capabilities in AI given how era-defining this technology will be in national security and in our economy,” Vivek Chilukuri of the Center for a New American Security, a center-left think tank, told me. “A company’s going to argue for this, that’s what companies do. But the interest of any one company should not be trumping the national security of the United States.
Moving further right, there’s a MAGA-aligned faction that is skeptical of foreign wars such as Trump’s conflict in Iran — but even some of them are still quite antagonistic to China.
Take, for instance, Trump’s onetime campaign manager and White House adviser Steve Bannon. He’s been furiously protesting Huang’s influence on the administration for more than a year — in September 2025, he argued that Huang should be arrested for being “an agent of influence of the Chinese Communist Party,” and argued we needed to “shut down” China’s “access to technology, chips, and training.”
Advocates and politicians focused on economic issues and reining in corporate power also have long criticized Nvidia. Oren Cass of the center-right group American Compass wrote an article titled “Break up Nvidia” last year, arguing that “its excessive concentration of power is exactly what antitrust law intends to combat.”
Meanwhile, the left, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), a longtime critic of Big Tech, has frequently suggested Huang was corruptly influencing the Trump administration. At a hearing in June, she mentioned that Huang or his company had donated to Trump’s inauguration and his White House ballroom project. “If it’s not plain old-fashioned bribery, it sure smells like it,” she said.
Many in the AI safety advocacy world have also long criticized — and feared — Nvidia. That’s in part because they hope slowing down sales of AI chips abroad could slow what they view as a dangerous race to superintelligence. Additionally, after AI safety fears hit the mainstream in September due to Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation and viral warnings, Huang took an increasingly public role in dismissing such fears.
Other AI safety advocates cite the company as having a chilling effect on public debate. “For months now, I’ve heard about widespread fear among think tank researchers and policy experts who publish work against Nvidia’s interests,” AI safety researcher Steven Adler wrote last year. “If you speak with people in-the-know at AI companies, fear of retaliation from Nvidia is a major concern when staking out policy positions.”
Indeed, OpenAI and Anthropic are highly dependent on Nvidia for its chips, so open criticism of the company is not common. Yet those big two US AI labs have been at odds with Nvidia in urging the Trump administration to do more to crack down on Chinese access to advanced chips, and to more heavily scrutinize Chinese “open source” AI models.
But to Huang and others in his camp, the growth of Chinese AI is a feature, not a bug. Sacks, for instance, has repeatedly argued that “open weight” or “open source” models — which make their parameters publicly available, in contrast to the proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic — would help avert “an unsafe and dystopian future where advanced AI capabilities are centralized and controlled by only a few hands.” The leading open weight models are currently from Chinese companies.
Huang has also used a more straightforward argument: that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States of America.
“American technology has to win across the world at every single layer,” he said in May. “If we can export chips, we should.”
Now it will be left to Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, to carry that message, instead of a rock-star founder with a global cult following that’s drawn comparisons to Steve Jobs at his peak at Apple. Her first task: taking stock of all the powerful actors across the political, advocacy, and business world rooting for her to fail. Perhaps DeepSeek could help make a list?

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

The Karnataka government has recently issued a joint circular, with multiple concerned departments on board, on measures to ensure the well-being of students across all schools, colleges, hostels, residential schools, and training institutions in the State.
These measures include conducting mandatory check-ups for all girls in schools by a gynaecologist, the provision of sex education, and the creation of awareness among children regarding child rights, issues concerning teenage pregnancies, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, child marriage, and the Child Helpline (1098). Furthermore, the installation of CCTV cameras has been made mandatory in all schools and colleges.
A warning has also been issued stating that failure to prevent — or negligence in addressing — cases of child marriage, teenage pregnancy, and incidents falling under the POCSO Act, 2012, will result in both legal action and disciplinary proceedings against the officials concerned.
The circular is a culmination of a series of measures initiated in June 2025 over concerns about rising cases of child marriage and teenage pregnancy in the State.
Child Protection Committee
Among the measures prescribed is the formation of Child Protection Committees in educational institutions across the State. The committee, comprising parents, children, and teachers, must meet once every three months, and the proceedings of these meetings should be duly recorded, the circular noted.
Schools and residential schools must install complaint boxes and take measures to address the grievances of girl students. It has been mandated that experienced and qualified counsellors be appointed in schools and Pre-University (PU) colleges to address the mental health and other challenges faced by adolescent students. Teachers must persuade parents to re-enrol girls who have dropped out of school and ensure that they continue their education until the age of 18. They must also take measures to prevent school-going children from being subjected to child labour.
Children should be provided with appropriate education to help them understand and identify issues such as crimes against children, child labour, child trafficking, sexual abuse, and child marriage through both formal and informal educational curricula. They should also be taught to recognise any form of abuse, violence, discrimination, or exploitation directed against them, whether within educational institutions or elsewhere, the circular said.
“If a girl student in a school or residential school remains absent for more than three days without providing any notification, the principal must inform the gram panchayat and the child helpline (1098) in writing. The Health Department has stated that appropriate legal action must be taken against shops selling abortion pills without a doctor’s prescription, as well as against doctors and members of the public involved in unauthorised abortion activities,” the circular said.
Substance abuse
Additionally, the guidelines emphasise the need to raise awareness among children about the dangers of substance abuse and drug addiction, alongside conducting regular screenings for such issues. They stipulate that such awareness should also be integrated into the school curriculum.

More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
Heading out of town for the holidays? There's still time to get your flu shot
More people are getting the flu than usual this fall, according to the latest influenza tracking numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Flu started a bit early this year, so it's out there and spreading," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. "So people who are thinking of Thanksgiving travel need to get their protection as quickly as possible."
The flu shot takes about ten days to reach its full efficacy, so there's still time to get one before Thanksgiving, Schaffner says. And the sooner someone gets it, the better – especially because people will be gathering in enclosed spaces for the holidays.
AAA predicts that this year, around 82 million people will travel more than 50 miles over Thanksgiving break, including 73 million by car.
Getting the vaccine doesn't mean someone won't get the flu – but it does mean they'll be less likely to wind up in the hospital from influenza-related complications. Those include pneumonia and secondary bacterial infections.
"It can strike a healthy person at any age and put them in the emergency room. Flu is like that," Schaffner says.
People at the highest risk are seniors, young children and people with underlying health conditions.
Schaffner also says not enough people are getting their COVID boosters.
"Somehow they think that COVID has disappeared," he says. "But the people who are admitted to my hospital with COVID are invariably people who are not up to date with their vaccinations, as with flu. That COVID vaccine helps keep you out of the hospital. It is still a threat. It hasn't gone away."
People should have no trouble finding available vaccines for the flu, COVID and the highly contagious respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, at their local pharmacies and health care providers' offices, says Claire Hannan, the executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, adding that vaccination season is in "full swing."
"Now is definitely the time to get vaccinated," says Hannan. "Influenza is circulating, people are traveling, people are getting ready for Thanksgiving, the holidays. And the best protection you can get is from the vaccine."

Kerala HC dismisses lawyer’s plea for contempt action against trial judge in actress assault case
Kochi, The Kerala High Court on Tuesday dismissed a plea by a lawyer from the prosecution team in the 2017 actress assault case seeking contempt action against the trial judge, ruling that such proceedings cannot be initiated on the basis of hearsay or media reports.
The High Court asked the media to bear in mind that oral observations made by judges and lawyers should not be treated as news, particularly when their publication could hurt a party.
The lawyer's plea alleged that the judge had made defamatory remarks about her conduct during the proceedings.
Justice P V Kunhikrishnan dismissed the plea filed by lawyer T B Mini, who had also sought the expunction of the remarks allegedly made against her by trial judge Honey M Varghese, saying there was no evidence to establish that the judicial officer had made any defamatory remarks.
The High Court said Mini's allegations were based on hearsay and media reports, and there was no evidence to show that the judge had made any defamatory observations against the lawyer.
"This court cannot initiate contempt proceedings against the judicial officer based on the petitioner's hearsay version of an alleged statement made by the judicial officer in an open court, which is not in the official records, but only in the air. Based on such hearsay versions, this court cannot initiate any proceedings against a judicial officer," Justice Kunhikrishnan said.
The High Court said judges speak through their judgments and that courtroom dialogue may sometimes be necessary to decide a case or persuade a lawyer to advance arguments.
"It is improper for the media to make this news, as it will cause serious damage to the lawyers and the judges too," it said.
It observed that remarks made by a presiding officer in the courtroom may be momentary, but their circulation could embarrass the person against whom they are directed.
"Lawyers deserve dignity and fair treatment, and they should not leave the court, after arguing a case, feeling that the court insulted or humiliated them," it added.
The High Court advised members of the Bar not to be swayed by social media reactions merely because a judge made certain observations in open court with good intentions.
"The dialogues in the courtroom should be confined to the courtroom itself. Judges or lawyers may not intend any harm when they make comments or jokes in court, because a serious courtroom, where only interpretations of law and facts are discussed, can be boring for judges, lawyers, and litigants, and a joke can ease the mood and atmosphere."
It said it was improper for the media to report such exchanges between a lawyer and a judge in a manner that tarnished the image of either.
Justice Kunhikrishnan said the media should, based on their journalistic experience, exercise discretion in deciding what to ignore and what to highlight.
"Equally, members of the Bar should not be carried away by social media reactions. In such situations, let us neither amplify a colleague's embarrassment nor rush to hold the bench in contempt without having the full picture and the context in which any remarks are made by the judge," the High Court said.
It said the response of the Bar and the media should be guided by professional solidarity, restraint and mutual respect rather than the impulse to share.
The High Court expressed confidence that the media knew what to report and what not to, and would continue to uphold journalistic principles in the future.

The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 combines a stylish translucent design with smooth linear switches, a compact 75% layout, multi-device connectivity, and excellent battery life. It’s great for everyday typing, but limited customization, closely packed keys, and a premium price may put some buyers off.
ASUS has a wide range of product categories, and its mechanical keyboards are quite popular among gamers.
ASUS also offers standard mechanical keyboards for regular users. The company recently sent us its recently announced Jelly75 keyboard for review. It features a 75% layout, a unique translucent design, and multi-device connectivity. The keyboard also comes with a slightly higher price tag of Rs 7,999 (US $129.99)
I have been using this keyboard for the past several days, and in this review, you will learn everything about the keyboard, including the good and the bad things, and also learn if this Jelly75 keyboard is worth the price for what it offers.
Table of Contents
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review: Design, Typing Experience, and Everyday Use
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Unboxing
You get a fairly simple package when you unbox the ASUS Jelly75 KD201. Inside, you find the keyboard, a USB-A to USB-C cable, a 2.4GHz wireless receiver, a quick start guide, and warranty documentation.
However, ASUS doesn’t provide a keycap puller or even a switch puller out of the box.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Design and Build Quality
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard is available in two colors: Volt Green and Orange Meadow. I received the Volt Green variant of the Jelly75, which comes with a translucent chassis and a combination of white, black, and mint green keys. This color combination makes it very attractive for a vibrant and unique desktop setup.
If you don’t like contrasting looks, the Orange Meadow color variant, which offers muted colors and a retro-looking design, is the best choice, which I personally prefer.
But the Volt Green variant also looks good in person and stands out more than the regular black-and-white finishes on most mechanical keyboards.
The standout feature on both variants is the translucent design, so you can see parts of the internal keyboard structure through the casing.
However, the body and keys are made of polycarbonate, but it’s solidly built, and the weight adds extra rigidity.
The steel plate inside the keyboard adds to its weight, bringing it to about 1.19 kg.
While the weight helps the keyboard stay stable during typing, it can be inconvenient if you plan to carry it often.
Since the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard uses a 75% layout, it measures about 326.2 x 142.1 x 39.5 mm, which takes up less space than traditional full-size keypads but more than smaller percentage keypads.
If you are not familiar with keyboard percentages, here is a detailed visual guide we created to help you understand different keyboard layouts.
The keys are densely packed together, and there is not much space between them; also, there is no gap between functional keys and the regular keys, especially around the arrow key cluster, where, until you get used to this layout, there is a high chance that you can accidentally mispress the other keys.
Also, the keyboard doesn’t have any knobs, which would have been a nice addition for direct volume control. Additionally, the Caps Lock key doesn’t come with any light indication to show it’s active.
The rubber pads on the bottom help it stay stable and in place without sliding on a smooth desk surface.
The keyboard also comes with adjustable kickstands that let you set three typing-angle positions.
While the design is attractive, the translucent, lighter-colored keycaps make dirt more visible. It also supports a wireless receiver, but the keypad doesn’t have a dedicated compartment to store it, which is inconvenient, especially if you plan to carry it between workspaces. It won’t be much of a concern if you plan to connect it via Bluetooth, but it’s something you should know.
Continuing with the design, you will find the ASUS logo on the bottom right, a toggle to switch between connection types on the top, and a USB-C charging port on the top left.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Keyboard Layout and Ergonomics
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 uses a 75% keyboard layout, which is a sweet spot between portability and functionality.
Unlike smaller 60% or 65% layouts, it includes a function row at the top and navigation keys on the right.
However, it doesn’t include a separate number pad, which full-size keyboards often have.
This compact layout has all essential keys and doesn’t miss anything, especially if you are coming from notebooks or a Mac.
This layout works for writing, programming, office work, and even standard gaming.
Although you get a dedicated number row below the function keys, a dedicated number pad is still more convenient, especially if your work involves entering numbers regularly.
However, the keys are densely packed, with negligible gaps between them.
ASUS has also included a dedicated Copilot key near the arrow key cluster, which could accidentally launch Windows Copilot, especially until you get used to this densely packed layout.
In terms of key design, ASUS used tall, squarish-rounded keycaps instead of the flatter options found on many keyboards.
While this makes them look unique, it may take time to get used to, especially if you are switching from a MacBook or another low-profile keyboard.
Since these keys are taller, I recommend a separate wrist rest, especially if you plan to use the keyboard lying flat.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Switches, Keycaps and Typing Experience
Typing experience is one of the most important things to consider when buying a mechanical keyboard, since you spend several hours every day writing, coding, or working on documents.
The ASUS Jelly75 comes with linear mechanical switches that offer 4mm of total key travel.
However, you won’t get tactile feedback when you press the keys. Unlike tactile switches, which have a noticeable bump when pressed, the Jelly75’s linear mechanism presses the keys gently, creating a smooth typing experience.
I personally prefer tactile feedback because I am used to my MacBook keyboard, but many also prefer smooth switches for longer typing sessions.
ASUS also rates the switches at 50 million keystrokes, which should last longer with regular use.
The keyboard also offers a gasket-mounted structure. ASUS calls it Uni-cushion technology, where it uses cushioning between the internal keyboard layout assembly and the outer body to help absorb vibrations.
This is especially useful if you press the keys harder, as the chassis absorbs vibration and stays steady overall.
The keycaps have a rigid feel. You won’t get rattling, wobbling, or uneven keypresses even on the larger keys like the spacebar.
As a mechanical keyboard, the ASUS Jelly75 offers hot-swappable switches, so you can remove and replace individual switches without soldering.
If you prefer tactile switches, you can also replace linear switches with tactile options.
However, ASUS doesn’t include a switch puller in the box, so you will need to buy it separately if you plan to swap the keys.
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard comes with a white backlight instead of RGB backlighting. It keeps the keyboard looking cleaner.
You can adjust the white backlighting to four brightness levels using the dedicated keys on your keyboard, including Fn + F9 shortcuts.
You can also turn off the backlight completely, which can help extend battery life further.
However, the backlight illuminates the area around the keys and doesn’t illuminate the letters and symbols printed on the keys; instead, it glows around them.
This won’t be an issue if you are already used to this keyboard layout and type without looking at the keyboard, but if you look at the keys while typing, the lighting may not be as helpful in low light.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Connectivity and Multi-Device Switching
Another big advantage of the ASUS Jelly75 KD201 keyboard is its connectivity. If you use multiple devices, such as a Windows PC, MacBook, or iPad, you can connect this keyboard to all of them wirelessly and switch between them easily.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports three connectivity options: Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, and a wired USB connection, and it can connect up to five devices using all three connection types.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports Bluetooth 3.0 and 5.0, and it can remember up to three Bluetooth devices.
To pair your devices, switch the keyboard to Bluetooth mode and hold Fn + 1, 2, or 3 for more than three seconds.
Once paired, you can easily switch between devices using the corresponding shortcuts.
You can pair up to three devices via Bluetooth. It also supports a 2.4 GHz wireless connection using the included USB receiver. ASUS says the wireless range is about 10 meters.
You can also connect the keyboard using the USB cable provided in the box.
The USB cable is long and suitable for any desktop layout, and its braided design lets you fold it easily and keeps it tngle-free.
However, as I said before, the main limitation is that it lacks a dedicated compartment for storing the 2.4GHz receiver if you plan to carry the keyboard between workplaces.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Customization
You won’t get much customization on the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard. Instead, ASUS kept it simple with a plug-and-play design.
It supports dedicated shortcuts to switch between Windows and MacBook layouts and offers several function-key shortcuts.
You can use Fn + F1, F2, and F3 to mute or adjust the volume, and F6-F8 to control music playback. It also includes shortcuts for switching between applications, searching, and launching Launchpad on macOS and Windows Search and Spotlight on macOS.
The keyboard also includes a dedicated Microsoft Copilot key, which lets you launch Copilot directly from your keyboard.
However, one noticeable downside is that, unlike other mechanical keyboards, it doesn’t include dedicated software for advanced key-mapping customization, so you can’t set custom shortcuts.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Battery Life
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 has a 4000mAh rechargeable battery. ASUS rates the keyboard as lasting up to 8500 hours on a single charge with the backlight off, which translates to roughly 354 days.
It can last days without needing to charge. I used this keyboard with the backlight on throughout the entire two-week review period. I didn’t have to charge it once.
Regarding charging, the Jelly75 uses a USB-C port and includes a USB-A to USB-C cable in the box. It supports up to 5W charging. You can also charge the keyboard by connecting it directly to your device. It also includes a useful wired USB mode, which can be convenient if you suddenly run out of battery.
The keyboard uses battery light indicators to show the remaining battery. When the battery level drops to 20%, the status light slowly flashes red and reminds you to charge it. While charging, the indicator flashes, and when it’s fully charged, the light turns solid white. You can also check the remaining battery life in the Bluetooth settings for the connected device.
Asus MD105 Wireless Mouse Review
Along with the Jelly75 keyboard, ASUS also sent the MD105 wireless mouse, which pairs well with it. Interestingly, it comes in two color variants: Volt Green, which perfectly matches your keyboard if you picked up the Volt Green variant, and Milky White, which suits the Orange variant.
In terms of design, the MD105 mouse looks like a conventional mouse with a slightly wider body, and it comes with a dedicated thumb rest designed for right-hand users that offers great support, especially if you are a creator and plan to use the mouse for several hours a day.
It feels very light and weighs just 66 grams without a battery, and although it’s slightly wider, it isn’t as travel-friendly as other compact mice.
One feature I particularly like is the silent-click mechanism, which reduces clicking noise. This can be especially useful in shared offices and libraries, or when you’re working late at night.
The MD105 uses an optical sensor with three adjustable DPI settings, including 1200, 1600, and 2400. You can switch between them using the DPI button. Lower DPI settings offer more controlled cursor movement, while higher settings let you move the cursor faster.
For my big hands, the mouse feels perfectly compact, and my right finger rests comfortably on the support, making it comfortable to use.
Since it is lightweight, it is also quickly responsive and easy to move. For connectivity, the MD105 supports Bluetooth 5.0 and also offers 2.4 GHz wireless through the included USB receiver.
You can pair up to three devices: two via Bluetooth and one via the wireless receiver.
It also offers a wireless compartment in the mouse. If you are planning to use it with Bluetooth, you can safely store the wireless receiver in the compartment.
Since it supports multiple devices like the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard, it is also useful for switching between Windows and Mac computers.
A few months ago, I switched to a mouse with a built-in battery, but the MD105 comes with a single AA battery included in the box.
You need to replace it whenever you want, without waiting for the mouse to recharge. However, I prefer a rechargeable mouse, as mine also comes with a battery level indicator, so I can charge it.
If you can, this MD105 mouse suggests you need to keep an AA battery on hand in case it suddenly runs out of battery
The ASUS MD105 mouse is priced at Rs 1,699, which is a good value considering the ergonomics, comfort, and portability it offers.
It also has dedicated left-side switches for extra shortcuts, and its quiet operation, adjustable sensitivity, and multi-device connectivity make it a great buy if you are planning to get it alongside the Jelly75 keyboard.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review Verdict
At Rs 8,999 (US$129.99), ASUS faces stiff competition from brands like AULA, Royal Kludge, and Keychron, which offer feature-packed mechanical keyboards with hot-swappable switches, RGB lighting, and dedicated volume knobs.
Some keyboards, like Royal Kludge, also offer a small dedicated display that shows useful information such as battery status and connection mode.
However, ASUS Jelly75 bets on its design, with colorful, translucent, rounded keycaps that make it one of the most distinctive-looking keyboards.
The gasket-mounted construction, linear switches, and multi-device connectivity also make it a great everyday companion with a simple plug-and-play device for a productive and attractive-looking desktop setup. However, if you want a fully customizable keyboard experience with a dedicated knob and customizable software, this might be a limitation.

India has voted against a draft UN General Assembly resolution calling on nations to establish a moratorium on the death penalty.
The 193-member UNGA adopted, by recorded vote, the resolution on Friday (November 13, 2026) introduced by Mexico on ‘Moratorium on the use of the death penalty’, with 133 countries voting in favour of the resolution, 33 against and 16 abstentions.
India, along with Bahrain, China, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Japan, Kuwait, Maldives, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the U.S., voted against the resolution.
The resolution expressed deep concern about the continued application of the death penalty and reaffirmed the right of all countries to develop their own legal systems, including determining appropriate legal penalties in accordance with international law.
It called upon all States to establish a moratorium on executions, with a view to abolishing the death penalty. It also called upon States which have abolished the death penalty not to reintroduce it.
The resolution expressed deep concern that, despite the global trend towards limiting the application of the death penalty, there was a significant surge in reported executions in 2025.
The resolution called upon all States to progressively restrict the use of the death penalty and not to impose capital punishment for offences committed by persons below 18 years of age or whose age above 18 years at the time of the commission of the crime cannot be accurately determined.
It also called for restricting the use of the death penalty on pregnant women or on persons with mental or intellectual disabilities, as well as on older persons, and to reduce the number of offences for which the death penalty may be imposed, including by removing the mandatory application of the death penalty.
